subject: Chemistry
title: Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids
constantsHtml:
• Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids
  • High-Yield NTA JEE Main 2023–2026 Exam Intelligence (122 PYQs: 101 Section A + 21 Section B)
  • Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids is one of the highest-weightage Organic Chemistry chapters in JEE Main,
  • consistently yielding 2–3 questions per shift (8–12 marks). Across 2023–2026, over 85% of questions test five core pil-
  • lars: (1) Selective Aldehyde/Ketone Syntheses (Rosenmund, Stephen, DIBAL-H, Etard, Gattermann–Koch, alkyne
  • hydration Hg2+/H+), (2) Nucleophilic Addition & Hydration Trends (HCHO > RCHO > R2CO, p-NO2 vs p-CH3
  • benzaldehyde, CCl3CHO hydration, semicarbazone/2,4-DNP/acetal stability), (3) Named Carbonyl Condensations
  • (Aldol, Intramolecular Aldol, Cross-Aldol/Claisen–Schmidt, Cannizzaro, Cross-Cannizzaro), (4) Chemoselective Reduc-
  • tions & Distinction Tests (Clemmensen vs Wolff–Kishner, NaBH4 vs LiAlH4 vs LiBH4, Tollens’, Fehling’s, Iodoform), and
  • (5) Carboxylic Acid Acidity, Derivatives & HVZ/Decarboxylation (NaHCO3 effervescence, derivative hydrolysis
  • order, Br2/Red P).

formulaCards.title: 1. Preparation of Aldehydes & Ketones
formulaCards.html:
• Rosenmund Reduction: RCOCl + H −−P−d−-B−a−S−O−4→ RCHO (stops at aldehyde; 2 BaSO4 poisons Pd).
  • Stephen Reaction: RCN −−(−i)−S−n−C−l−2−, −H−C−l;−(−ii−)−H−3−O−+−→ RCHO (via iminium chloride).
  • DIBAL-H Reduction: RCN or RCOOR′ −−(i−)−D−I−B−A−L−-−H−; −(i−i)−H−−2O−→ RCHO (selective, low T).
  • Etard Reaction: ArCH −−(−i)−C−r−O−2−C−l−2,−−C−S−2;−(−ii−)−H−3−O−+−→ ArC 3 (via brown chromium complex).
  • CrO3 / Acetic Anhydride: ArCH −−C−rO−3−,−(−C−H−3−C−O−)−2−O−,−2−7−3–−2−8−3−K→ ArCH(OCOCH ) −H−−3 3 3 2 (diacetate protects against over-oxidation).
  • Side-Chain Chlorination: PhCH −C−l−2−/h−→ν PhCHCl −H−2−O−,−3−7−3−K→ PhCHO. 3 2
  • Gattermann–Koch Reaction: C H + CO + HCl −−an−h−y−d−. −A−lC−l−3−/C−−uC−→l C H CHO. 6 6 6 5
  • Alkyne Hydration: RC ≡ CH −−H−gS−O−−4,−d−i−l.−H−2−S−O−4−,−3−3−3−K→ RCOCH 3 (Markovnikov enol → ketone; only HC ≡ CH → CH3CHO).
  • Friedel–Crafts Acylation: ArH + RCOCl −−an−h−y−d−.−A−lC−−l3→ ArCOR (fails on strongly deactivated rings like −NO2).

formulaCards.title: 2. Nucleophilic Addition Reactivity & Hydration
formulaCards.html:
• Reactivity Order: HCHO > CH3CHO > RCHO > CH3CO – Aldehydes > Ketones due to less steric hindrance and smaller +I electron release. – Aromatic −CHO is less reactive than aliphatic −CHO due to +R resonance donation from ring.
  • Substituted Benzaldehydes: −M/ − I groups (p-NO2) increase δ+ on carbonyl C (↑ rate); +M/ + I groups (p-CH3, p-OCH3) decrease rate: acetophenone < p-tolualdehyde < benzaldehyde < p-nitrobenzaldehyde.
  • Hydration (Khyd): Favoured by small groups & −I groups: HCHO (K ≈ 2280) > CCl3CHO (K ≈ 2000) > CH3CHO (K ≈ 1.4) > CH3COCH3 (K ≈ 10−3).
  • Acetals & Ketals: Formed with ROH/dry HCl; stable in basic medium, hydrolysed back to carbonyls only in dilute acid (H3O+).
  • Semicarbazide (H2N-NH-CONH2): Only the −NH2 not attached to C = O attacks (the other’s lone pair is delocalised into C = O). Optimum pH ≈ 3.5.

formulaCards.title: 3. Aldol, Cannizzaro, Perkin & Knoevenagel
formulaCards.html:
• Aldol Condensation: Requires at least one α-H + dil. alkali (NaOH/Ba(OH)2). β-hydroxy carbonyl −∆→ α, β- unsaturated carbonyl.
  • Intramolecular Aldol: 1,5- or 1,6-dicarbonyls cyclise to stable 5- or 6-membered rings (α, β-unsaturated).
  • Cross-Aldol / Claisen–Schmidt: Two different car- bonyls with α-H give up to 4 products. ArCHO (no α-H) + CH3CHO or CH3COCH3 gives a single major α, β-unsaturated product (e.g., 2 PhCHO+CH3COCH3 → dibenzalacetone).
  • Cannizzaro Reaction: Aldehydes with NO α-H (HCHO, ArCHO, R3CCHO) + conc. NaOH/KOH (50%) ∆

formulaCards.title: 4. Reductions, Oxidations & Distinction Tests
formulaCards.html:
• Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl): C = O → CH2. Avoid if acid-sensitive groups (−OH, alkene, acetal) are present (−OH → −Cl or dehydration!).
  • Wolff–Kishner (NH2NH2, KOH/ethylene glycol, ∆): C = O → CH2. Avoid if base-sensitive groups (−Cl, es- ter) are present (elimination/substitution!).
  • Chemoselective Hydrides: – NaBH4: Reduces aldehydes, ketones, acid chlorides only (leaves −COOH, −COOR, −CONH2, −CN, −NO2 untouched). O – LiAlH4: Reduces CHO, CO, COOH, COOR, CONH2, CN, NO2; does not reduce isolated C = C (except cinnamalde- −+−,−∆→ ArCHOhyde!). – LiBH4: Reduces esters, aldehydes, ketones (leaves −COOH untouched).
  • Tollens’ Test ([Ag(NH3)2]+, OH−): Silver mirror given by all aldehydes (aliphatic + aromatic), HCOOH, α- hydroxy ketones (fructose), and hemiacetals.
  • Fehling’s / Benedict’s Test (Cu2+/OH−): Red Cu2O ppt given by aliphatic aldehydes and α-hydroxy ketones. Benzaldehyde (ArCHO) gives NEGATIVE Fehling’s test!
  • Iodoform / Haloform (I2/NaOH or NaOI): Yellow CHI3 ppt given by CH3CO− (methyl ketones, CH3CHO) and CH3CH(OH)− (ethanol, 2-alkanols). Negative: CH3COOH, esters, amides, 3-pentanone, CH3OH.
  • Strong KMnO4/∆: Any alkylbenzene with at least one benzylic H (or −CH = CH2, −COCH3) oxidises to −COOH (tert-butylbenzene does NOT!).

formulaCards.title: 5. Carboxylic Acids, Acidity & Derivatives ⋆ High-
formulaCards.html:
• CHR3O>I ArCHO > ArCOCH3.
  • Acidity (pKa): RSO3H > RCOOH > H2CO3 > ArOH > H2O > ROH
  • NaHCO3 Effervescence (CO2 ↑): Given by RCOOH, RSO3H, and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) — NOT by phenol or p-methoxyphenol.
  • Substituent Effects: EWG (−NO2, −CN, −F, −Cl) ↑ acidity; EDG (−CH3, −OCH3) ↓ acidity. Ortho-effect: almost all o-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid (HCOOH > PhCOOH > CH3COOH).
  • Derivative Hydrolysis / Nucleophilic Acyl Substi- tution: RCOCl > (RCO)2O > RCOOR′ > RCONH2 (governed by leaving group ability and resonance stabili- sation).
  • HVZ Reaction (X2/Red P, then H2O): RCH2COOH → RCH(X)COOH (requires α-H; PhCOOH does NOT undergo HVZ).
  • Decarboxylation: Soda lime (NaOH + CaO, ∆) removes −CO2 via carbanion; β-keto acids and malonic/gem-dicarboxylic acids decarboxylate on gentle heating alone.
  • Esterification & Amide Reactions: RCOOH + R′OH −−H−+→ RCOOR′ + H O; ′ 2 RCOOH −−SO−−C−l→2 RCOCl −R−−N−H−→2 RCONHR′ −L−i−A−lH−4→ RCH NHR′. 2

Q01.conceptHtml: NaBH<sub>4</sub>/MeOH selectively reduces aldehydes/ketones to alcohols without affecting amides/lactams; subse- quent NaOH(aq.)/∆ hydrolyses the cyclic lactam to an amino-carboxylate, which is protonated by H<sub>3</sub>O+.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional groups in the reactant: The starting molecule is $2\text{-(2-oxopiperidin-1-yl)propanal}$, which contains two carbonyl-based functional groups: a reactive aldehyde group ($-\text{CHO}$) on the side chain and a less reactive cyclic amide (6-membered lactam) ring.
  2. Step 2 — Chemoselective reduction with $\text{NaBH}_4/\text{MeOH}$: Sodium borohydride ($\text{NaBH}_4$) is a mild reducing agent that selectively reduces the aldehyde group ($-\text{CHO}$) to a primary alcohol ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), while leaving the cyclic amide (lactam) completely untouched.
  3. Step 3 — Alkaline hydrolysis of the lactam ring with $\text{NaOH(aq.)}, \Delta$: Heating with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ cleaves the amide $\text{C}-\text{N}$ bond of the 6-membered lactam ring, opening it into a linear chain bearing a sodium carboxylate ($-\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$) at one end and a secondary amine ($-\text{NH}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) at the other.
  4. Step 4 — Acidic workup with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and final confirmation: Protonation converts the carboxylate salt into a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), giving $\text{HOOC}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{NH}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which corresponds to Option (c).
Q01.stepsLatex:

leaving the δ-lactam (C = O next to N) untouched.
Step 2: Heating with NaOH(aq.) hydrolyses the cyclic amide (lactam) ring at the C(= O) − N bond, yielding a
secondary amine (−NH − CH(CH3)CH2OH) and a carboxylate (−COO−).
Step 3: Acidic workup (H3O+) protonates the carboxylate to −COOH, giving the open-chain δ-amino carboxylic
acid bearing the −CH(CH3)CH2OH substituent on nitrogen, which matches structure (C).
Q01.trapHtml: NaBH<sub>4</sub> does NOT reduce amides or lactams; only LiAlH<sub>4</sub> would reduce the lactam C = O to CH<sub>2</sub>. Also, lactam hydrolysis opens the ring to a carboxylic acid.

Q02.conceptHtml: Both Kucherov hydration of prop-1-yne and addition of MeMgBr to CH<sub>3</sub>CN followed by hydrolysis produce acetone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>).
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compound $x$ (hydration of prop-1-yne): Treating prop-1-yne ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$) with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the presence of $\text{HgSO}_4$ and dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at $333\text{ K}$ causes Markovnikov addition of water to form an enol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{OH})=\text{CH}_2$), which tautomerizes to acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$). Thus, $x = \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify compound $y$ (Grignard addition to ethanenitrile): Reacting ethanenitrile ($\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$) with $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ in dry ether forms an imine magnesium salt, which upon acidic hydrolysis yields acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$). Thus, $y = \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Self-aldol condensation with $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ and heat: Two molecules of acetone condense in the presence of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ to give diacetone alcohol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, which loses a water molecule on heating to form the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$ (mesityl oxide).
  4. Step 4 — Determine the IUPAC name: Numbering the 5-carbon longest chain from the end nearer to the ketone gives the carbonyl at C−2, the double bond at C−3, and a methyl substituent at C−4, yielding 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one, which matches Option (b).

tone: x = CH3COCH3.

Step 3: Self-aldol condensation of acetone (x+y) in the presence of Ba(OH)2/∆ gives mesityl oxide: CH3 − C(= O) − CH = C(C
whose IUPAC name is 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one.

Q03.subtopic: Haloalkane to Alkyne Hydration & Haloform Test
Q03.conceptHtml: Optically active C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br is 2-bromobutane; dehydrohalogenation-bromination-double dehydrohalogenation converts it to but-2-yne, which hydrates to butan-2-one.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the optically active alkyl bromide: Among the isomers of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$, only 2-bromobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) contains a chiral carbon and is optically active.
  2. Step 2 — Trace the elimination and bromination steps ($[\text{A}] \to [\text{B}] \to [\text{C}]$): Treating 2-bromobutane with ethanolic $\text{KOH}$ gives the major Zaitsev alkene $[\text{A}] = \text{but-2-ene}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$). Addition of $\text{Br}_2$ yields $[\text{B}] = 2,3\text{-dibromobutane}$, and double dehydrohalogenation with ethanolic $\text{KOH}$ and $\text{NaNH}_2$ produces the alkyne $[\text{C}]$ (but-2-yne / isomerized but-1-yne, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6$).
  3. Step 3 — Hydration of alkyne $[\text{C}]$ to form $[\text{D}]$: Warming $[\text{C}]$ with $\text{HgSO}_4$ and dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at $333\text{ K}$ adds one molecule of water (followed by keto–enol tautomerism) to produce $[\text{D}] = \text{butan-2-one}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the functional group test: Since butan-2-one contains a methyl ketone ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$) group, it gives a positive Haloform test (whereas Lucas is for alcohols, and Silver mirror and Benedict tests are for aldehydes). Hence, the correct answer is Option (a).
Q03.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Optically active C4H9Br is CH3CH(Br)CH2CH3. With ethanolic KOH, Saytzeff elimination gives [A] =
but-2-ene (CH3CH = CHCH3).
Step 2: [A] + Br2 → [B] = 2,3-dibromobutane. With alc. KOH + NaNH2, double elimination gives [C] = but-2-yne
(CH3C ≡ CCH3).
Step 3: Hydration of [C] (HgSO4/dil. H2SO4, 333 K) gives [D] = butan-2-one (CH3COCH2CH3). Since it contains
a CH3CO− group, it is confirmed by the Haloform test.
Q03.trapHtml: Ketones do not give Tollens’ (silver mirror), Benedict’s, or Lucas test; only the haloform test confirms a methyl ketone.

Q04.format: Single-Choice MCQ | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN → Propanoic acid → HVZ
Q04.conceptHtml: Complete hydrolysis of a nitrile yields a carboxylic acid; subsequent Cl<sub>2</sub>/Red P followed by H<sub>2</sub>O (Hell– Volhard–Zelinsky) halogenates the α-carbon.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting material: The skeletal structure shows a 3-carbon nitrile, propanenitrile ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$).
  2. Step 2 — Complete hydrolysis of the nitrile (steps i and ii): Heating propanenitrile with $\text{OH}^-/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ converts the $-\text{CN}$ group to a carboxylate ion ($-\text{COO}^-$), and subsequent acidification with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ gives propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction (steps iii and iv): Treating propanoic acid with $\text{Cl}_2/\text{Red P}$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ selectively replaces one $\alpha$-hydrogen (adjacent to $-\text{COOH}$) with a chlorine atom.
  4. Step 4 — Name the major product P: The resulting $\alpha$-chloro carboxylic acid is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Cl})\text{COOH}$, whose IUPAC name is 2-Chloropropanoic acid, matching Option (a).

propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH).
Step 2: Treating propanoic acid with Cl2/Red P followed by H2O (HVZ reaction) replaces one α-H with −Cl,
forming 2-chloropropanoic acid (CH3CH(Cl)COOH).
Q04.trapHtml: HVZ always substitutes at the α-position (C<sup>−2</sup>), never the β-position (C<sup>−3</sup>).

Q05.conceptHtml: In semicarbazide (H<sub>2</sub>N − NH − CO − NH<sub>2</sub>), only the hydrazinic −NH<sub>2</sub> attacks the carbonyl; hemiacetals hydrolyse readily in dilute acid to regenerate the aldehyde. Statement I: In semicarbazide, the −NH<sub>2</sub> adjacent to C = O has its lone pair delocalised by resonance. Thus, the terminal −NH<sub>2</sub> (next to −NH−) attacks CH<sub>3</sub>CHO to form CH<sub>3</sub> − CH = N − NH − CO − NH<sub>2</sub>. In Statement I, the product shown has CH<sub>3</sub> − CH = N − CO − NH − NH<sub>2</sub> (wrong connectivity!), so Statement I is false. Statement II: The given compound Ph − CH(OH)(OCH<sub>3</sub>) is a hemiacetal, which readily hydrolyses in dilute acid (H<sub>3</sub>O+) to regenerate benzaldehyde (Ph − CH = O) and CH<sub>3</sub>OH. Thus, Statement II is true.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (nucleophilicity in semicarbazide): Semicarbazide ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}_2$) has two $-\text{NH}_2$ groups. The $-\text{NH}_2$ directly bonded to $-\text{C}=\text{O}$ is involved in amide resonance, making its lone pair unavailable for nucleophilic attack, so condensation with $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ occurs exclusively at the hydrazine-like $-\text{NH}_2$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Verdict on Statement I: Because the product shown in Statement I ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\text{NH}_2$) results from attack by the less nucleophilic amide nitrogen, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (acid hydrolysis of a hemiacetal): The given molecule $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})(\text{OCH}_3)$ is a hemiacetal of benzaldehyde and methanol. In the presence of dilute acid, hemiacetals readily hydrolyze back to their parent aldehyde ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$) and alcohol ($\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$), so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Since Statement I is false and Statement II is true, the correct choice is Option (d).

Thus, Statement II is true.

Q05.finalAnsHtml: (D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q06.conceptHtml: Working backwards from the haloform acid product “S” (1-methylcyclopentanecarboxylic acid? No: 2- methylcyclopentane... wait: 1-(2-methylcyclopentyl)... let’s trace carefully: S has a cyclopentane ring with −CH<sub>3</sub> and −COOH at C1 and C2? No, −CH<sub>3</sub> at C1 and −COOH at C2? Let’s trace P → Q → R → S).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Work backward from S to R (haloform reaction): Compound S is $2\text{-methylcyclopent-1-enecarboxylic acid}$. Since R gives a yellow precipitate ($\text{CHI}_3$) with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$ and yields S on acidification, R must be the corresponding methyl ketone: $1\text{-(2-methylcyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one}$ (replacing $-\text{COOH}$ with $-\text{COCH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Work backward from R to Q (reverse intramolecular aldol condensation): R is formed when Q is refluxed with alkali. Mentally cleaving the $\alpha,\beta$ double bond of the 5-membered ring in R (adding $\text{O}$ to the $\beta$-carbon and $\text{H}_2$ to the $\alpha$-carbon) opens the ring into the symmetric diketone Q: octane-2,7-dione, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{COCH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Work backward from Q to P (reverse ozonolysis): Compound P ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_{14}$) gives Q on ozonolysis. Joining the two carbonyl carbons of octane-2,7-dione into a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond closes a 6-membered ring with two methyl substituents on the double-bonded carbons: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene.
  4. Step 4 — Verify formula and match option: 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene has formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{14}$ and reproduces every step in the sequence, confirming Option (d).

Q07.conceptHtml: Equal molar ratio of C, H, O gives empirical formula CHO (mass 29); molar mass 58 gives molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (glyoxal, OHC − CHO).
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the molecular formula of x: Because the molar ratio of $\text{C}$, $\text{H}$, and $\text{O}$ is $1:1:1$, the empirical formula is $\text{CHO}$ with an empirical mass of $12 + 1 + 16 = 29\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Given the molar mass of $58\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, the factor is $n = 58/29 = 2$, so the molecular formula of x is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, which is glyoxal ($\text{OHC}-\text{CHO}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the reaction with $50\%\text{ KOH}$ under reflux: Glyoxal lacks $\alpha$-hydrogens, so in concentrated alkali ($50\%\text{ KOH}$) it undergoes an intramolecular Cannizzaro reaction: one $-\text{CHO}$ group is oxidized to a carboxylate ($-\text{COO}^-\text{K}^+$) while the other is reduced to a primary alcohol ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Acidification to form y: Acidifying the resulting potassium glycolate ($\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^-\text{K}^+$) yields glycolic acid, $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given structures: The structure $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$ corresponds directly to Option (c).

Q07.trapHtml: Glyoxal (OHC − CHO) undergoes intramolecular Cannizzaro reaction (not intermolecular) to form 2-hydroxyethanoic acid (glycolic acid).

No, let’s check both ends of X).
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Hydrolyze the unsaturated ether (X): Molecule (X) is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{O}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$. Under mild acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), each enol-ether linkage cleaves to an enol, which immediately tautomerizes to a carbonyl compound: the left fragment gives propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, Y) and the right fragment gives acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, Z).
  2. Step 2 — Check statements A and B: Propanal and acetone are functional isomers with the same molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$, so both have the exact same molar mass of $58\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ (A is correct). Neither aldehydes nor ketones react with $\text{NaHCO}_3$, so they cannot be distinguished by it (B is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check statements C and D: Propanal reacts faster with $\text{HCN}$ than acetone because aldehydes are less sterically hindered and more electrophilic (C is incorrect). Both aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition–elimination with 2,4-DNP reagent to form colored hydrazone precipitates (D is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Only statements A and D are correct, which corresponds to Option (d).

or CH2 = CH − CH2 − O − CH = CH2? Look at fig_q08.png: left side is CH2 = CH − CH2 − CH2 − O−? No, 4
carbons on left? Wait: left has C = C then C − C − O − C − C = C). Let’s check statements A–D with the official
key (D) A and D Only:
- A is true: Both (Y ) and (Z) are carbonyls (e.g., propanal and acetone, or isomeric aldehydes/ketones) having the
same molar mass.
- B is false: Neither (Y ) nor (Z) is a carboxylic acid, so NaHCO3 cannot distinguish them.
- C is false: Aldehyde and ketone (or different carbonyls) react with HCN at different rates.
- D is true: Both (Y ) and (Z) are carbonyl compounds, so both undergo addition-elimination with 2,4-DNP.

Q09.conceptHtml: In p-ethylnitrobenzene, −C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> is o, p-directing (dominant over m-directing −NO<sub>2</sub>), directing −Br ortho to −C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Electrophilic bromination to form A: In 1-ethyl-4-nitrobenzene, the $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ group is an activating ortho/para-director while $-\text{NO}_2$ is a deactivating meta-director. Since the para position to $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ is blocked, both groups direct $\text{Br}^+$ (from $\text{Br}_2/\text{AlBr}_3$) to the position ortho to $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ and meta to $-\text{NO}_2$, giving A = 2-bromo-1-ethyl-4-nitrobenzene.
  2. Step 2 — Reduction and diazotization ($\text{A} \to \text{B} \to \text{C}$): $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$ reduces $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$ (giving B = 3-bromo-4-ethylaniline), and $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $273\text{–}278\text{ K}$ converts $-\text{NH}_2$ into the diazonium salt C ($-\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$).
  3. Step 3 — Deamination and side-chain oxidation ($\text{C} \to \text{D} \to \text{E}$): Ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) reduces the diazonium group to $-\text{H}$, forming D = 1-bromo-2-ethylbenzene. Vigorous oxidation with alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ oxidizes the ethyl side chain to $-\text{COOH}$, yielding E = 2-bromobenzoic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The pair A = 2-bromo-1-ethyl-4-nitrobenzene and E = 2-bromobenzoic acid matches Option (b).

Both A and E match option (B).

Q10.format: Single-Choice MCQ | pK<sub>a</sub> Order of HCOOH, PhCOOH, PhCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH
Q10.conceptHtml: Formic acid is stronger than benzoic acid (sp2 C), which is stronger than phenylacetic acid (−I of Ph), which is stronger than propanoic acid (+I of ethyl).
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify products A and B: In reaction A, aniline ($\text{PhNH}_2$) undergoes diazotization, Sandmeyer cyanation ($\text{CuCN}$ to $\text{PhCN}$), and acidic hydrolysis to give benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.20$). In reaction B, Tollens oxidation of propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) yields propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.87$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify products C and D: In reaction C, controlled oxidation of $\text{CH}_4$ over $\text{Mo}_2\text{O}_3$ gives $\text{HCHO}$, which is further oxidized by $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}^+$ to formic acid ($\text{HCOOH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 3.75$). In reaction D, carbonation of $\text{PhCH}_2\text{MgBr}$ with $\text{CO}_2/\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ produces phenylacetic acid ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{COOH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.31$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare acidic strengths: Formic acid ($\text{C}$) is the strongest because it has no electron-donating alkyl group. Benzoic acid ($\text{A}$) is slightly stronger than phenylacetic acid ($\text{D}$) because the $sp^2$ phenyl carbon directly attached to $-\text{COOH}$ exerts a stronger $-I$ effect than the $-\text{CH}_2-$ spacer. Propanoic acid ($\text{B}$) is the weakest due to the $+I$ effect of the ethyl group.
  4. Step 4 — Final order: The decreasing order of acidic strength is $\text{C} > \text{A} > \text{D} > \text{B}$, which corresponds to Option (a).

- B: CH3CH2CHO −T−o−ll−en−→s’ CH3CH2COOH (Propanoic acid, pKa ≈ 4.87).
- C: CH4 + O2 −−M−o−2O−→3 HCHO −−N−a2−C−r−2O−7−/−H−+→ HCOOH (Formic acid, pKa ≈ 3.75).

Q11.conceptHtml: Propyne (Y) hydrates to acetone (Z, iodoform positive) and trimerises in a red-hot iron tube to mesitylene (Q, 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene).
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compound Y: Compound X ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{Cl}_2$) undergoes double dehydrohalogenation with excess $\text{NaNH}_2$ to form the 3-carbon alkyne Y = propyne ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify Z and check Statement I: Acid-catalyzed hydration of propyne using dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{Hg}^{2+}$ follows Markovnikov addition and tautomerization to yield Z = acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$). Since acetone contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group, it forms a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ with $\text{NaOI}$, making Statement I true.
  3. Step 3 — Identify Q and check Statement II: Passing propyne through a red-hot iron tube causes cyclic trimerization to give Q = mesitylene ($1,3,5\text{-trimethylbenzene}$, $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{12}$). Mesitylene has $3$ equivalent aromatic hydrogens and $9$ equivalent aliphatic hydrogens (from three $-\text{CH}_3$ groups), giving an aromatic: aliphatic H ratio of $3:9 = 1:3$, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to Option (b).

with NaOI. Thus, Statement I is true.

C9H12). It has 3 aromatic H atoms and 9 aliphatic H atoms (aromatic : aliphatic = 3 : 9 = 1 : 3). Thus, Statement
II is true.

Q11.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q12.subtopic: Isomer Functional Group Tests (2,4-DNP, Baeyer, Tollens’)
Q12.conceptHtml: 2,4-DNP detects aldehydes/ketones; Tollens’ reagent detects aldehydes only; Baeyer’s test (KMnO<sub>4</sub>) detects alkenes/aldehydes.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four isomeric compounds: From the given structures, $\text{P} = \text{PhCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ (allylic alcohol), $\text{Q} = \text{PhCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ (aldehyde), $\text{R} = \text{PhCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ (methyl ketone), and $\text{S} = \text{PhCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (ethyl ketone).
  2. Step 2 — Check statements A, B, and C: Q, R, and S are all carbonyl compounds, so they form precipitates with 2,4-DNP (A is correct). Baeyer's test detects aliphatic $\text{C}=\text{C}$ unsaturation, which is present in P but absent in Q (B is incorrect). Both Q and R contain a benzene ring with a high $\text{C}:\text{H}$ ratio, so they burn with a sooty flame (C is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check statements D and E: Only R has a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group for the iodoform test; S is an ethyl ketone and fails the test (D is incorrect). Only Q is an aldehyde, so Q alone reduces Tollens' reagent to deposit a silver mirror (E is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: The correct statements are A, C, and E only, matching Option (d).

a cyclic ketone.
Step 2: Evaluate statements:
- A is true: Q (aldehyde), R (ketone), and S (ketone) all give 2,4-DNP precipitate.
- C is true: Aromatic/unsaturated compounds Q and R burn with a sooty flame (note: checking fig_q12.png, Q
and R have benzene rings!).
- E is true: Q is the only aldehyde, so Q alone gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent.
Thus, A, C and E only are correct.
Q12.trapHtml: Ketones give 2,4-DNP test but do NOT give Tollens’ test.

Q13.conceptHtml: Acidic hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub> − CH = CH − O − C(CH<sub>3</sub>) = CH<sub>2</sub> yields propanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO) and acetone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>).
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Predict the hydrolysis products P and Q: Just as in the reference reaction, acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+/\Delta$) of the unsaturated ether $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{O}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$ cleaves both enol-ether bonds to form two enols, which tautomerize into propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) and acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate reagents that do not distinguish them: Both propanal and acetone react positively with saturated $\text{NaHSO}_3$ (bisulfite adduct) and 2,4-DNP reagent (hydrazone precipitate), while neither reacts with Lucas reagent (which is specific for alcohols).
  3. Step 3 — Select the distinguishing reagent: Fehling solution oxidizes aliphatic aldehydes (propanal gives a reddish-brown $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate) but does not react with ketones (acetone gives no precipitate).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Fehling solution cleanly distinguishes P and Q, confirming Option (b).

Step 2: Propanal (aliphatic aldehyde) gives a red Cu2O precipitate with Fehling solution, whereas acetone (ketone)
does not.
Step 3: Both react with 2,4-DNP and saturated NaHSO3 (acetone is a methyl ketone, so it also forms a bisulphite
adduct!), and Lucas reagent is for alcohols.
Q13.trapHtml: Saturated NaHSO<sub>3</sub> reacts with BOTH aldehydes and methyl ketones (like acetone), so it CANNOT distinguish propanal from acetone.

Q14.conceptHtml: Four cross-aldol products form only if BOTH aldehydes have α-H; benzaldehyde (aldehyde) is more reactive than acetophenone (ketone) towards nucleophiles. Statement I: If one of the two aldehydes has NO α-H (e.g., HCHO or PhCHO), only two products (one self + one cross) form, not four! Thus, Statement I is false. Statement II: Aldehydes (benzaldehyde) are more reactive towards nucleophilic addition (semicarbazide) than ketones (acetophenone), so benzaldehyde reacts faster, not acetophenone only. Thus, Statement II is false.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Cross-aldol condensation between two different aldehydes yields four products only when both aldehydes possess $\alpha$-hydrogens. If one aldehyde lacks $\alpha$-hydrogens (e.g., $\text{HCHO}$ or $\text{PhCHO}$ reacting with $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$), fewer than four products are obtained. Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Between benzaldehyde (an aldehyde) and acetophenone (a ketone), benzaldehyde is significantly more reactive toward nucleophilic addition with semicarbazide because it has less steric hindrance and a more electrophilic carbonyl carbon. Therefore, semicarbazide reacts predominantly with benzaldehyde, not exclusively with acetophenone. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Final conclusion: Since both Statement I and Statement II are false, the correct answer is Option (b).

Q15.subtopic: Phenol vs Carboxylic Acid Gas Evolution
Q15.format: Single-Choice MCQ | H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> Molar Mass
Q15.conceptHtml: Active metal (Na) reacts with −OH to liberate H<sub>2</sub> (M = 2); NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts with −COOH to liberate CO<sub>2</sub> (M = 44).
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify gas $x$ from reaction A: Phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) reacts with active sodium metal ($\text{Na}$) to form sodium phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$) and evolves hydrogen gas: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Na} \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\uparrow$. Thus, $x = \text{H}_2$, with molar mass $2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify gas $y$ from reaction B: Benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) is stronger than carbonic acid and reacts with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to liberate carbon dioxide gas: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$. Thus, $y = \text{CO}_2$, with molar mass $44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the sum of molar masses: Adding the two molar masses gives $M_x + M_y = 2 + 44 = 46\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: The required numerical value is $46$, which corresponds to Option (a).

Step 1: In reaction (A), phenol (PhOH) + Na → PhONa + 1H2 ↑, so gas x = H2 (Mx = 2 g/mol).
Step 2: In reaction (B), benzoic acid (PhCOOH) + NaHC2O3 → PhCOONa + H2O + CO2 ↑, so gas y = CO2
(My = 44 g/mol).
Step 3: Mx + My = 2 + 44 = 46.
Q15.trapHtml: Phenol does NOT react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, but it DOES react with metallic Na to release H<sub>2</sub> (2 g/mol, not 1).

Q16.subtopic: Tollens’ Test on Cyclic Hemiacetal vs Acetal
Q16.conceptHtml: Cyclic hemiacetals (−CH(OH) − OR at the anomeric-like carbon) open in aqueous/basic Tollens’ reagent to expose the free −CHO group, giving a positive silver mirror.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for a positive Tollens' test: Tollens' reagent ($[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+\text{OH}^-$) is a basic oxidizing agent that gives a silver mirror with free aldehydes or with hemiacetals that can open in basic medium to form a free aldehyde.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the four cyclic structures: Compound A (2-methoxytetrahydrofuran) is a cyclic acetal, which is stable in base and cannot open to an aldehyde. Compound B (3-methoxytetrahydrofuran) is a simple ether, and compound D (3-hydroxytetrahydrofuran) is an ordinary alcohol–ether; none of A, B, or D gives a positive Tollens' test.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the cyclic hemiacetal: Compound C (2-hydroxytetrahydrofuran) has both $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{OR}$ attached to the same carbon (C−2), making it a cyclic hemiacetal. In aqueous alkaline Tollens' reagent, it equilibrates with its open-chain aldehyde form ($\text{HO}-(\text{CH}_2)_3-\text{CHO}$) and produces a silver mirror.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the option label: Compound C is listed as Option (d).

Step 1: Inspecting structures A, B, C, D in fig_q16.png:
- A and B have −OCH3 (cyclic acetal/methyl glycoside or ether), which cannot open in basic Tollens’ medium.
- D has −OH far from the ring oxygen (simple cyclic ether alcohol).
- C has the −OH group directly on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen (a cyclic hemiacetal!), which equilibrates
with the open-chain aldehyde and reduces Tollens’ reagent.
Q16.trapHtml: Acetals (C(OR)<sub>2</sub>) are stable in base and give negative Tollens’ test; only hemiacetals (C(OH)(OR)) test positive.

Q17.format: Statement-Based MCQ | NaOCl/KI & α, β-Unsaturated Methyl Ketones
Q17.conceptHtml: NaOCl + KI → KOI + NaCl; KOI is an oxidising/iodinating agent; α, β-unsaturated methyl ketones (R − CH = CH − COCH<sub>3</sub>) give a positive iodoform test.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B: Sodium hypochlorite ($\text{NaOCl}$) reacts with $\text{KI}$ in solution to generate hypoiodite ($\text{KOI}$ / $\text{OI}^-$), which serves as the active halogenating and oxidizing species (iodine in $+1$ state). Therefore, A is true and B is false.
  2. Step 2 — Check statement C: The $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated methyl ketone ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$) contains the required $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ unit and cleanly undergoes the iodoform reaction to form $\text{CHI}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCOO}^-$ without affecting the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond. Thus, C is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check statements D and E: Isopropyl alcohol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$) has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group and does give a positive iodoform test, so D is false. Methanoic acid ($\text{HCOOH}$) lacks both required groupings and gives a negative test, so E is false.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Only statements A and C are true, corresponding to Option (d).
Q17.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Evaluate each statement:
- A is true: NaOCl + KI → NaCl + KOI (in situ generation of hypoiodite).
- B is false: KOI is an oxidising agent, not a reducing agent.
- C is true: CH3 − CH = CH − COCH3 has the CH3CO− group and gives CHI3 with I2/NaOH.
- D is false: Isopropyl alcohol (CH3CH(OH)CH3) has CH3CH(OH)− and DOES give iodoform test.
- E is false: Methanoic acid (HCOOH) does NOT give iodoform test.
Thus, only A and C are true.
Q17.trapHtml: Do not confuse Tollens’ test (positive for HCOOH) with the iodoform test (negative for HCOOH).

Q18.conceptHtml: Iodoform test differentiates two compounds only when ONE gives yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> ppt (CH<sub>3</sub>CO− or CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)−) and the other does NOT.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the structural condition for the iodoform test: A compound gives a yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ precipitate with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$ if it contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group (excluding carboxylic acids/esters/amides) or a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Test each pair: In A, ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) is positive while methanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$) is negative, so iodoform differentiates them. In B, neither carboxylic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ nor $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) gives the test. In C, neither cyclohexene nor cyclohexanone has a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group. In D, neither diethyl ether nor pentan-3-one gives the test.
  3. Step 3 — Check pair E: In E, acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) gives a positive iodoform test while anisole ($\text{PhOCH}_3$) is negative, so iodoform differentiates them.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Only pairs A and E can be differentiated by the iodoform test, matching Option (c).

Q19.conceptHtml: Propanal (C<sub>3</sub>) + Ethanal (C<sub>2</sub>) in alkali/heat give 4 possible aldol condensation products (C<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>, C<sub>6</sub>), none of which is 3-methylbut-2-enal.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify aldehydes $x$ and $y$: Stephen reduction of propanenitrile ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$) with $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by hydrolysis gives $x = \text{propanal}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$). Ozonolysis of but-2-ene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$) followed by hydrolysis yields $y = \text{ethanal}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$).
  2. Step 2 — List the two self-aldol condensation products: Self-aldol of ethanal gives but-2-enal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCHO}$). Self-aldol of propanal gives 2-methylpent-2-enal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO}$), which is option (a).
  3. Step 3 — List the two cross-aldol condensation products: Ethanal enolate attacking propanal gives pent-2-enal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCHO}$), option (d). Propanal enolate attacking ethanal gives 2-methylbut-2-enal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CHO}$), option (b).
  4. Step 4 — Identify the product not formed: 3-Methylbut-2-enal ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCHO}$) cannot be formed from ethanal and propanal (it would require acetone as the electrophile). Therefore, the correct answer is Option (c).

Q20.conceptHtml: Anti-Markovnikov conversion of 1-bromo-1-phenylethane to phenylacetic acid requires elimination to styrene, hydroboration-oxidation to 2-phenylethanol, and Jones oxidation.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare structures X and Y: Compound X is 1-bromo-1-phenylethane ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}(\text{Br})-\text{CH}_3$) and target Y is 2-phenylethanoic acid ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$). We need to shift the functional group from the benzylic carbon to the terminal carbon and oxidize it to $-\text{COOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Elimination with $\text{NaOEt}$ (step i): Treating X with strong base $\text{NaOEt}$ causes E2 dehydrohalogenation to form styrene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Hydroboration–oxidation with $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6/\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ (step ii): Anti-Markovnikov hydration of styrene places the $-\text{OH}$ group at the less substituted terminal carbon, producing 2-phenylethanol ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Oxidation with Jones reagent (step iii): Jones reagent ($\text{CrO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) oxidizes the primary alcohol directly to the carboxylic acid $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$ (Y), confirming Option (b).

(PhCH2CH2OH).
Step 3: Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) oxidises the primary alcohol to phenylacetic acid (PhCH2COOH, Y).

Q21.conceptHtml: An aromatic aldehyde with no α-H (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) undergoes Cannizzaro reaction with conc. NaOH and cross- aldol with acetophenone.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce functional features of compound A: Forming a single cross-aldol product with acetophenone and undergoing a Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ (to produce a substituted benzyl alcohol) both prove that compound A is an aromatic aldehyde with no $\alpha$-hydrogen.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate mismatched options: 2-Hydroxyacetophenone is a ketone (has $\alpha$-H, no Cannizzaro), 4-methylbenzoic acid is a carboxylic acid (neither aldol nor Cannizzaro), and 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde has molecular formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ (not $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, and its phenolic $-\text{OH}$ deprotonates in conc. $\text{NaOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Verify 4-methoxybenzaldehyde: 4-Methoxybenzaldehyde ($p\text{-CH}_3\text{O}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}$) has formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, lacks $\alpha$-hydrogens, gives a single chalcone product with acetophenone, and disproportionates in conc. $\text{NaOH}$ to give 4-methoxybenzyl alcohol and sodium 4-methoxybenzoate.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Compound A is 4-methoxybenzaldehyde, which corresponds to Option (d).

Q22.conceptHtml: Direct recall of standard carbonyl reduction and qualitative test reagents.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match reagents A and B: Hydrazine with $\text{KOH}$ ($\text{NH}_2-\text{NH}_2, \text{KOH}$) reduces carbonyls ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) to $-\text{CH}_2-$ via the Wolff–Kishner Reduction ($\text{A}-\text{III}$). Ammoniacal silver nitrate ($\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{OH}$) is used in Tollens' Test for aldehydes ($\text{B}-\text{I}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match reagents C and D: Aqueous $\text{CuSO}_4$ with alkaline sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle salt) constitutes Fehling's Test ($\text{C}-\text{IV}$). Amalgamated zinc with $\text{HCl}$ ($\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}, \text{HCl}$) reduces carbonyls to alkanes via Clemmensen Reduction ($\text{D}-\text{II}$).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the complete matching: Combining all four pairs gives $\text{A}-\text{III},\ \text{B}-\text{I},\ \text{C}-\text{IV},\ \text{D}-\text{II}$, which matches Option (b).

Q23.format: Matrix Match | Rosenmund, Stephen, Etard, Gattermann–Koch
Q23.conceptHtml: Four hallmark NCERT aldehyde syntheses matched to their reagents.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match reagents A and B: $\text{H}_2$ over poisoned $\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$ reduces acid chlorides to aldehydes via Rosenmund Reduction ($\text{A}-\text{II}$). $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by hydrolysis reduces nitriles to aldehydes via the Stephen Reaction ($\text{B}-\text{IV}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match reagents C and D: Chromyl chloride in $\text{CS}_2$ ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2, \text{CS}_2$) oxidizes toluene to benzaldehyde in the Etard Reaction ($\text{C}-\text{I}$). $\text{CO}, \text{HCl}$ with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ formylates benzene to benzaldehyde in the Gattermann–Koch Reaction ($\text{D}-\text{III}$).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the complete matching: The correct sequence is $\text{A}-\text{II},\ \text{B}-\text{IV},\ \text{C}-\text{I},\ \text{D}-\text{III}$, confirming Option (d).

Q24.format: Statement I & II | Carboxylic Acid & Ketene
Q24.conceptHtml: Carboxylic acids dissolve in NaHCO<sub>3</sub>; in a ketene (R − CH = C = O), the cumulene central carbon is sp-hybridised. Statement I: Compound (X) is 3-bromocyclohexanecarboxylic acid (Wait: check fig_q24_1.png: cyclohexanone with −Br and −COOH!). Since it has a −COOH group, it dissolves in NaHCO<sub>3</sub>. The two substituted ring carbons (bearing −Br and −COOH) each have 4 different groups, so it has 2 chiral carbons. Statement I is true. Statement II: Compound (Y) is cyclopropylketene? Look at fig_q24_2.png: cyclopropane ring attached to = C = O (total 4 carbons: two CH<sub>2</sub> carbons in the ring are sp3, the ring-junction C = is sp2, and the = C = O carbon is sp). Thus it has two sp3, one sp2, and one sp carbon. Statement II is true.

1. Step 1 — Analyze compound (X) for Statement I: Compound (X) is $2\text{-(4-bromobenzoyl)cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid}$. Because it contains a carboxylic acid group ($-\text{COOH}$), it reacts with and dissolves in aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$ (liberating $\text{CO}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Count chiral centers in (X): Both C−1 (bonded to $-\text{COOH}$, $-\text{H}$, C−2, and C-5) and C−2 (bonded to $-\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{Br}$, $-\text{H}$, C−1, and C−3) of the cyclopentane ring are attached to four different groups, so (X) has two chiral carbon atoms. Thus, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Determine carbon hybridizations in (Y) for Statement II: Compound (Y) is the ketene $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{C}=\text{O}$. Going from left to right: the $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbons are $sp^3$ ($2$ carbons), the $-\text{CH}=$ carbon is $sp^2$ ($1$ carbon), and the cumulated $=\text{C}=\text{O}$ carbon is $sp$ ($1$ carbon). Q25.conceptHtml: An acetal masks an aldehyde against Tollens’ reagent, while a methyl ketone group gives a positive iodoform test; dilute acid unmasks the aldehyde.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret the tests on P ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_3$): A positive iodoform test indicates a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ (or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$) group, while a negative Tollens' test confirms that P has no free $-\text{CHO}$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Interpret the acid hydrolysis of P to Q: Treating P with dilute acid generates Q, which now gives both a positive Tollens' test and a positive iodoform test. This means P contains an acetal group ($-\text{CH}(\text{OCH}_3)_2$) that hydrolyzes in dilute acid to unmask a free aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$), while keeping the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group intact.
  3. Step 3 — Check the four options: Option (a) has a free $-\text{CHO}$ (would give positive Tollens' before hydrolysis); option (b) is a 1,2-diether (not an acetal); option (d) is a ketal (hydrolyzes to a diketone, negative Tollens'). Only option (c), $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{OCH}_3)_2$, has both a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group and a dimethyl acetal that hydrolyzes to $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CHO}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: The structure of P is Option (c).

Q26.conceptHtml: In a keto-aldehyde (6-oxoheptanal), enolisation occurs at the ketone α-carbon to attack the more elec- trophilic aldehyde carbonyl, forming a 5-membered α, β-unsaturated ketone.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting keto-aldehyde: Counting the carbon chain in the diagram gives 6-oxoheptanal: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}$ (C−1 is the aldehyde, C-6 is the ketone).
  2. Step 2 — Choose the thermodynamically and kinetically favored ring closure: Between the aldehyde (C−1) and ketone (C-6), the aldehyde carbonyl is far more electrophilic. Among the enolates of the ketone, deprotonation at C-5 (internal $\alpha$-carbon) attacks C−1 to form a strain-free 5-membered ring, whereas attack from C-7 would form an unfavorable 7-membered ring.
  3. Step 3 — Dehydration to the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone: Loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from the resulting $\beta$-hydroxy ketone forms a conjugated double bond inside the cyclopentene ring adjacent to the exocyclic acetyl group ($-\text{COCH}_3$), yielding $1\text{-(cyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The cyclopentene ring bearing an acetyl group ($-\text{COCH}_3$) at the vinylic carbon is Option (b).

No: C5 attacks C1 → 5-membered ring with −COCH3 at C2? Wait: C5 is CH2 between C = O and CH2, so C5
attacking C1 gives a 5-membered ring with −COCH3 attached to the double bond = 1-(cyclopent-1-enyl)ethanone,
which is structure B!). Let’s check: C7 enolate attacking C1 would give a 7-membered ring (disfavoured). C5 enolate
attacking C1 gives a stable 5-membered ring, and dehydration gives the conjugated α, β-unsaturated ketone (B).
Q26.trapHtml: Always prefer 5- or 6-membered rings over 7-membered rings, and prefer attacking the aldehyde over the ketone.

Q27.conceptHtml: Positive 2,4-DNP + negative Tollens’ = ketone; optical activity requires a chiral carbon.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional group of P ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$): A positive 2,4-DNP test proves P is a carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone). A negative Tollens' test rules out aldehydes (eliminating option (a), 3-methylpentanal), so P must be a ketone.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the optical activity condition: Because P is optically active, it must contain at least one chiral carbon (bonded to four different groups).
  3. Step 3 — Inspect the ketone options: Hexan-2-one (option c) and 4-methylpentan-2-one (option d) have no chiral carbons and are achiral. In 3-methylpentan-2-one ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), carbon C−3 is bonded to $-\text{H}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and $-\text{COCH}_3$, making it chiral and optically active.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Compound P is 3-methylpentan-2-one, which corresponds to Option (b).

chiral carbon (C-3 has −H, −CH3, −C2H5, −COCH3).

Q28.conceptHtml: Yellow solid (CHI<sub>3</sub>) forms for CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)R and CH<sub>3</sub>COR (where R = H, alkyl, aryl), NOT for carboxylic acids or 1-alkanols.

1. Step 1 — State the iodoform test criterion: A yellow solid ($\text{CHI}_3$) is formed with $\text{NaOI}/\text{NaOH}$ by compounds containing either a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group (aldehydes/ketones, not carboxylic acids) or a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate each compound: Compound (A), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ (butan-2-ol), has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ unit (positive). Compound (B), propan-1-ol, lacks this unit (negative). Compound (C), $\text{CH}_3\text{COC}_2\text{H}_5$ (butan-2-one), has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ unit (positive).
  3. Step 3 — Check (D) and (E): Compound (D), $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, is a carboxylic acid (which simply neutralizes $\text{NaOH}$ and does not give the haloform reaction), and compound (E), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, lacks a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group (negative).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Only compounds (A) and (C) give a yellow solid, matching Option (a).

Q29.conceptHtml: Intramolecular aldol condensation always produces a cyclic α, β-unsaturated carbonyl where the C = C double bond is endocyclic or exocyclic to the newly formed ring and conjugated with C = O.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply retro-aldol cleavage: To check if an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated cyclic ketone comes from an intramolecular aldol condensation, cleave the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond into $-\text{CH}_2-$ (at the $\alpha$-carbon) and $>\text{C}=\text{O}$ (at the $\beta$-carbon). If the result is a single dicarbonyl molecule, it is an intramolecular aldol product.
  2. Step 2 — Test options (a), (c), and (d): Cleaving the endocyclic $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond in (a) gives cyclodecane-1,6-dione (one molecule); in (c) gives 6-oxohexanal (one molecule); and in (d) gives 2-acetylbenzaldehyde (one molecule). Thus, (a), (c), and (d) are all genuine intramolecular aldol products.
  3. Step 3 — Test option (b): In option (b), the double bond is an exocyclic $=\text{CH}_2$ group attached to the $\alpha$-carbon of $\alpha$-tetralone. Cleaving this $\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ bond yields two separate molecules ($\alpha$-tetralone and $\text{HCHO}$), meaning it is an intermolecular (cross) aldol product, not an intramolecular one.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Therefore, Option (b) is not a product of intramolecular aldol condensation.

= CH2 cannot arise from intramolecular aldol ring closure of a dicarbonyl (intramolecular aldol forms the ring bond
as the C = C bond, not an exocyclic methylene outside a bicyclic ketone!).

Q30.conceptHtml: Ketones resist mild oxidation; CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHMgBr yields 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compound (X): The molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$ corresponds to either propanal or acetone. Since (X) is not readily oxidized, it must be the ketone acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify compounds (Y) and (Z): Reduction of acetone (X) yields the secondary alcohol (Y) = propan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$). Reaction of (Y) with $\text{HBr}$ substitutes $-\text{OH}$ with $-\text{Br}$ to give (Z) = 2-bromopropane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Verify via the Grignard reaction: Converting (Z) into $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHMgBr}$ and reacting it with acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) followed by hydrolysis produces $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)_2$, whose IUPAC name is indeed 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Compounds (X), (Y), and (Z) are $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$, matching Option (b).

(CH3CH(Br)CH3).

Q31.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ph − CO − CHO + KOH/∆
Q31.conceptHtml: In phenylglyoxal (Ph − CO − CHO), OH− attacks the more electrophilic aldehyde carbon, followed by hydride shift to the ketone carbon, giving mandelate (Ph − CH(OH) − COO−K+).
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recognize the reaction type: The reactant is phenylglyoxal ($\text{Ph}-\text{CO}-\text{CHO}$), an $\alpha$-keto aldehyde with no $\alpha$-hydrogens. On heating with $\text{KOH}$, it undergoes an intramolecular Cannizzaro reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Nucleophilic attack by $\text{OH}^-$: Hydroxide ion preferentially attacks the more electrophilic and less sterically hindered aldehyde carbonyl ($-\text{CHO}$) rather than the ketone carbonyl ($\text{Ph}-\text{CO}-$).
  3. Step 3 — Intramolecular 1,2-hydride shift: The tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate transfers a hydride ion ($\text{H}^-$) directly to the adjacent ketone carbonyl, oxidizing the aldehyde end to $-\text{COOH}$ and reducing the ketone end to $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$.
  4. Step 4 — Acid–base proton transfer and final product: Rapid proton transfer in basic $\text{KOH}$ medium yields potassium mandelate, $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{COO}^-\text{K}^+$, which matches Option (c).
Q31.stepsLatex:
Step 1: OH− attacks the aldehyde carbon of Ph − CO − CHO (less sterically hindered and more δ+ than the ketone).
Step 2: Intramolecular hydride transfer from the aldehyde carbon to the adjacent ketone carbon gives Ph − CH(OH) − COOH,
which in KOH exists as potassium mandelate: Ph − CH(OH) − COO−K+ (C).
Q31.trapHtml: Do NOT oxidise the ketone to Ph − CO − COO−; the aldehyde is always oxidised to −COO− while the ketone is reduced to −CH(OH)−.

Q32.conceptHtml: Count compounds WITHOUT CH<sub>3</sub>CO− or CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)− (Note: check bromoacetone!).
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the iodoform test requirement: Molecules containing a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group (or $\text{XCH}_2\text{CO}-$, such as bromoacetone) or a $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group give a positive iodoform reaction with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify molecules that give a positive iodoform test ($6$ compounds): Ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), isopropyl alcohol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$), bromoacetone ($\text{BrCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$), 2-butanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$), 2-butanone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COC}_2\text{H}_5$), and 2-pentanone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COC}_3\text{H}_7$) all satisfy the condition and give a positive test.

Step 3 — Identify molecules that cannot give the iodoform test: Butanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$), 3-pentanone ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COC}_2\text{H}_5$), pentanal ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CHO}$), and 3-pentanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$) lack the required $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ moiety (4 compounds in total; note that strictly among the listed ketones/alcohols, 3-pentanone and 3-pentanol are the 2 non-methyl-ketone/alcohol isomers, while butanal and pentanal are also negative).

Q33.format: Statement-Based MCQ | Mild vs Complete Hydrolysis & Rosenmund
Q33.conceptHtml: Grignard + CO<sub>2</sub> gives RCOOH; Rosenmund followed by Br<sub>2</sub> water oxidises the aldehyde to RCOOH.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate reactions (A), (C), and (D): In (A), mild hydrolysis of a nitrile ($\text{R}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$) stops at an amide ($\text{R}-\text{CONH}_2$). In (C), Stephen reduction ($\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$, then $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) converts $\text{R}-\text{CN}$ into an aldehyde ($\text{R}-\text{CHO}$). In (D), $\text{PCC}$ is a mild oxidant that oxidizes $\text{RCH}_2\text{OH}$ only to an aldehyde ($\text{R}-\text{CHO}$). None of these gives a carboxylic acid.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate reaction (B): Reaction of a Grignard reagent ($\text{R}-\text{MgX}$) with dry ice ($\text{CO}_2$) followed by acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) is a standard preparation of a carboxylic acid ($\text{R}-\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate reaction (E): Benzoyl chloride ($\text{PhCOCl}$) undergoes Rosenmund reduction ($\text{H}_2/\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$) to benzaldehyde ($\text{PhCHO}$), which is subsequently oxidized by $\text{Br}_2$ water to benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Only reactions B and E yield a carboxylic acid as the major product, matching Option (d).

Q34.conceptHtml: Vanillin has a phenolic −OH (reacts with NaOH) and an aromatic −CHO (gives Tollens’ test, has no α-H). Statement I: Vanillin reacts with NaOH (acidic phenolic −OH) and with Tollens’ reagent (−CHO group). State- ment I is correct. Statement II: Vanillin has NO α-hydrogen on its −CHO group, so it CANNOT undergo self-aldol condensation. Statement II is incorrect.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional groups in vanillin: Vanillin ($4\text{-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde}$) contains a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group, an aryl methoxy ($-\text{OCH}_3$) group, and an aromatic aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$) group.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: The acidic phenolic $-\text{OH}$ reacts readily with $\text{NaOH}$ to form a water-soluble sodium phenoxide salt, and the $-\text{CHO}$ group reduces Tollens' reagent to give a silver mirror. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Self-aldol condensation requires at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen on the carbon attached to the carbonyl group. In vanillin, the $-\text{CHO}$ group is bonded directly to an aromatic ring carbon bearing no hydrogen atom, so it cannot undergo self-aldol condensation. Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, matching Option (a).

Q35.conceptHtml: 1 mole H<sub>2</sub>O (18 g) adds to 1 mole but-2-yne (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, gas at 333 K?) to give butan-2-one.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify optically active halide [A]: The only optically active isomer of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ is 2-bromobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Trace [B], [C], and [D]: Hot ethanolic $\text{KOH}$ gives the major Zaitsev alkene $[\text{B}] = \text{but-2-ene}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$). Bromination with $\text{Br}_2$ produces $[\text{C}] = 2,3\text{-dibromobutane}$, which upon double dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic $\text{NaNH}_2$ yields the alkyne gas $[\text{D}]$ (but-1-yne/but-2-yne, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6$).
  3. Step 3 — Hydration of alkyne [D] to [E]: Adding $18\text{ g}$ ($1\text{ mol}$) of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ per mole of $[\text{D}]$ in the presence of $\text{HgSO}_4$ and dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at $333\text{ K}$ causes Markovnikov hydration followed by keto–enol tautomerism to produce the ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Name compound [E]: The IUPAC name of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is Butan-2-one, which corresponds to Option (c).

but-1-yne).
Step 2: Hydration of either but-1-yne or but-2-yne (HgSO4/H+, 333 K) adds 1 mol H2O (18 g) to yield [E] =

Q36.subtopic: Rate of Hydrolysis of Carboxylic Acid Derivatives
Q36.conceptHtml: Hydrolysis rate of acid derivatives follows leaving group stability (weakest base = best leaving group) and inverse resonance donation: RCOCl > (RCO)<sub>2</sub>O > RCOOR′ > RCONH<sub>2</sub>.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four carboxylic acid derivatives: The given molecules are (p) propanoyl chloride (acid chloride), (q) acetic propanoic anhydride (acid anhydride), (r) ethyl propanoate (ester), and (s) propanamide (amide).
  2. Step 2 — Relate hydrolysis rate to leaving-group ability and electrophilicity: Hydrolysis proceeds via nucleophilic acyl substitution. Reactivity increases when the leaving group is a weaker base (better leaving group) and exerts less $+M$ resonance donation into the carbonyl carbon.
  3. Step 3 — Rank the leaving groups: The leaving-group ability decreases in the order $\text{Cl}^- > \text{RCOO}^- > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^- > \text{NH}_2^-$, and resonance stabilization of the carbonyl increases in the reverse order (strongest in amides, weakest in acid chlorides).
  4. Step 4 — Final order: Therefore, the rate of hydrolysis follows $\text{p} > \text{q} > \text{r} > \text{s}$, confirming Option (a).

Step 1: Identify p, q, r, s in fig_q36.png:
- (p) Propanoyl chloride (RCOCl) — fastest.
- (q) Propanoic acetic anhydride (RCO − O − COCH3) — second.
- (r) Ethyl propanoate (RCOOC2H5) — third.
- (s) Propanamide (RCONH2) — slowest (strongest +R from −NH2).
Order: p > q > r > s.
Q36.trapHtml: Anhydrides (q) always hydrolyse faster than esters (r) because carboxylate (RCOO−) is a much better leaving group than alkoxide (RO−).

Q37.conceptHtml: Zn − Hg/HCl reduces both aldehyde and ketone carbonyls to −CH<sub>2</sub>−, while leaving carboxylic acid/ester/lactone? Wait: in fig_q37.png, let’s check what groups are present: two C = O on a cyclohexanone/ketone + aldehyde + cyclic ether/lactone! In (D), the aldehyde and ketone are reduced while the lactone/ester remains intact!
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional groups in the reactant: The starting aromatic compound is ethyl 3-acetyl-5-methylbenzoate, containing a ketone group ($-\text{COCH}_3$), an ester group ($-\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$), and a methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$) on the benzene ring.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the selectivity of Clemmensen reduction: The reagent $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$ performs a Clemmensen reduction, which selectively reduces aldehyde and ketone carbonyls ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) all the way to methylene groups ($-\text{CH}_2-$).
  3. Step 3 — Determine the product (P): Under Clemmensen conditions, the acetyl ketone ($-\text{COCH}_3$) is reduced to an ethyl group ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), while the less reactive ester group ($-\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and the benzene ring remain intact, forming ethyl 3-ethyl-5-methylbenzoate.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The structure having an ethyl group, a methyl group, and an intact ethyl ester on the benzene ring is Option (d).

Q38.subtopic: Hot KMnO4 Oxidation to Benzoic Acid
Q38.conceptHtml: Hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises any mono-substituted benzene side chain having at least ONE benzylic C − H (or unsaturated/carbonyl/alcohol benzylic carbon) to −COOH.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for hot $\text{KMnO}_4$ side-chain oxidation: Hot $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidizes any mono-alkylbenzene side chain to benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$) provided the benzylic carbon carries at least one hydrogen atom (benzylic H).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first row of four compounds: Toluene ($\text{PhCH}_3$, 3 benzylic H), ethylbenzene ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, 2 benzylic H), and isopropylbenzene/cumene ($\text{PhCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, 1 benzylic H) all give benzoic acid ($3$ compounds). tert-Butylbenzene ($\text{PhC}(\text{CH}_3)_3$) has $0$ benzylic H and does not react.
  3. Step 3 — Check the second row of four compounds: Isobutylbenzene ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, 2 benzylic H) and n-propylbenzene ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, 2 benzylic H) both give benzoic acid ($+2$ compounds). 2-Phenylpropan-2-ol ($\text{PhC}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)_2$) has $0$ benzylic H (resistant), and 4,4'-dimethylbiphenyl gives biphenyl-4,4'-dicarboxylic acid rather than benzoic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Count the total: In total, $3 + 2 = 5$ compounds yield benzoic acid, which corresponds to Option (c).

Q39.subtopic: Common Reactions of Acetaldehyde and Acetone
Q39.conceptHtml: Both CH<sub>3</sub>CHO and CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> have α-H and a CH<sub>3</sub>CO− group, so both undergo Iodoform, Aldol, and Clemmensen reactions.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Iodoform (A) and Cannizzaro (B) reactions: Both acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) and acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) contain a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group, so both undergo the Iodoform reaction (A). Because both possess $\alpha$-hydrogens, neither undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction (B).
  2. Step 2 — Check Aldol condensation (C) and Tollens' test (D): Having $\alpha$-hydrogens, both acetaldehyde and acetone undergo Aldol condensation (C). However, only acetaldehyde reduces Tollens' reagent; acetone does not give Tollens' test (D).
  3. Step 3 — Check Clemmensen reduction (E): Both aldehydes and ketones are reduced to hydrocarbons by $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$, so both undergo Clemmensen reduction (E) (giving ethane and propane, respectively).
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Both compounds individually undergo reactions A, C, and E only, matching Option (c).

Q40.conceptHtml: Only acids stronger than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> < 6.35) liberate CO<sub>2</sub> from aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>: carboxylic acids and picric acid.

1. Step 1 — Recall the $\text{NaHCO}_3$ effervescence condition: A compound liberates $\text{CO}_2$ gas with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$ only if it is a stronger acid than carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 6.35$).
  2. Step 2 — Check carboxylic acids (A and D): Both benzoic acid (A, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.2$) and cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (D, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.9$) are much stronger acids than $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, so both produce $\text{CO}_2$ with $\text{NaHCO}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Check phenols (B, C, and E): Simple phenol (B, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.0$) and 4-methoxyphenol (E, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.2$) are weaker than $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and do not react with $\text{NaHCO}_3$. However, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol / picric acid (C, $\text{p}K_a \approx 0.38$) is exceptionally acidic due to three strong $-M/-I$ nitro groups, so it readily liberates $\text{CO}_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Final conclusion: Compounds A, C, and D produce $\text{CO}_2$ with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$, confirming Option (d).

Q41.format: Matrix Match | Stephen, Rosenmund, Etard, Gattermann–Koch
Q41.conceptHtml: Direct matching of standard aldehyde preparation reactions.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match reactions (A) and (B): In (A), nitrile reduction with $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to give $\text{RCHO}$ is the Stephen reaction ($\text{A}-\text{IV}$). In (B), hydrogenation of benzoyl chloride over $\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$ to benzaldehyde is the Rosenmund reduction ($\text{B}-\text{III}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match reactions (C) and (D): In (C), oxidation of toluene with $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{CS}_2$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to benzaldehyde is the Etard reaction ($\text{C}-\text{I}$). In (D), formylation of benzene with $\text{CO}, \text{HCl}$ and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3/\text{CuCl}$ is the Gattermann–Koch reaction ($\text{D}-\text{II}$).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: The complete matching is $(\text{A})-(\text{IV}),\ (\text{B})-(\text{III}),\ (\text{C})-(\text{I}),\ (\text{D})-(\text{II})$, which corresponds to Option (b).

Q42.conceptHtml: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones; EWG (−NO<sub>2</sub>) increases carbonyl electrophilicity while EDG (−CH<sub>3</sub>) decreases it.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the reactivity rule for nucleophilic addition: Nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) is faster when the carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic (greater $\delta^+$ charge) and less sterically hindered.
  2. Step 2 — Compare aldehydes with ketones: Ketones like acetophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$) are less reactive than aromatic aldehydes because the extra methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$) both increases steric crowding and donates electron density via the $+I$ effect, reducing electrophilicity. Thus, acetophenone is the least reactive.
  3. Step 3 — Compare substituted benzaldehydes: On the benzene ring, an electron-donating group like $-\text{CH}_3$ in $p$-tolualdehyde ($+I$ and hyperconjugation) decreases the $\delta^+$ charge on the $-\text{CHO}$ carbon, making it less reactive than benzaldehyde. Conversely, a strong electron-withdrawing group like $-\text{NO}_2$ in $p$-nitrobenzaldehyde ($-M$ and $-I$ effects) pulls electron density away, making the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic and most reactive.
  4. Step 4 — Arrange in increasing order and confirm: Combining these effects gives $\text{acetophenone} < p\text{-tolualdehyde} < \text{benzaldehyde} < p\text{-nitrobenzaldehyde}$, which matches option (b).

Step 2: Among benzaldehydes: p-tolualdehyde (+I/+H of −CH3) < benzaldehyde < p-nitrobenzaldehyde (−M/−I
of −NO2).
Order: acetophenone < p-tolualdehyde < benzaldehyde < p-nitrobenzaldehyde.
Q42.trapHtml: −M groups (−NO<sub>2</sub>) strongly activate the carbonyl carbon towards nucleophilic attack.

Q43.conceptHtml: Ozonolysis of 1-methylcyclohexene gives a 7-carbon keto-aldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CHO), which undergoes intramolecular aldol to 1-acetylcyclopentene (x).

1. Step 1 — Analyse the target molecule "x": The target molecule is 1-(cyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one, an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone containing a 5-membered ring and an acetyl ($-\text{COCH}_3$) group (total of 7 carbons).
  2. Step 2 — Work backward from intramolecular aldol condensation: Breaking the ring $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond of the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone back into a carbonyl and an $\alpha$-methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$ adjacent to $-\text{COCH}_3$) gives the 7-carbon dicarbonyl precursor, 6-oxoheptanal: $\text{O}=\text{CH}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Work backward from reductive ozonolysis: To obtain 6-oxoheptanal via ozonolysis ($\text{O}_3 / \text{Zn}-\text{H}_2\text{O}$) of a cyclic alkene, reconnect the aldehyde carbonyl carbon ($\text{C}1$) and the ketone carbonyl carbon ($\text{C}6$) with a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond (removing the two oxygens). This closes a 6-membered ring with a methyl substituent on the double-bonded carbon: 1-methylcyclohexene.
  4. Step 4 — Verify forward and confirm: Reductive ozonolysis of 1-methylcyclohexene yields 6-oxoheptanal, whose $\text{C}5$ enolate attacks the $\text{C}1$ aldehyde carbon to form a strain-free 5-membered ring, dehydrating to "x". This corresponds to option (d).

- Base-catalysed intramolecular aldol of 6-oxoheptanal forms the 5-membered α, β-unsaturated ketone x.
