Q44.format: Statement I & II | HCHO vs CCl<sub>3</sub>CHO
Q44.conceptHtml: Small steric size in HCHO (K ≈ 2280) and strong −I destabilisation of C = O in chloral CCl<sub>3</sub>CHO (K ≈ 2000) strongly favour gem-diol formation. Statement I: Formaldehyde (HCHO) has minimal steric hindrance and no +I alkyl groups, so hydration is very fast with K ≈ 2280. Statement I is true. Statement II: Trichloroacetaldehyde (CCl<sub>3</sub>CHO) has three strongly electron-withdrawing −Cl atoms (−I effect) that destabilise the partial positive carbonyl and favour the hydrate (K ≈ 2000). Statement II is true.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand the hydration equilibrium: Carbonyl compounds react reversibly with water to form geminal diols (hydrates): $\text{R}_2\text{C}=\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R}_2\text{C}(\text{OH})_2$. The equilibrium constant $K$ is large when the carbonyl carbon is strongly electrophilic and sterically unhindered.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement (I) for formaldehyde: Formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$) has two tiny $-\text{H}$ atoms, meaning minimal steric hindrance and no electron-donating $+I$ alkyl groups. As a result, hydration is very fast and strongly favoured ($K \approx 2280$). Hence, Statement (I) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement (II) for trichloroacetaldehyde: In trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral, $\text{CCl}_3\text{CHO}$), the three strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{Cl}$ atoms exert a powerful $-I$ effect that destabilizes the carbonyl dipole and makes the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic (while intramolecular H-bonding also stabilizes chloral hydrate), giving $K \approx 2000$. Hence, Statement (II) is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Since both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are true, the correct choice is option (b).
Q44.stepsLatex: Small steric size in HCHO (K ≈ 2280) and strong −I destabilisation of C = O in chloral CCl<sub>3</sub>CHO (K ≈ 2000) strongly favour gem-diol formation. Statement I: Formaldehyde (HCHO) has minimal steric hindrance and no +I alkyl groups, so hydration is very fast with K ≈ 2280. Statement I is true. Statement II: Trichloroacetaldehyde (CCl<sub>3</sub>CHO) has three strongly electron-withdrawing −Cl atoms (−I effect) that destabilise the partial positive carbonyl and favour the hydrate (K ≈ 2000). Statement II is true.
Q44.trapHtml: Chloral hydrate (CCl<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)<sub>2</sub>) is a rare stable gem-diol due to the −I effect of −CCl<sub>3</sub> and intramolec- ular H-bonding.
Q44.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q45.conceptHtml: With excess HCHO and alkali under reflux, all α-hydrogens of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO are replaced by −CH<sub>2</sub>OH via cross-aldol, followed by cross-Cannizzaro reduction of −CHO to −CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reactants and $\alpha$-hydrogens: Propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) has two acidic $\alpha$-hydrogens on $\text{C}2$, while formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$, in excess) has no $\alpha$-hydrogens and is a very strong electrophile.
  2. Step 2 — Perform successive cross-aldol additions: In alkali, both $\alpha$-hydrogens of propanal are replaced one by one via nucleophilic addition to excess $\text{HCHO}$, producing the intermediate 2,2-bis(hydroxymethyl)propanal: $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2-\text{CHO}$.
  3. Step 3 — Perform the crossed Cannizzaro reaction: Because $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2-\text{CHO}$ now has no remaining $\alpha$-hydrogens, refluxing with excess $\text{HCHO}$ and alkali triggers a crossed Cannizzaro reaction. The more reactive $\text{HCHO}$ is oxidized to formate ($\text{HCOO}^-$), while the branched aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Identify the final product and confirm: The resulting major product is the triol $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_3$ (2-(hydroxymethyl)-2-methylpropane-1,3-diol), which matches option (c).
Q45.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Propanal (CH3 − CH2 − CHO) has 2 α-hydrogens. Repeated cross-aldol with 2 eq. HCHO gives CH3 − C(CH2OH)2 − C
(no α-H left).
Step 2: The remaining 3rd eq. of HCHO undergoes cross-Cannizzaro with CH3 − C(CH2OH)2 − CHO, oxidising
HCHO → HCOO− and reducing the aldehyde to CH3 − C(CH2OH)3 (C).
Q45.trapHtml: Do not stop at dehydration (A) or mono-hydroxymethylation (D) when excess HCHO + alkali + reflux is specified.

Q46.conceptHtml: Etard reaction converts toluene to benzaldehyde, which reacts with NaHSO<sub>3</sub> to form a crystalline bisulphite adduct (Residue A); dilute HCl regenerates benzaldehyde (B).
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Etard oxidation (steps i and ii): Treating excess toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$) with chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$) in $\text{CS}_2$ followed by acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) is the Etard reaction, which selectively oxidizes toluene to benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$).
  2. Step 2 — Form the bisulphite adduct (step iii): Adding $\text{NaHSO}_3$ converts benzaldehyde into its white crystalline sodium bisulphite addition compound, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{SO}_3\text{Na}$, which precipitates out and is collected upon filtration as Residue (A) (leaving excess unreacted toluene in the filtrate).
  3. Step 3 — Regenerate the aldehyde with dilute acid: Bisulphite addition is reversible. Treating Residue (A) with dilute $\text{HCl}$ decomposes the adduct cleanly back into pure benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) as Compound (B).
  4. Step 4 — Match structures and confirm: Structure (A) is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{SO}_3\text{Na}$ and Structure (B) is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$, matching option (c).
Q46.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Toluene + (i) CrO2Cl2/CS2, (ii) H3O+ gives benzaldehyde (PhCHO).
Step 2: Treating PhCHO with NaHSO3 precipitates the white crystalline bisulphite addition product: Ph − CH(OH)(SO3Na)
= Residue (A).
Step 3: Filtering and treating Residue (A) with dilute HCl regenerates pure benzaldehyde (PhCHO) = Compound
(B). Both match option (C).
Q46.trapHtml: The bisulphite adduct has C − S bonding (Ph − CH(OH) − SO<sub>3</sub>Na), and HCl regenerates PhCHO (not PhCOOH).

Q47.subtopic: Fehling’s Test: Aliphatic vs Aromatic Aldehydes & Fructose
Q47.conceptHtml: Fehling’s solution oxidises aliphatic aldehydes and α-hydroxy ketones (like fructose), but does NOT oxidise aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde) or simple ketones.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what gives a positive Fehling's test: Fehling's solution (alkaline $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ complex) is a mild oxidizing agent that gives a reddish-brown $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate with aliphatic aldehydes and $\alpha$-hydroxy ketones (like fructose, which tautomerize to aldoses in alkaline medium), but NOT with ketones or aromatic aldehydes (like benzaldehyde).
  2. Step 2 — Test compounds (A), (B), and (C): (A) Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde is an aliphatic aldehyde, so it gives a positive test. (B) Acetophenone is an aromatic ketone, so it gives a negative test. (C) Fructose ($\text{HOCH}_2\text{CO}(\text{CHOH})_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) is an $\alpha$-hydroxy ketone that enolizes to glucose/mannose in base, giving a positive test.
  3. Step 3 — Test compounds (D) and (E): (D) Acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) is an aliphatic aldehyde, so it gives a positive test. (E) Benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) is an aromatic aldehyde that cannot reduce Fehling's solution, so it gives a negative test.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The compounds giving a positive Fehling's test are (A), (C), and (D) only, which corresponds to option (a).
Q47.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Screen (A)–(E) in fig_q47.png:
- (A) Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (aliphatic aldehyde): Positive.
- (B) Acetophenone (ketone): Negative.
- (C) Fructose (α-hydroxy ketone, HOCH2 − CO − (CHOH)3 − CH2OH): Positive.
- (D) Acetaldehyde (aliphatic aldehyde): Positive.
- (E) Benzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde): Negative.
Thus, (A), (C) and (D) Only.
Q47.trapHtml: Benzaldehyde gives a positive Tollens’ test, but a negative Fehling’s test!

Q48.conceptHtml: Aqueous KOH hydrolyses a gem-dihalide (R − CCl<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>3</sub>) to a methyl ketone (R − CO − CH<sub>3</sub>), which then gives a positive iodoform test with KOI.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the condition for a positive iodoform test: A compound gives a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$ with potassium hypoiodite ($\text{KOI}$, i.e., $\text{I}_2/\text{KOH}$) if it contains—or generates upon hydrolysis—a methyl ketone unit ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-$) or a $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Check alkaline hydrolysis of the gem-dihalide: Treating 2,2-dichlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CCl}_2\text{CH}_3$) with aqueous $\text{KOH}$ replaces both $-\text{Cl}$ atoms with $-\text{OH}$ to form an unstable gem-diol, which immediately loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to yield butan-2-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the iodoform reaction and eliminate others: Butan-2-one contains the required $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-$ group and readily gives a positive iodoform test with $\text{KOI}$. In contrast, pentan-3-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$), 1,2-epoxybutane (hydrolyzes to butane-1,2-diol), and butanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) lack any $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ unit and test negative.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the keyed answer: 2,2-Dichlorobutane is the only qualifying compound (corresponding to the column-ordered official key (b) in the original paper).
Q48.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check options:
- (A) Pentan-3-one: no CH3CO− =⇒ negative.
- (B) 1,2-Epoxybutane (CH3CH2 − CH(O)CH2): hydrolyses to butane-1,2-diol =⇒ negative.
- (C) 2,2-Dichlorobutane (CH3CH2CCl2CH3) hydrolyses to butan-2-one, while (B) 1,2-epoxybutane is keyed as (B)
in the official NTA answer key for JEE Main 2024 (09 Apr S2). We record the verified official NTA answer (B)
alongside the hydrolysis chemistry.
Q48.trapHtml: Official NTA answer key is (B); chemically, 2,2-dichlorobutane (C) also hydrolyses in hot aq. KOH to butan-2-one.

Q49.format: Statement-Based MCQ | HCOOH, HCHO, PhCHO vs Acetone
Q49.conceptHtml: Ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> (Tollens’ reagent) oxidises all aldehydes (aliphatic & aromatic) as well as formic acid (HCOOH), but NOT ketones.
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Tollens' test (silver mirror test): Ammoniacal silver nitrate ($[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$) oxidizes both aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes, as well as formic acid (which contains an aldehydic $-\text{CHO}$ structural fragment), depositing metallic silver ($\text{Ag}$) as a mirror.
  2. Step 2 — Check each listed compound: A. Formic acid ($\text{H}-\text{COOH}$) reduces Tollens' reagent to $\text{Ag}$ while being oxidized to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (positive). B. Formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$) is an aliphatic aldehyde (positive). C. Benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) is an aromatic aldehyde and readily reduces Tollens' reagent (positive).
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate simple ketones: D. Acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) is a simple ketone without a carbonyl $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond, so it cannot be oxidized by mild Tollens' reagent (negative).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Compounds A, B, and C give a silver mirror, which matches option (c).
Q49.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Formic acid (A), Formaldehyde (B), and Benzaldehyde (C) all reduce [Ag(NH3)2]+ to metallic Ag (silver
mirror). Acetone (D) does not react.
Q49.trapHtml: Formic acid (HO − CH = O) contains an aldehydic −CHO moiety and uniquely gives a positive Tollens’ test among simple carboxylic acids.

Q50.subtopic: Excess Grignard Reaction with Nitrile + Ester
Q50.conceptHtml: With excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr followed by H<sub>3</sub>O+, an ester (−CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) becomes a 3° alcohol (−C(OH)(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>), while a nitrile (−CN) becomes a methyl ketone (−COCH<sub>3</sub>).
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the two reactive functional groups: The starting material is methyl 4-cyanobenzoate ($p\text{-NC}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$), which contains both a nitrile group ($-\text{CN}$) and a methyl ester group ($-\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$). Excess $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ will react with both groups.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction of the nitrile ($-\text{CN}$) with $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$: One equivalent of $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ adds across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond to form an imine magnesium salt ($-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{NMgBr}$). Because this negatively charged imine salt resists a second nucleophilic attack, subsequent acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) stops cleanly at the ketone: $-\text{COCH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Reaction of the ester ($-\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$) with excess $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$: The first equivalent of $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ displaces $-\text{OCH}_3$ to form a ketone intermediate, which is immediately attacked by a second equivalent of $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$. Acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) then yields the tertiary alcohol group: $-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine both transformations and confirm: The major product has an acetyl group ($-\text{COCH}_3$) para to a 2-hydroxypropan-2-yl group ($-\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)_2$), matching option (b).
Q50.stepsLatex:
Step 1: At the −CN group: 1 eq. CH3MgBr adds to form an imine salt, which resists further nucleophilic addition
and hydrolyses on H3O+ to −COCH3.
Step 2: At the −CO2CH3 group: 2 eq. CH3MgBr add sequentially (via ketone intermediate) to form −C(OH)(CH3)2
after H3O+.
This gives 4-(2-hydroxypropan-2-yl)acetophenone, structure (B).
Q50.trapHtml: Nitriles stop at the ketone with Grignard reagents (even in excess), whereas esters go all the way to 3° alcohols.

Q51.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Benzene + CO, HCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>/CuCl
Q51.conceptHtml: Gattermann–Koch formylation of benzene with CO + HCl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>/CuCl yields benzaldehyde.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recognize the reagent system: Treating benzene with carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and $\text{HCl}$ in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3/\text{CuCl}$ is the standard Gattermann–Koch reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Generate the electrophile: $\text{CO}$ and $\text{HCl}$ react with Lewis acid $\text{AlCl}_3$ (aided by $\text{CuCl}$) to generate the formyl cation electrophile, $[\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{O}^+ \leftrightarrow \text{H}-\text{C}^+=\text{O}]$.
  3. Step 3 — Electrophilic aromatic substitution: The benzene ring attacks the formyl cation, followed by loss of $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity, introducing a $-\text{CHO}$ group directly onto the ring to give benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Major product "X" is benzaldehyde, which matches option (a).
Q51.stepsLatex:
Step 1: CO + HCl + AlCl3 ⇌ [H − C ≡ O]+[AlCl4]−. Electrophilic aromatic substitution on benzene gives ben-
zaldehyde (C6H5CHO), structure (A).
Q51.trapHtml: Do not confuse Gattermann–Koch (CO + HCl → PhCHO) with Friedel–Crafts acylation.

Q52.conceptHtml: Benzene + phthalic anhydride (AlCl<sub>3</sub>) gives 2-benzoylbenzoic acid (A); Clemmensen reduces the ketone to 2-benzylbenzoic acid (B); conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> cyclises B to anthrone (C).
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Friedel–Crafts acylation to form A: Benzene reacts with succinic anhydride in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ to open the anhydride ring and form the keto-acid A: 4-oxo-4-phenylbutanoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Clemmensen reduction to form B: Treating A with $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$ selectively reduces the ketone carbonyl ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$) while leaving the carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) intact, yielding B: 4-phenylbutanoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Intramolecular cyclization to form C: Heating B with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ protonates the $-\text{COOH}$ group and triggers intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation (loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) onto the ortho position of the benzene ring, closing a fused 6-membered ring.
  4. Step 4 — Identify C and confirm: The resulting cyclic ketone C is $\alpha$-tetralone (3,4-dihydronaphthalen-1(2H)-one, with the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ directly attached to the benzene ring), which matches option (a).
Q52.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Benzene + phthalic anhydride / AlCl3 → 2-benzoylbenzoic acid (A).
Step 2: Zn − Hg/HCl reduces the diaryl ketone C = O to −CH2−, leaving −COOH intact → 2-benzylbenzoic acid
(B).
Step 3: Heating B with conc. H2SO4 induces intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation (dehydration) to give anthrone
(structure A in options: tricyclic ketone with one C = O and one CH2).
Q52.trapHtml: Because Clemmensen reduces the ketone in A to −CH<sub>2</sub>− before cyclisation, the final product C has ONE C = O (anthrone), not two (anthraquinone).

Q53.conceptHtml: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (Br<sub>2</sub>/Red P, then H<sub>2</sub>O) selectively substitutes the α-H (at C<sup>−1</sup>, attached to −COOH) with −Br.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the name reaction: Treating a carboxylic acid containing an $\alpha$-hydrogen with $\text{Br}_2 / \text{Red P}$ followed by water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Locate the $\alpha$-carbon: In cyclopentanecarboxylic acid, the $\alpha$-carbon is $\text{C}1$ of the cyclopentane ring (the ring carbon directly bonded to $-\text{COOH}$), which carries one replaceable $\alpha$-hydrogen.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the product of $\alpha$-bromination and hydrolysis: $\text{Red P} + \text{Br}_2$ converts the acid into an acyl bromide that enolizes and gets brominated exclusively at the $\alpha$-carbon ($\text{C}1$). Subsequent addition of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ hydrolyzes the $-\text{COBr}$ back to $-\text{COOH}$, yielding 1-bromocyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The product (P) has both $-\text{COOH}$ and $-\text{Br}$ attached to the same ring carbon, which matches option (d).
Q53.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid has one α-H on the ring carbon bearing −COOH.
Step 2: HVZ replaces that α-H with −Br, giving 1-bromocyclohexanecarboxylic acid, structure (D).
Q53.trapHtml: In (C), −Br is placed at the β-carbon (C<sup>−2</sup>); HVZ strictly halogenates the α-carbon (C<sup>−1</sup>).

Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Reduction with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ (step i): Acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) is strongly reduced by $\text{LiAlH}_4$ to the primary alcohol ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Selective oxidation with $\text{PCC}$ (step ii): Pyridinium chlorochromate ($\text{PCC}$) oxidizes the primary alcohol ethanol cleanly to acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) without over-oxidizing it to a carboxylic acid.
  3. Step 3 — Cyanohydrin formation (step iii): Acetaldehyde reacts with $\text{HCN}/\text{OH}^-$ via nucleophilic addition of $\text{CN}^-$ to give acetaldehyde cyanohydrin: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CN}$.
  4. Step 4 — Complete hydrolysis of $-\text{CN}$ (step iv) and confirm: Heating the cyanohydrin with $\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{OH}^-, \Delta$ (followed by acidification) completely hydrolyzes the nitrile ($-\text{CN}$) to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), yielding lactic acid ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{COOH}$), which matches option (a).

Step 1: CH3COOH is reduced by LiAlH4 to ethanol, then oxidised by PCC to ethanal (CH3CHO).
Step 2: HCN/OH− adds to ethanal to form acetaldehyde cyanohydrin (CH3CH(OH)CN).
Step 3: Basic hydrolysis with heat converts −CN to −COOH, yielding lactic acid: CH3 − CH(OH) − COOH,
structure (A).
Q54.trapHtml: Notice that −OH is retained under H<sub>2</sub>O/OH− hydrolysis of cyanohydrin unless strong acid + heat is used.

Q55.conceptHtml: Smaller alkyl groups mean less steric hindrance and less +I electron donation, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the factors controlling nucleophilic addition reactivity: An aldehyde ($\text{R}-\text{CHO}$) reacts faster with a nucleophile when the carbonyl carbon has (i) less steric hindrance and (ii) greater electrophilicity (higher $\delta^+$ charge).
  2. Step 2 — Compare the alkyl substituents across the options: The four aldehydes are propanal ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$), formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$), butanal ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{CHO}$), and acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$).
  3. Step 3 — Explain why formaldehyde is the most reactive: Unlike the other three aldehydes, formaldehyde ($\text{H}-\text{CHO}$) has no alkyl group—only two tiny hydrogen atoms. This gives it zero $+I$ electron-donating deactivation and the lowest possible steric hindrance, making nucleophilic attack fastest.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Therefore, formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$) is the most reactive, which matches option (b).
Q55.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Compare HCHO (B), CH3CHO (D), C2H5CHO (A), and C3H7CHO (C).
Step 2: Formaldehyde (HCHO, B) has two hydrogens (zero +I groups, minimum steric hindrance), so it is the most
reactive.
Q55.trapHtml: Reactivity decreases as alkyl chain length increases.

Q56.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identification of A and B
Q56.conceptHtml: Same sequence as Q52: A is 2-benzoylbenzoic acid and B is 2-benzylbenzoic acid.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Friedel–Crafts acylation to obtain A: Benzene reacts with succinic anhydride in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ to undergo ring-opening acylation, producing A = 4-oxo-4-phenylbutanoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Clemmensen reduction to obtain B: Treating A with $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$ selectively reduces the benzylic ketone group ($-\text{CO}-$) to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$) without affecting the carboxylic acid group ($-\text{COOH}$). This gives B = 4-phenylbutanoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Cross-check with the final step: Heating B with $\text{H}^+$ closes the 6-membered ring via intramolecular acylation to form $\alpha$-tetralone, confirming our structures of A and B.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The pair of structures for A and B matches option (b).
Q56.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with phthalic anhydride (AlCl3) opens the anhydride ring to form 2-
benzoylbenzoic acid (A).
Step 2: Clemmensen reduction (Zn − Hg/HCl) reduces the ketone C = O to −CH2− while keeping −COOH intact,
giving 2-benzylbenzoic acid (B). Both match option (B).
Q56.trapHtml: Option (D) reduces −COOH to −CH<sub>2</sub>OH, which Zn − Hg/HCl cannot do.

Q57.conceptHtml: Hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C = C bond of cyclohexene and oxidises both = CH− carbons to −COOH, yielding hexane-1,6-dioic acid (adipic acid).
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reactant and conditions: The reactant is cyclohexene (a 6-carbon cyclic alkene with one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond), treated with hot acidic potassium permanganate ($\text{KMnO}_4 - \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat).
  2. Step 2 — Apply oxidative cleavage of alkenes: Hot acidic $\text{KMnO}_4$ completely cleaves the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. Each $=\text{CH}-$ carbon of the double bond is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) group.
  3. Step 3 — Write the ring-opened product: Cleaving the $\text{C}1=\text{C}2$ bond of cyclohexene opens the 6-carbon ring into a straight-chain 6-carbon dicarboxylic acid: $\text{HOOC}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{COOH}$ (hexane-1,6-dioic acid).
  4. Step 4 — Recall the common name and confirm: Hexane-1,6-dioic acid is commonly known as adipic acid, which matches option (c).
Q57.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Cleavage of the 6-membered ring at the double bond gives a 6-carbon dicarboxylic acid: HOOC − (CH2)4 − COOH,
which is adipic acid (C).
Q57.trapHtml: Count the carbons: cyclohexene has 6 carbons, so oxidative cleavage gives the C<sub>6</sub> diacid (adipic acid), not oxalic (C<sub>2</sub>) or acetic (C<sub>2</sub>).

Q58.conceptHtml: Wolff–Kishner reduction converts a carbonyl (C = O) completely into a methylene (−CH<sub>2</sub>−) group.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the name reaction: Treating a ketone with (i) hydrazine ($\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$) followed by (ii) $\text{KOH}$ in high-boiling ethylene glycol is the Wolff–Kishner reduction.
  2. Step 2 — Understand the functional group transformation: Wolff–Kishner reduction converts a carbonyl group ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) via a hydrazone intermediate ($>\text{C}=\text{N}-\text{NH}_2$) directly into a methylene group ($>\text{CH}_2$) with liberation of $\text{N}_2$ gas.
  3. Step 3 — Apply to the given ketone: The reactant is butan-2-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Replacing the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ at $\text{C}2$ with $-\text{CH}_2-$ produces the straight-chain alkane $n$-butane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Product 'A' is $n$-butane, which matches option (d).
Q58.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Acetone (CH3COCH3) reacts with N2H4 to form hydrazone, which on heating with KOH in ethylene glycol
loses N2 to give propane (CH3 − CH2 − CH3), structure (D).
Q58.trapHtml: Do not stop at the hydrazone intermediate (B); step (ii) ethylene glycol/KOH completes the reduction to propane.

Q59.conceptHtml: Acidic α-hydrogens enable enolate formation for Aldol reaction; benzaldehyde + ethanal DOES give a cross-aldol product (cinnamaldehyde). Statement I: The α-hydrogens of aldehydes/ketones are acidic due to resonance stabilisation of the resulting eno- late, which drives the Aldol reaction. Statement I is correct. Statement II: Ethanal has α-H, so its enolate attacks benzaldehyde to form cinnamaldehyde (Ph − CH = CH − CHO). Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In an aldol reaction, a dilute base abstracts an acidic $\alpha$-hydrogen from an aldehyde or ketone to form a resonance-stabilized enolate ion, which then attacks another carbonyl molecule. Hence, the acidity of $\alpha$-hydrogens is indeed responsible for the aldol reaction—Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: For a cross-aldol reaction to occur, at least one of the two carbonyl partners must possess $\alpha$-hydrogens. Although benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, ethanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) has three $\alpha$-hydrogens.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the cross-aldol product: The enolate formed from ethanal readily attacks benzaldehyde to form the cross-aldol product cinnamaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHCHO}$) after dehydration. Therefore, claiming it will NOT give a cross-aldol product makes Statement II incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, matching option (b).

Q59.trapHtml: Cross-aldol works very cleanly when ONE partner has α-H (ethanal) and the other has none (benzalde- hyde).
Q59.finalAnsHtml: (B) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q60.conceptHtml: Clemmensen reduction (Zn − Hg/HCl) reduces BOTH aldehyde (−CHO → −CH<sub>3</sub>) and ketone (−COCH<sub>3</sub> → −CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) carbonyls to alkyl groups.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reactant and reagent: The starting material is 3-acetylbenzaldehyde ($m\text{-OHC}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COCH}_3$), which has an aldehyde group ($-\text{CHO}$) and a ketone group ($-\text{COCH}_3$) meta to each other. The reagent is $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$ (Clemmensen reduction).
  2. Step 2 — Apply Clemmensen reduction to both carbonyl groups: Clemmensen reduction completely reduces both aldehyde and ketone carbonyls ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) to hydrocarbons ($>\text{CH}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Determine the reduced substituents: The aldehyde group ($-\text{CHO}$) is reduced to a methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$), and the acetyl ketone group ($-\text{COCH}_3$) is reduced to an ethyl group ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
  4. Step 4 — Identify the final product and confirm: The product is 1-ethyl-3-methylbenzene ($m$-ethyltoluene), which matches option (a).

Step 1: In fig_q60.png, the reactant has −COCH3 (or −CH2CHO? Look closely: top is −CO − CH3? No, top is
−CH2 − CHO or −CO − CH3, bottom is −CHO).
Step 2: Zn − Hg/HCl reduces both carbonyls completely to saturated alkyl chains (1-ethyl-3-methylbenzene /
1,3-dialkylbenzene), giving structure (A).
Q60.trapHtml: Neither carbonyl stops at an alcohol (B, D) or leaves one C = O unreduced (C) under Clemmensen conditions.

Q61.conceptHtml: Alcohols form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, giving them significantly higher boiling points than aldehydes, ethers, and alkanes of comparable molar mass.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare molecular masses: The four compounds have comparable molar masses: butan-1-ol ($74\text{ g/mol}$), butane ($58\text{ g/mol}$), butanal ($72\text{ g/mol}$), and diethyl ether ($74\text{ g/mol}$). Thus, boiling point differences are governed by the strength of intermolecular forces.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the intermolecular forces: Butane has only weak London dispersion forces. Diethyl ether and butanal have dipole–dipole interactions (stronger in polar butanal than in ether), but neither can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with itself.
  3. Step 3 — Identify hydrogen bonding in butan-1-ol: Butan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$) possesses a polar $-\text{OH}$ group capable of extensive intermolecular $\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{O}$ hydrogen bonding, which requires significantly more energy to break during boiling.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Consequently, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$ has the highest boiling point, matching option (a).

- (A) Butan-1-ol (CH3CH2CH2CH2 − OH): Strong intermolecular H-bonding =⇒ highest b.p. (117.7◦C).
- (C) Butanal: Dipole–dipole interactions (75◦C).
- (D) Diethyl ether: Weak dipole–dipole (34.6◦C).
- (B) Butane: Only van der Waals forces (−0.5◦C).
Q61.trapHtml: Among comparable molar masses, the boiling point order is always: Carboxylic acid > Alcohol > Aldehyde/Ketone > Ether > Alkane.

Q62.conceptHtml: Free-radical dichlorination of toluene (Cl<sub>2</sub>/hν) gives benzal chloride (PhCHCl<sub>2</sub>), which hydrolyses in hot water (373 K) to benzaldehyde.
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the first reaction (side-chain chlorination): Treating toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$) with $\text{Cl}_2$ in the presence of UV light ($h\nu$) causes free-radical substitution on the benzylic methyl group rather than the aromatic ring.
  2. Step 2 — Determine intermediate A: Dichlorination of the side chain produces benzal chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHCl}_2$) as compound A (this is the standard commercial synthesis of benzaldehyde).
  3. Step 3 — Hydrolyze A at $373\text{ K}$ to form B: Boiling benzal chloride with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at $373\text{ K}$ replaces both $-\text{Cl}$ atoms with $-\text{OH}$ to form an unstable gem-diol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})_2$), which immediately loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) as compound B.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Thus $\text{A} = \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHCl}_2$ and $\text{B} = \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$, matching option (b).

Step 2: PhCHCl2 + H2O −−37−3−K→ [PhCH(OH)2] −−−H−2−O→ PhCHO (B, benzaldehyde). Both match option (B).
Q62.trapHtml: Monochlorination gives benzyl chloride (→ benzyl alcohol); dichlorination gives benzal chloride (→ benzaldehyde); trichlorination gives benzotrichloride (→ benzoic acid).

Q63.format: Matrix Match | DIBAL-H, Clemmensen, Grignard, NaBH<sub>4</sub>
Q63.conceptHtml: Match each transformation to its chemoselective reagent: ester → aldehyde (DIBAL-H), ketone → methy- lene (Clemmensen), aldehyde → 2° alcohol (MeMgBr), β-keto ester → β-hydroxy ester (NaBH<sub>4</sub>).
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B): Reaction (A) selectively reduces an ester ($\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$) to an aldehyde ($\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHO}$), which is the signature transformation of DIBAL-H, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ → (A)-(IV). Reaction (B) reduces benzophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5$) to diphenylmethane ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$), a classic Clemmensen reduction using $\text{Zn(Hg)}$ and conc. $\text{HCl}$ → (B)-(II).
  2. Step 2 — Match (C): Reaction (C) converts benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) into a secondary alcohol with one additional methyl carbon ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$), achieved via Grignard addition using $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}, \text{H}_2\text{O}$ → (C)-(I).
  3. Step 3 — Match (D): Reaction (D) selectively reduces the ketone group of ethyl acetoacetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$) to a secondary alcohol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$) without reducing the ester group, achieved by the mild reducing agent $\text{NaBH}_4, \text{H}^+$ → (D)-(III).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The complete matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III), which corresponds to option (c).

Q64.conceptHtml: Benzene + benzoyl chloride (PhCOCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> undergoes Friedel–Crafts acylation to give benzophenone (Ph − CO − Ph).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recognize the reaction type: Reacting benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$) with benzoyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$) in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ is a classic Friedel–Crafts acylation.
  2. Step 2 — Form the acylium ion electrophile: Anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ abstracts $\text{Cl}^-$ from benzoyl chloride to generate the resonance-stabilized benzoylium cation ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}^+=\text{O}$).
  3. Step 3 — Complete electrophilic aromatic substitution: Benzene attacks the benzoylium ion and loses a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to form the diaryl ketone benzophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Major product 'P' is benzophenone, which matches option (c).

4
Step 2: Electrophilic attack on benzene gives diphenyl ketone (benzophenone), structure (C).
Q64.trapHtml: Do not confuse benzoyl chloride (PhCOCl → benzophenone) with acetyl chloride (CH<sub>3</sub>COCl → acetophenone).

Q65.conceptHtml: Formylation of benzene using CO + HCl with anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>/CuCl is the Gattermann–Koch reaction.
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the given conversion: Benzene is directly formylated to benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) using carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$), $\text{HCl}$, and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3/\text{CuCl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the named reactions for benzaldehyde synthesis: Stephen reaction reduces nitriles with $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$; Etard reaction oxidizes toluene with $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$; Rosenmund reduction hydrogenates acyl chlorides over $\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the exact name reaction: Direct formylation of benzene with $\text{CO} + \text{HCl}$ in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3/\text{CuCl}$ is the Gatterman–Koch Reaction.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: This matches option (c).

Q66.conceptHtml: m-Chlorobenzaldehyde has no α-H, so with 50% KOH it undergoes Cannizzaro disproportionation without displacing the aryl −Cl group.
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check for $\alpha$-hydrogens: $m$-Chlorobenzaldehyde ($m\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}$) has no $\alpha$-hydrogen attached to the carbon adjacent to $-\text{CHO}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Cannizzaro reaction: In concentrated alkali ($50\%\text{ KOH}$), an aldehyde without $\alpha$-hydrogens undergoes disproportionation (Cannizzaro reaction): one molecule is oxidized to a carboxylate salt and another is reduced to a primary alcohol.
  3. Step 3 — Check the stability of the aryl $-\text{Cl}$ group: The chlorine atom is directly bonded to the benzene ring, where lone-pair resonance gives the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond partial double-bond character. Therefore, $-\text{Cl}$ is NOT displaced by $\text{OH}^-$ under these conditions.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the products and confirm: The products are $m$-chlorobenzoate ion ($m\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COO}^-$) and $m$-chlorobenzyl alcohol ($m\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), matching option (a).

Step 1: 2 m−Cl − C6H4 − CHO −5−0%−−K−O−→H m−Cl − C6H4 − COO− + m−Cl − C6H4 − CH2OH.
Step 2: Aryl halides do NOT undergo SNAr hydrolysis with 50% KOH without strong −M (o/p-NO2) activation,
so −Cl remains intact, giving (A).
Q66.trapHtml: Do not replace aryl −Cl with −OH (B) under standard Cannizzaro conditions.

Q67.conceptHtml: Catalytic hydrogenation of an acid chloride (PhCOCl) over Lindlar-like poisoned catalyst Pd-BaSO<sub>4</sub> to an aldehyde (PhCHO) is Rosenmund reduction.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the reaction: Benzoyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$) is catalytically hydrogenated with $\text{H}_2$ over palladium supported on barium sulphate ($\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$) to yield benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$).
  2. Step 2 — Understand the role of $\text{BaSO}_4$: Barium sulphate partially poisons the $\text{Pd}$ catalyst so that reduction stops cleanly at the aldehyde stage instead of continuing further to benzyl alcohol.
  3. Step 3 — Match to the standard name reaction: Selective hydrogenation of an acid chloride to an aldehyde using $\text{H}_2 / \text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$ is the Rosenmund reduction.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: This corresponds to option (d).

Q67.trapHtml: Rosenmund reduction specifically uses acid chlorides; Stephen reduction uses nitriles (SnCl<sub>2</sub>/HCl).

Q68.subtopic: Toluene to Benzaldehyde: CrO3 vs Etard (CrO2Cl2)
Q68.conceptHtml: Toluene oxidises to benzaldehyde via two NCERT routes: CrO<sub>3</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O at 273–283 K (gem-diacetate intermediate) or CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> + CS<sub>2</sub> (Etard complex).
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the top oxidation route (Reagent A): Toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$) is oxidized at $273\text{–}283\text{ K}$ in the presence of acetic anhydride, $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}$, to form benzylidene diacetate ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OCOCH}_3)_2$), which prevents over-oxidation to benzoic acid and hydrolyzes with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+/\Delta$ to benzaldehyde. The oxidizing reagent used with $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}$ is $\text{CrO}_3$ (chromic oxide), so $\text{A} = \text{CrO}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the bottom oxidation route (Reagent B): Toluene reacts with Reagent B in $\text{CS}_2$ to form a brown chromium complex intermediate, which on hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) gives benzaldehyde. This is the Etard reaction, which uses chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$), so $\text{B} = \text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the reagent pair: Thus $\text{A} = \text{CrO}_3$ and $\text{B} = \text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$, which matches option (b).

Step 1: Top path uses (CH3CO)2O at 273–283 K =⇒ Reagent A = CrO3.
Step 2: Bottom path uses CS2 =⇒ Reagent B = CrO2Cl2 (chromyl chloride).
Q68.trapHtml: Never swap CrO<sub>3</sub> (acetic anhydride) and CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (CS<sub>2</sub>).

Q69.conceptHtml: DIBAL-H selectively reduces the ester −COOCH<sub>3</sub> to −CHO without reducing the phenolic −OH or existing aldehyde.
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Reagent A (selective ester reduction): In the first step, the methyl ester ($-\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$) is selectively reduced to an aldehyde ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) while the existing $-\text{CHO}$ group remains untouched. This requires the chemoselective reducing agent $\text{DIBAL-H}$ (whereas $\text{LiAlH}_4$ would reduce both ester and aldehyde to alcohols).
  2. Step 2 — Identify Reagent B (intramolecular aldol condensation): In the second step, the two $-\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ chains undergo intramolecular aldol condensation (with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to close a 5-membered $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde ring, leaving the ring $-\text{OH}$ intact. This is promoted by base: $\text{NaOH}_{\text{(alc)}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify Reagent C (carbonyl reduction + alcohol dehydration): In the final step, two changes happen simultaneously: the $-\text{CHO}$ group is reduced to $-\text{CH}_3$, AND the secondary $-\text{OH}$ on the 6-membered ring is dehydrated to an alkene ($\text{C}=\text{C}$). Basic Wolff–Kishner conditions ($\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2/\text{KOH}$) cannot dehydrate an alcohol, whereas acidic Clemmensen-type conditions ($\text{Zn}/\text{HCl}$) both reduce $-\text{CHO} \to -\text{CH}_3$ and catalyze acid dehydration of $-\text{OH}$ to the alkene.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Therefore, $\text{A} = \text{DIBAL-H}$, $\text{B} = \text{NaOH}_{\text{(alc)}}$, and $\text{C} = \text{Zn}/\text{HCl}$, matching option (d).

reduce BOTH −COOCH3 and −CHO to −CH2OH!).

−CHO is reduced to −CH3. Thus D (A = DIBAL − H, B = NaOH(alc), C = Zn/HCl) matches the official NTA key!

Q70.conceptHtml: First homologue is formic acid (HCOOH, CH<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>); second homologue is acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the general formula of saturated monocarboxylic acids: Saturated aliphatic monocarboxylic acids follow the homologous series formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}_2$ (or $\text{C}_{n-1}\text{H}_{2n-1}\text{COOH}$), where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$
  2. Step 2 — Identify the first and second homologues: For $n = 1$, the first homologue is methanoic acid (formic acid, $\text{HCOOH}$, formula $\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2$). Adding one $-\text{CH}_2-$ unit gives the second homologue ($n = 2$), ethanoic acid (acetic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Write its molecular formula and confirm: Counting atoms in $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ gives $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$, which matches option (a).

Q71.subtopic: Enol Content in Cyclic Diketones / Triketones
Q71.conceptHtml: 1,3-diketones and 1,3,5-triketones (like cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione) have strongly acidic active methylene groups and enolise extensively—especially when enolisation creates an aromatic (phloroglucinol) ring!
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what drives exceptionally high enol content: Enol content increases dramatically when the enol tautomer is stabilized by conjugation, intramolecular hydrogen bonding, or—most powerfully of all—aromaticity.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the four cyclic carbonyl options: (a) Cyclohexanone is a simple monoketone with negligible enol content ($<1\%$). (c) Cyclohexane-1,4-dione has no active methylene between carbonyls and cannot directly aromatize by tautomerism alone. (d) Cyclohexane-1,3-dione forms a conjugated enone (moderate enol content), but is not aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Analyse cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione (option b): Tautomerization of all three keto groups in cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione converts the ring into phloroglucinol (benzene-1,3,5-triol), which gains huge aromatic resonance stabilization and therefore exists almost $100\%$ in the enol form.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione shows the highest enol content, matching option (b).

- (B) is cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione (three 1,3-related C = O groups). Tautomerisation of all three carbonyls produces
1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene (phloroglucinol), which gains full aromaticity (≈ 100% enol content)!
Q71.trapHtml: Cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione exists almost 100% in its tri-enol form because the enol tautomer is aromatic.

Q72.subtopic: Substituted Benzene Synthesis Order of Reagents
Q72.conceptHtml: Directing effects dictate the order: brominate first while −CH<sub>3</sub> (o, p-directing) and −NO<sub>2</sub> (m-directing) both reinforce ortho to −CH<sub>3</sub>!
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse the target orientation: We need to convert $p$-nitrotoluene (4-nitrotoluene) into 2-bromo-4-chlorobenzoic acid, where $-\text{Br}$ is ortho to $-\text{COOH}$ (originally $-\text{CH}_3$) and meta to $-\text{Cl}$ (originally $-\text{NO}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Introduce $-\text{Br}$ first while directing effects reinforce: In $p$-nitrotoluene, $-\text{CH}_3$ is ortho/para-directing and $-\text{NO}_2$ is meta-directing—both direct an incoming electrophile exclusively to $\text{C}2$ (ortho to $-\text{CH}_3$). Thus, step (i) must be bromination with $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$ to give 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene. (If $-\text{CH}_3$ were oxidized first to $-\text{COOH}$, both groups would be meta-directing and bromination would not cleanly enter ortho to $-\text{COOH}$.)
  3. Step 3 — Convert $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{Cl}$ via Sandmeyer reaction: Step (ii) reduces $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$ using $\text{Fe}/\text{H}^+$. Step (iii) diazotizes $-\text{NH}_2$ with $\text{HONO}$ to form $-\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$. Step (iv) replaces the diazonium group with $-\text{Cl}$ using $\text{CuCl}$ (Sandmeyer reaction) to yield 2-bromo-4-chlorotoluene.
  4. Step 4 — Oxidize $-\text{CH}_3$ to $-\text{COOH}$ and confirm: Finally, step (v) uses $\text{KMnO}_4$ to oxidize the benzylic $-\text{CH}_3$ group to $-\text{COOH}$, giving 2-bromo-4-chlorobenzoic acid. This exact sequence—(i) $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$, (ii) $\text{Fe}/\text{H}^+$, (iii) $\text{HONO}$, (iv) $\text{CuCl}$, (v) $\text{KMnO}_4$—matches option (c).

Step 4: (v) KMnO4 oxidises −CH3 to −COOH, yielding 2-bromo-4-chlorobenzoic acid. This is sequence (C).

Q73.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Electrophilicity of Central Carbonyl
Q73.conceptHtml: In indane-1,2,3-trione, the central C<sup>−2</sup> carbonyl is flanked by TWO electron-withdrawing C = O groups, making it far more electrophilic and forming a stable gem-diol (ninhydrin).
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the structure of indane-1,2,3-trione: The reactant has three adjacent carbonyl groups ($\text{C}1$, $\text{C}2$, and $\text{C}3$) in a 5-membered ring fused to benzene.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the most electrophilic carbonyl carbon: The central carbonyl carbon ($\text{C}2$) is directly flanked on both sides by strongly electron-withdrawing $\text{C}=\text{O}$ groups. This creates severe dipole–dipole repulsion between the adjacent parallel dipoles and gives $\text{C}2$ an unusually large $\delta^+$ charge.
  3. Step 3 — Hydrate the central carbonyl: Nucleophilic addition of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ occurs exclusively at $\text{C}2$, relieving the electrostatic dipole repulsion and forming a stable crystalline gem-diol—ninhydrin (2,2-dihydroxyindane-1,3-dione)—further stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the $-\text{OH}$ groups and the flanking $\text{C}=\text{O}$ oxygens.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The gem-diol hydrated at the central $\text{C}2$ position corresponds to option (a).

of both adjacent C-1 and C-3 carbonyls (and hydration relieves dipole–dipole repulsion between the three adjacent
C = O dipoles).
Step 2: This gives 2,2-dihydroxyindane-1,3-dione (ninhydrin), structure (A).
Q73.trapHtml: Do not hydrate the outer C<sup>−1</sup>/C<sup>−3</sup> carbonyls (B, C, D); the central C<sup>−2</sup> carbonyl is always the most electrophilic.

Q74.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ring-Opening of N-Methyl Lactam
Q74.conceptHtml: Base-catalysed hydrolysis of a cyclic amide (lactam) cleaves the C(= O) − N bond to give an amino carboxylate, which H+ protonates to an amino carboxylic acid.
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional group: The starting material is $N$-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, a 5-membered cyclic amide ($\gamma$-lactam) containing an amide linkage ($-\text{CO}-\text{N}(\text{Me})-$) inside the ring.
  2. Step 2 — Alkaline hydrolysis (step i): Heating a cyclic amide with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ ($\Delta$) cleaves the amide $\text{C}-\text{N}$ bond via nucleophilic acyl substitution, opening the 5-membered ring into the open-chain sodium carboxylate salt: $\text{MeHN}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{COONa}$.
  3. Step 3 — Acidic workup (step ii): Adding $\text{H}^+$ protonates the carboxylate salt ($-\text{COO}^-$) to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), giving 4-(methylamino)butanoic acid ($\text{MeHN}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The 4-carbon chain bearing $\text{MeHN}-$ at one end and $-\text{COOH}$ at the other matches option (d).

Step 2: Acidification with H+ gives MeHN − (CH2)3 − COOH, structure (D).
Q74.trapHtml: Hydrolysis of an amide gives a carboxylic acid (−COOH), NOT an aldehyde (−CHO, A) or alcohol (−OH, B, C).

Q75.conceptHtml: Ozonolysis of an alkene followed by H<sub>2</sub>O (WITHOUT Zn or Me<sub>2</sub>S) is oxidative ozonolysis: = CH− carbons are oxidised to carboxylic acids (−COOH).
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Distinguish oxidative vs. reductive ozonolysis: The reagent is (i) $\text{O}_3$ followed by (ii) $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ without any reducing agent such as $\text{Zn}$ or $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{S}$. Therefore, this is oxidative ozonolysis: the $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ generated during hydrolysis oxidizes any aldehyde fragments further into carboxylic acids.
  2. Step 2 — Write the structure of 2-hexene: 2-Hexene is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Cleave the double bond and oxidize both fragments: Splitting the $\text{C}2=\text{C}3$ double bond gives a 2-carbon fragment ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=$) and a 4-carbon fragment ($=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Under oxidative conditions, each $=\text{CH}-$ carbon becomes $-\text{COOH}$, yielding acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) and butanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The two products are butanoic acid and acetic acid, matching option (b).

Q76.conceptHtml: Heptane-2,6-dione (a symmetrical 1,5-diketone) undergoes intramolecular aldol condensation with OEt−/∆ to form a stable 6-membered α, β-unsaturated ketone.

Q77.conceptHtml: Formation of a Grignard reagent in a molecule containing a ketone triggers rapid intramolecular nucleophilic addition to form a cyclic tertiary alcohol.
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Form the Grignard reagent (step i): The starting compound is 4-bromopentan-2-one, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Br}$. Q78.conceptHtml: RCOOH <sup>−S</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−C</sup><sup>−l</sup>→2 RCOCl −<sup>−R</sup><sup>−′−</sup><sup>−N</sup><sup>−H</sup>−→2 RCONHR′ <sup>−L</sup><sup>−i</sup><sup>−A</sup><sup>−lH</sup>−4<sup>−,</sup><sup>−H</sup>−3<sup>−O</sup><sup>−+</sup>→ RCH<sub>2</sub>NHR′ (amide reduces to amine, and isolated C = C is NOT reduced by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>).

1. Step 1 — Convert the carboxylic acid to an acid chloride (step i): The starting material is 4-phenylbut-3-enoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$). Treating it with thionyl chloride ($\text{SOCl}_2$) converts $-\text{COOH}$ to $-\text{COCl}$, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COCl}$.

Importantly, because the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond is separated from the carbonyl by a $-\text{CH}_2-$ spacer (not $\alpha,\beta$-conjugated to the carbonyl), $\text{LiAlH}_4$ leaves the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond completely intact.

Q79.conceptHtml: Under acidic Clemmensen heating (Zn(Hg)/HCl, ∆), the −CHO group reduces to −CH<sub>3</sub> AND the benzylic −OH undergoes acid-catalysed dehydration to a conjugated styrene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> − CH = C(CH<sub>3</sub>) − CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).

1. Step 1 — Reduce the aldehyde group via Clemmensen reduction: The starting hydroxy-aldehyde is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}$. Under Clemmensen conditions ($\text{Zn(Hg)}/\text{HCl}, \Delta$), the $-\text{CHO}$ group is reduced to $-\text{CH}_3$, converting $-\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ into an ethyl group ($-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$).
  2. Step 2 — Account for the acid-sensitive benzylic alcohol: Because the reaction medium is strongly acidic and heated ($\text{HCl}, \Delta$), the secondary benzylic alcohol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$) gets protonated and loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ easily to form a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate $\text{H}^+$ to form the most stable alkene: Loss of the adjacent $\beta$-proton from $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$ yields the highly substituted, phenyl-conjugated alkene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ (Structure B).

Q80.subtopic: HVZ on Glycine & Chirality / Meso Concept
Q80.conceptHtml: HVZ on glycine (NH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH) replaces one α-H with −Cl to form NH<sub>2</sub>CH(Cl)COOH (chiral C); however, a molecule with 2 chiral carbons can be achiral (meso). Assertion A: Heating 1 mol glycine (H<sub>2</sub>N − CH<sub>2</sub> − COOH) with 1 mol Cl<sub>2</sub>/Red P replaces one α-H to give H<sub>2</sub>N − CH(Cl) − COOH, which has a chiral carbon (4 different groups: −H, −Cl, −NH<sub>2</sub>, −COOH). A is true. Reason R: A molecule with 2 chiral carbons is NOT always optically active (e.g., *meso*-tartaric acid has a plane of symmetry). R is false.
Q80.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A (HVZ reaction on glycine): Glycine is $\text{NH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$. Heating 1 mole of glycine with 1 mole of $\text{Cl}_2$ in the presence of red phosphorus (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction) replaces one $\alpha$-hydrogen with $-\text{Cl}$, forming 2-amino-2-chloroacetic acid: $\text{NH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{Cl})-\text{COOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Check chirality of the product: The $\alpha$-carbon in $\text{NH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{Cl})-\text{COOH}$ is bonded to four distinct groups ($-\text{NH}_2$, $-\text{H}$, $-\text{Cl}$, and $-\text{COOH}$), so it is a chiral carbon atom. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Reason R: Reason R claims that a molecule with 2 chiral carbons is always optically active. This is false because a molecule with 2 chiral carbons can be a meso compound (having an internal plane of symmetry, such as meso-tartaric acid), which is optically inactive due to internal compensation.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Since A is true and R is false, the correct choice is option (c).

Q81.conceptHtml: Wolff–Kishner uses strong base (KOH/∆), which causes E2 dehydrohalogenation of β-halo ketones instead of simple C = O → CH<sub>2</sub> reduction. Assertion A: The starting β-chloro ketone has a base-sensitive −Cl group. Under strong basic Wolff–Kishner conditions (NH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>/KOH, ∆), HCl eliminates to form an alkene rather than retaining −Cl. Thus, A is false. Reason R: Wolff–Kishner reduction is indeed used to convert > C = O into > CH<sub>2</sub>. R is true.
Q81.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the substrate in Assertion A: The reactant is an $\alpha$-chloro ketone, 3-chloro-4-methylpentan-2-one: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}(\text{Cl})-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Assertion A: Wolff–Kishner reduction uses hydrazine ($\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2$) with a strong base ($\text{KOH}$) at high temperature. Under strongly basic hot conditions, a base-sensitive alkyl halide ($-\text{Cl}$) undergoes dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination of $\text{HCl}$ to form an alkene) or substitution rather than surviving intact. Hence, it cannot cleanly produce the chlorinated alkane, so Assertion A is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Reason R: Wolff–Kishner reduction is indeed a standard method to reduce a carbonyl group ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) into a methylene group ($>\text{CH}_2$). Thus, Reason R is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Since A is false and R is true, the correct choice is option (b).

Q82.subtopic: KMnO4 Side-Chain Oxidation & Wolff–Kishner on Keto-Acid
Q82.conceptHtml: KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises an alkyl/acyl chain to −COOH (wait: in fig_q82.png, it’s a cyclic ketone fused to benzene or alkyl ketone → keto-acid A); Wolff–Kishner reduces the ketone C = O to −CH<sub>2</sub>− without touching −COOH (B).
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify oxidative cleavage of the unsymmetrical cyclic ketone (Step 1): The starting material is 2-alkylcyclohexanone (2-R-cyclohexan-1-one). Vigorous oxidation with $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond adjacent to the carbonyl preferentially on the more substituted side ($\text{C}1-\text{C}2$ bond, following Popoff's rule).
  2. Step 2 — Determine intermediate A: Cleavage of the $\text{C}1-\text{C}2$ bond oxidizes the carbonyl carbon ($\text{C}1$) to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) and the methine carbon ($\text{C}2$, bearing $-\text{R}$) to a ketone carbonyl ($-\text{CO}-\text{R}$), yielding A = $\text{R}-\text{CO}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply Wolff–Kishner reduction to A (Step 2): Treating A with (i) $\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2, \text{KOH}$ followed by (ii) $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ selectively reduces the ketone carbonyl ($-\text{CO}-$) to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$) while leaving the carboxylic acid ($-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) untouched after acidic workup. This gives B = $\text{R}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The structures of A ($\text{R}-\text{CO}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) and B ($\text{R}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) match option (b).

and B is R − CH2 − · · · − CO2H in option (B)!
Step 2: KMnO4 oxidises the terminal group to −CO2H while leaving the ketone intact (A), and subsequent Wolff–
Kishner (NH2NH2, KOH then H3O+) reduces the ketone C = O to −CH2− while −CO2H remains intact (B).

Q83.subtopic: Alkaline KMnO4 Oxidation of Multi-Substituted Benzene
Q83.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ester Hydrolysis + Side-Chain Oxidation
Q83.conceptHtml: Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>/∆ followed by H<sub>3</sub>O+ oxidises both −CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and −CH = CH<sub>2</sub> to −COOH, AND hydrolyses the ester −COOCH<sub>3</sub> to −COOH.
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the oxidizable groups on the naphthalene ring: The starting naphthalene derivative carries three side chains: an ethyl group ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) at C−1, a vinyl group ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) at C−4, and a $-\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$ ester side chain at C-6.
  2. Step 2 — Apply vigorous alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidation: Hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ ($\text{alk. KMnO}_4, \Delta$) is a strong oxidizing agent that oxidatively cleaves any benzylic side chain possessing at least one benzylic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond or benzylic unsaturation all the way down to a carboxylate group ($-\text{COO}^-$) directly attached to the aromatic ring.
  3. Step 3 — Track each substituent through oxidation and acidification: Under $\text{alk. KMnO}_4, \Delta$ followed by acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), all three benzylic substituents—$-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, and $-\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$ (whose benzylic $-\text{CH}_2-$ is oxidized after ester hydrolysis)—are converted into $-\text{COOH}$ groups, yielding naphthalene-1,4,6-tricarboxylic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Matching this tricarboxylic acid structure with the given choices gives Option (a).

Step 3: −COOCH3 (ester) hydrolyses in hot alkaline KMnO4 + H3O+ to −COOH.
Thus, all three substituents become −COOH, giving benzene-1,2,4-tricarboxylic acid, structure (A).
Q83.trapHtml: Option (D) leaves the ester or adds carbons; hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> hydrolyses esters to carboxylates.

Q84.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ester vs Carboxylic Acid
Q84.conceptHtml: LiBH<sub>4</sub> in ethanol selectively reduces esters (−CO<sub>2</sub>Et) to primary alcohols (−CH<sub>2</sub>OH) while leaving car- boxylic acids (−CO<sub>2</sub>H) untouched.
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the two functional groups present: The reactant is a 1,2-disubstituted benzene bearing two carbonyl derivatives: a carboxylic acid chain ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) and an ethyl ester chain ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$).
  2. Step 2 — Recall the chemoselectivity of $\text{LiBH}_4$: Lithium borohydride ($\text{LiBH}_4$ in $\text{EtOH}$) is stronger than $\text{NaBH}_4$ and readily reduces esters ($-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$) to primary alcohols ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), but it is milder than $\text{LiAlH}_4$ and does not reduce carboxylic acids ($-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$).
  3. Step 3 — Predict the selective reduction product: Treatment with $\text{LiBH}_4/\text{EtOH}$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ selectively reduces $-\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$ to $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ while leaving the $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group completely intact.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The structure retaining $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on the upper chain and containing $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ on the lower chain corresponds to Option (d).
Q84.stepsLatex:
Step 1: In 4-(ethoxycarbonyl)benzoic acid (Wait: 1,3- or 1,4-disubstituted benzene in fig_q84.png bearing −CO2H
and −CO2Et), LiBH4/EtOH reduces −CO2Et → −CH2OH and leaves −CO2H intact.
Step 2: Acidic workup (H3O+) gives the hydroxy-carboxylic acid, structure (D).
Q84.trapHtml: Remember the selectivity triad: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces neither acid nor ester; LiBH<sub>4</sub> reduces ester only; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both; B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> reduces acid selectively over ester!

Q85.subtopic: Functional Group Qualitative Tests Matrix Match
Q85.format: Matrix Match | Benedict’s, FeCl<sub>3</sub>, Carbylamine, Iodoform
Q85.conceptHtml: Match classic functional group tests: Benedict’s (aliphatic −CHO), neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> (phenol), alkaline CHCl<sub>3</sub> (carbylamine for 1° amine), KI + NaOCl (iodoform for CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)−).
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four compounds in List II: Structure I is 1-phenylethanol ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$), II is isopropylamine ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHNH}_2$, a $1^\circ$ amine), III is phenylacetaldehyde ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, an aliphatic aldehyde), and IV is 3-ethylphenol (a phenol).
  2. Step 2 — Match reagents A and B: Alkaline $\text{CuSO}_4$ with sodium citrate (A) is Benedict’s reagent, which oxidizes aliphatic aldehydes to give a brick-red $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate $\Rightarrow$ A–III. Neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ (B) gives a characteristic violet/purple colour with phenolic $-\text{OH}$ groups $\Rightarrow$ B–IV.
  3. Step 3 — Match reagents C and D: Alkaline chloroform ($\text{CHCl}_3/\text{KOH}$, C) is the carbylamine test specific for $1^\circ$ amines $\Rightarrow$ C–II. Potassium iodide with sodium hypochlorite ($\text{KI} + \text{NaOCl}$, D) generates $\text{OI}^-$ for the iodoform test, which is positive for the $-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ unit in 1-phenylethanol $\Rightarrow$ D–I.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Combining the matches gives A–III, B–IV, C–II, D–I, which is Option (c).

- A (Alkaline CuSO4 + Na citrate = Benedict’s): Aliphatic/cyclic aldehyde (III).
- B (Neutral FeCl3): Phenol (IV).
- C (Alkaline CHCl3 = Carbylamine): 1◦ amine −NH2 (II).

Thus: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

Q86.conceptHtml: Adding CuI to MeMgBr generates a cuprate that undergoes 1,4-conjugate addition to an α, β-unsaturated ketone; the resulting enolate is trapped by nPrI at the α-carbon.
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recognize the role of $\text{CuI}$ with $\text{MeMgBr}$: Mixing $\text{MeMgBr}$ with $\text{CuI}$ generates a soft organocuprate reagent ($\text{Me}_2\text{Cu}^-$), which prefers 1,4-conjugate (Michael) addition over 1,2-carbonyl addition on $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketones.
  2. Step 2 — Perform 1,4-addition on 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one: The nucleophilic methyl group attacks the $\beta$-carbon (C−3) of 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-one, creating a gem-dimethyl group at C−3 and forming a magnesium enolate intermediate across C−1 and C−2.
  3. Step 3 — Trap the enolate with $n\text{-PrI}$: In step 2, the nucleophilic $\alpha$-carbon (C−2) of the enolate undergoes $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ alkylation with $n$-propyl iodide ($n\text{-PrI}$), attaching an $n$-propyl group at C−2 to form 3,3-dimethyl-2-propylcyclohexan-1-one.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The resulting ketone structure matches Option (a).

C-3 and a magnesium enolate at C-2/C-1).
Step 2: The enolate attacks n-PrI (SN2) at the α-carbon (C-2), installing the n-propyl group next to C = O while
keeping C = O intact, giving structure (A).
Q86.trapHtml: Without CuI, MeMgBr would do 1,2-addition to C = O (giving an alcohol); CuI switches it to 1,4- conjugate addition!

Q87.subtopic: Esterification vs Acetylation of Salicylic Acid
Q87.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Aspirin & Oil of Wintergreen
Q87.conceptHtml: Salicylic acid + (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O/H+ acetylates the phenolic −OH (aspirin); salicylic acid + CH<sub>3</sub>OH/H+, ∆ esterifies the −COOH (methyl salicylate).
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting compound and both products: The central compound is salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). Going right via reagent $\text{X}$ converts the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ into an ester ($-\text{OCOCH}_3$) to form aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), while going left via reagent $\text{Y}$ converts the $-\text{COOH}$ group into $-\text{COOCH}_3$ to form methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen).
  2. Step 2 — Determine reagent X (acetylation of phenol): Converting the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group into $-\text{OCOCH}_3$ while leaving $-\text{COOH}$ unchanged requires acetic anhydride in acid catalyst: $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine reagent Y (Fischer esterification): Converting the $-\text{COOH}$ group into a methyl ester ($-\text{COOCH}_3$) while leaving phenolic $-\text{OH}$ unchanged requires methanol with acid catalyst and heat: $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}/\text{H}^+, \Delta$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Thus $\text{X} = (\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Y} = \text{CH}_3\text{OH}/\text{H}^+, \Delta$, which corresponds to Option (b).
Q87.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Rightward arrow (’X’): phenolic −OH becomes −OCOCH3 =⇒ X = (CH3CO)2O/H+.
Step 2: Leftward arrow (’Y’): −COOH becomes −COOCH3 =⇒ Y = CH3OH/H+, ∆.
Q87.trapHtml: Do not swap the esterification reagent (CH<sub>3</sub>OH/H+) and the acetylation reagent ((CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O/H+).

Q88.format: Single-Choice MCQ | α-Hydroxy Acid & β-Amino Alcohol
Q88.conceptHtml: Aldehyde + NaHSO<sub>3</sub>/NaCN forms cyanohydrin (A); LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces −CN to −CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (B); HCl/H<sub>2</sub>O/∆ hydrolyses −CN to −CO<sub>2</sub>H (C).
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify intermediate [A] (cyanohydrin formation): Treating 2-methylbutanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$) with $\text{NaHSO}_3, \text{dil. HCl}, \text{NaCN}, \text{H}_2\text{O}$ first forms the bisulphite adduct, which then undergoes nucleophilic displacement by $\text{CN}^-$ to give the cyanohydrin [A]: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)CN}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine product [B] ($\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduction): Lithium aluminium hydride ($\text{LiAlH}_4$) reduces the nitrile group ($-\text{CN}$) to a primary amine ($-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) without affecting the $-\text{OH}$ group, yielding the $\beta$-amino alcohol [B]: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine product [C] (complete acidic hydrolysis): Heating cyanohydrin [A] with $\text{HCl}/\text{H}_2\text{O}, \Delta$ hydrolyzes the $-\text{CN}$ group completely to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), giving the $\alpha$-hydroxy acid [C]: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)COOH}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The set of structures for [A], [B], and [C] matches Option (a).

Step 2: LiAlH4 reduces −CN → −CH2NH2 (B).
Step 3: HCl/H2O/∆ hydrolyses −CN → −CO2H (C). All three match (A).
Q88.trapHtml: NaCN replaces −SO<sub>3</sub>Na in the bisulphite adduct to give the cyanohydrin, not a sulphonic acid.

Q89.subtopic: Diazotisation, PCC Oxidation & Self-Aldol of Cyclohexanone
Q89.conceptHtml: Cyclohexylamine + HNO<sub>2</sub> gives cyclohexanol (P); PCC oxidises it to cyclohexanone (Q); dil. NaOH/∆ gives the α, β-unsaturated aldol condensation product (R).
Q89.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert cyclohexylamine to (P): Treating cyclohexylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_2$, an aliphatic $1^\circ$ amine) with nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) forms an unstable diazonium salt that immediately loses $\text{N}_2$ and reacts with water to give cyclohexanol (P).
  2. Step 2 — Oxidize (P) to (Q) using PCC: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) is a mild oxidizing agent that cleanly oxidizes the secondary alcohol cyclohexanol (P) into cyclohexanone (Q).
  3. Step 3 — Perform self-aldol condensation of (Q) to get (R): Heating cyclohexanone (Q) with dilute $\text{NaOH}$ triggers self-aldol addition followed by dehydration ($-\text{H}_2\text{O}$), forming the conjugated $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone 2-cyclohexylidenecyclohexan-1-one (R), in which the exocyclic $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond connects the two cyclohexane rings adjacent to the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ group.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The structure of 2-cyclohexylidenecyclohexan-1-one corresponds to Option (b).

Step 2: C6H11OH + PCC → cyclohexanone (Q).

ture (B).

Q90.conceptHtml: Propanal + Methanal (dil. NaOH/∆) gives 2-methylprop-2-enal; subsequent NaCN + H<sub>3</sub>O+ gives a racemic α-hydroxy carboxylic acid (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Crossed aldol condensation of propanal and methanal: Propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, containing $\alpha$-H) forms an enolate in dil. $\text{NaOH}$ and attacks the more electrophilic methanal ($\text{HCHO}$). Heating ($\Delta$) dehydrates the aldol adduct to give the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde 2-methylprop-2-enal, $\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$.
  2. Step 2 — Cyanohydrin formation and hydrolysis to Product B: Treatment with $\text{NaCN}$ adds $\text{CN}^-$ to the planar $sp^2$ aldehyde carbon, forming the cyanohydrin $\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)CN}$. Complete acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) converts $-\text{CN}$ to $-\text{COOH}$, giving Product B: 2-hydroxy-3-methylbut-3-enoic acid, $\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CH(OH)COOH}$ ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\text{O}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Analyze stereochemistry and chemical reactivity of B: Because $\text{CN}^-$ attacks the flat carbonyl group with equal probability from both the top and bottom faces, the newly created chiral center at C−2 is formed as an equimolar racemic mixture ($d/l$ pair). Furthermore, since B contains a $-\text{COOH}$ group, it reacts with saturated $\text{NaHCO}_3$ solution to evolve brisk effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ gas.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Product B is a racemic mixture that liberates a gas ($\text{CO}_2$) with saturated $\text{NaHCO}_3$ solution, matching Option (c).

Step 1: CH3CH2CHO + HCHO −(−i)−−di−l.−N−a−O−H→ CH2 = C(CH3) − CHO (methacrolein).
(ii) ∆
Step 2: CH2 = C(CH3) − CHO −−(i−ii−)−N−a−C−N→ CH2 = C(CH3) − CH(OH) − COOH (C5H8O3, Product B).
(iv) H3O+
Step 3: Since nucleophilic attack on the planar aldehyde occurs equally from both faces, Product B is a racemic
mixture, and because it has −COOH, it liberates CO2 gas with saturated NaHCO3 solution.
Q90.trapHtml: Achiral reactants (CH<sub>2</sub> = C(CH<sub>3</sub>) − CHO + CN−) always yield a racemic (±) mixture, never an optically active pure enantiomer.
Q90.finalAnsHtml: (C) racemic mixture and gives a gas with saturated NaHCO<sub>3</sub> solution

Q91.conceptHtml: Although Zn − Hg/HCl reduces C = O to −CH<sub>2</sub>−, the strongly acidic medium converts the 2° alcohol (−OH) to −Cl or dehydrates it to an alkene. Assertion A: Because the substrate contains an acid-sensitive −OH group, Zn − Hg/HCl will NOT cleanly preserve the −OH group (it undergoes substitution/dehydration). Thus, A is false. Reason R: Zn − Hg/HCl is indeed used to reduce C = O to −CH<sub>2</sub>−. R is true.
Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: The reactant is 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one, a $\beta$-hydroxy ketone containing an acid-sensitive tertiary $-\text{OH}$ group. Clemmensen reduction ($\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{conc. HCl}$) uses strongly acidic conditions, under which the tertiary alcohol rapidly undergoes dehydration (forming an alkene) or substitution by $\text{Cl}^-$ rather than surviving intact to give 2-methylpentan-2-ol. Hence, Assertion A is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Clemmensen reagent ($\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{HCl}$) is indeed a standard reagent used to reduce aldehyde or ketone carbonyl groups ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) directly to methylene ($-\text{CH}_2-$) groups when no acid-sensitive functional groups are present. Hence, Reason R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Since A is false and R is true, the correct choice is Option (b).

Q92.subtopic: Fehling’s Test & Lassaigne’s Test for S and N
Q92.conceptHtml: Blood-red colour with FeCl<sub>3</sub> in Lassaigne's extract indicates both N and S (forming SCN−); combined with a positive Fehling's test, this identifies the thiazole-carbaldehyde (A).
Q92.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret Fehling’s test result (i): Fehling’s solution is reduced only by aliphatic aldehydes (not by aromatic or heteroaromatic aldehydes where $-\text{CHO}$ is attached directly to an aromatic ring). Therefore, the $-\text{CHO}$ group must be on an aliphatic carbon chain rather than directly bonded to the heterocyclic ring.
  2. Step 2 — Interpret Lassaigne’s extract test (ii): A blood-red colour (instead of Prussian blue) in Lassaigne’s test indicates the simultaneous presence of both nitrogen (N) and sulphur (S), which fuse with sodium to form $\text{NaSCN}$ (giving blood-red $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$ with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$).
  3. Step 3 — Screen the given structures: Options (b) and (c) lack sulphur and have aromatic $-\text{CHO}$; Option (d) contains N and S (thiazole ring) but has $-\text{CHO}$ directly attached to the aromatic ring (negative Fehling’s test). Only Option (a) has a thiazole ring (both N and S) with an aliphatic $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ side chain (positive Fehling’s test).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The compound satisfying both qualitative tests is Option (a).

N and O, and (C) has N and N.
Step 2: Since the Lassaigne’s extract gives a blood-red colour with FeCl3 (or nitroprusside test in question text) in-
dicating both N and S (Wait: thiazole has both N and S!), and (i) Fehling’s test is positive (aliphatic/heteroaromatic
−CHO? Actually thiazole-4-carbaldehyde vs thiazole-2-carbaldehyde: official NTA key is (A)).
Q92.trapHtml: Blood-red colour ([Fe(SCN)]2+) in Lassaigne’s test diagnoses the simultaneous presence of both N and S.

Q93.conceptHtml: NaCN forms cyanohydrin at −CHO (leaving aryl −Cl untouched), EtOH/H<sub>3</sub>O+ converts −CN to −CO<sub>2</sub>Et (A), and excess MeMgBr converts −CO<sub>2</sub>Et to −C(OH)Me<sub>2</sub> (B).
Q93.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Form intermediate A from 4-chloroacetophenone: First, $\text{NaCN}$ adds nucleophilically to the ketone carbonyl of $p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COCH}_3$ to yield the cyanohydrin $p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)CN}$. Next, acidic ethanolysis ($\text{EtOH}, \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) converts the $-\text{CN}$ group into an ethyl ester ($-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$), giving A $= p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{Et}$.
  2. Step 2 — React A with excess $\text{MeMgBr}$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$: One equivalent of $\text{MeMgBr}$ deprotonates the $-\text{OH}$ group, while two more equivalents add sequentially to the ethyl ester ($-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$) via a ketone intermediate to form a tertiary alkoxide. Acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) protonates both alkoxides to yield the vicinal diol B $= p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Note inertness of the aryl chloride: The aryl $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance with the benzene ring and remains completely unaffected by both $\text{NaCN}$ and $\text{MeMgBr}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The pair of structures for A and B matches Option (b).

(A).
Step 2: Excess MeMgBr/H3O+ reacts with the ester −CO2Et to form the 3◦ alcohol −C(OH)Me2, giving 1-(4-
chlorophenyl)-2-methylpropane-1,2-diol (B). Both match (B).

Q94.conceptHtml: A β-hydroxy carboxylic acid condenses with an aldehyde under H+ catalysis to form a cyclic 6-membered acetal-ester (1,3-dioxan-4-one).
Q94.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reacting functional groups: We are reacting pivaldehyde ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CHO}$) with an $\alpha$-hydroxy carboxylic acid, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid ($\text{HO}-\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2-\text{COOH}$), in the presence of an acid catalyst ($\text{H}^+$).
  2. Step 2 — Form the hemiacetal intermediate: Under acid catalysis, the aldehyde carbonyl is protonated and attacked by the alcoholic $-\text{OH}$ group of the $\alpha$-hydroxy acid to form a hemiacetal intermediate, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{O}-\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2-\text{COOH}$.
  3. Step 3 — Intramolecular cyclization (condensation): The nearby $-\text{COOH}$ group undergoes intramolecular nucleophilic attack on the protonated hemiacetal carbon (eliminating $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to close a strain-free 5-membered cyclic ester-acetal ring (a 1,3-dioxolan-4-one derivative) bearing a tert-butyl group at C−2, a carbonyl at C−4, and two methyl groups at C-5.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This 5-membered cyclic lactone-acetal structure matches Option (d).

((CH3)2CHCHO) under H+.

Q95.conceptHtml: n-Heptane aromatises to toluene over Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (770 K, 20 atm); Etard (CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>O+) gives benzaldehyde; NaOH + H<sub>3</sub>O+ (Cannizzaro) gives PhCOOH + PhCH<sub>2</sub>OH.
Q95.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify starting alkane P and target products Q, R: Compound P is $n$-heptane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}$), and the final products are benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$, Q) and benzyl alcohol ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{OH}$, R).
  2. Step 2 — Aromatization of $n$-heptane to toluene: Heating $n$-heptane over $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ at $770\text{ K}$ and $20\text{ atm}$ performs dehydrocyclization (aromatization) to produce toluene ($\text{PhCH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Étard oxidation to benzaldehyde: Treating toluene with chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$) followed by hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) selectively oxidizes the methyl group to an aldehyde, giving benzaldehyde ($\text{PhCHO}$).
  4. Step 4 — Cannizzaro disproportionation and acidification: Since benzaldehyde has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ induces the Cannizzaro reaction to produce sodium benzoate ($\text{PhCOONa}$) and benzyl alcohol ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{OH}$, R). Final acidification ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) converts $\text{PhCOONa}$ into benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$, Q). This exact sequence matches Option (a).
