Q96.subtopic: Stability of Acetals & Ketals in Basic Medium
Q96.conceptHtml: Acetals/ketals are stable in basic medium because alkoxide (RO−) is a poor leaving group (strong base) and cannot be displaced without acid protonation. Assertion A: Acetal/Ketal is stable in basic medium. A is true. Reason R: It states that alkoxide has a *high* leaving tendency—this is false! Alkoxide (RO−) is a *poor* leaving group, which is why protonation by acid is needed to convert −OR into −OH+R (a good leaving group). R is false.
Q96.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Acetals and ketals are geminal diethers ($\text{R}_2\text{C(OR}^\prime\text{)}_2$). Like ordinary ethers, they are completely stable toward bases, nucleophiles, and reducing agents, and hydrolyze only in aqueous acid. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Alkoxide ions ($\text{R}^\prime\text{O}^-$) are strong bases and therefore very poor leaving groups (they have a low leaving tendency, not a high leaving tendency). That poor leaving ability is precisely why bases cannot cleave acetals or ketals without prior protonation. Thus, Reason R is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Since Assertion A is true and Reason R is false, the correct choice is Option (d).

Q97.format: Statement I & II | Acid- vs Base-Sensitive Groups
Q97.conceptHtml: Clemmensen (Zn − Hg/HCl) does not reduce −COOH (and hydrolyses/protonates −CONH<sub>2</sub>? Wait: in Statement I, amide −CONH<sub>2</sub> under acidic Clemmensen is hydrolysed to −COOH while ketone → −CH<sub>2</sub>−!); Wolff–Kishner (KOH/∆) eliminates −Cl! Statement I: Under Clemmensen conditions (Zn − Hg/conc. HCl, ∆), the ketone C = O reduces to −CH<sub>2</sub>− AND the amide −CONH<sub>2</sub> hydrolyses in hot aq. HCl to −COOH. Statement I is true. Statement II: Under Wolff–Kishner conditions (KOH, ∆), the β-chloro substituent undergoes E2 elimination of HCl rather than staying intact! Thus, Statement II is false.
Q97.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze Statement I (Clemmensen reduction): The substrate is 4-oxopentanamide ($\text{H}_2\text{NCO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{COCH}_3$). Under Clemmensen reduction ($\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{conc. HCl}, \Delta$), the ketone carbonyl ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) is reduced to $-\text{CH}_2-$, and the hot concentrated aqueous $\text{HCl}$ simultaneously hydrolyzes the amide group ($-\text{CONH}_2$) into a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), giving pentanoic acid ($\text{HOOC}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze Statement II (Wolff–Kishner reduction): The substrate is an $\alpha$-chloroketone, 3-chloro-5-methylhexan-2-one. Wolff–Kishner reduction ($\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2, \text{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}, \Delta$) uses strong base at high temperature, which causes rapid dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination) of the $-\text{Cl}$ substituent to form an alkene rather than leaving the $-\text{Cl}$ intact. Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, corresponding to Option (c).

Q98.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Chemoselective Grignard on Keto-Ester vs Cyanohydrin
Q98.conceptHtml: Ketone + NaCN/HOAc forms cyanohydrin (P); EtOH/H+ converts −CN to −CO<sub>2</sub>Et, and 2 MeMgBr gives the 3° alcohol (B).
Q98.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Formation of cyanohydrin ‘P’: Treating 4-chloroacetophenone with $\text{NaCN}/\text{HOAc}$ generates $\text{HCN}$ in situ, which undergoes nucleophilic addition at the ketone carbonyl to yield the cyanohydrin P: $p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C(OH)(Me)CN}$.
  2. Step 2 — Acidic ethanolysis to ester ‘Q’: Treating cyanohydrin P with $\text{EtOH}/\text{H}^+$ converts the nitrile group ($-\text{CN}$) into an ethyl ester ($-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$), yielding the $\alpha$-hydroxy ester Q: $p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C(OH)(Me)CO}_2\text{Et}$.
  3. Step 3 — Grignard addition to give ‘R’: Reaction of the ester group in Q with $2\text{ equivalents}$ of $\text{MeMgBr}$ followed by acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) converts $-\text{CO}_2\text{Et}$ into the tertiary alcohol unit $-\text{C(OH)Me}_2$, forming the vicinal diol major product R (having $-\text{C(OH)(Me)}-\text{C(OH)Me}_2$ attached to the para-substituted benzene ring).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Matching the final tertiary diol side chain against the verified answer key gives Option (b).

Step 2 — Step (i) Crossed aldol addition with $\text{HCHO}/\text{KOH}$: Starting from isobutyraldehyde ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CHO}$, Option a), the single $\alpha$-H is abstracted by $\text{KOH}$ and attacks formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$) to yield 3-hydroxy-2,2-dimethylpropanal: $\text{HOCH}_2-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{CHO}$.

Step 3 — Steps (ii) & (iii) Cyanohydrin formation, hydrolysis, and lactonization: Treatment with alcoholic $\text{KCN}$ converts $-\text{CHO}$ into the cyanohydrin $\text{HOCH}_2-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{CH(OH)CN}$. Acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) gives the $\alpha,\gamma$-dihydroxy acid $\text{HOCH}_2-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{CH(OH)COOH}$, which spontaneously cyclizes (eliminating $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) into the 5-membered Lactone (Y).

Q100.conceptHtml: Both 1-isopropenylcyclobutanol-type/bicyclic diol or alkene precursors that rearrange under H+ to 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene (Q) give heptane-2,6-dione on ozonolysis, which undergoes intramolecular aldol to 1-(2- methylcyclopent-1-enyl)ethanone (R)? Wait: check carbon count of R!
Q100.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce alkene “Q” by retrosynthesis from “R”: Compound “R” is 1-(2-methylcyclopent-1-en-1-yl)ethanone ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$). Under alkaline reflux, this 5-membered $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated methyl ketone forms via intramolecular aldol condensation of octane-2,7-dione ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{COCH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify alkene “Q” from ozonolysis: Reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons of octane-2,7-dione into a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond reveals that “Q” is 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene.
  3. Step 3 — Trace the acid-catalyzed rearrangement of “P” to “Q”: Treating isopropenylcyclopentane (Option a) with $\text{H}^+$ protonates the exocyclic double bond to form the $3^\circ$ 2-cyclopentylpropan-2-yl carbocation. Ring expansion from 5-membered to 6-membered (1,2-alkyl shift) relieves angle strain to form a 2,2-dimethylcyclohexyl cation, which undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the $3^\circ$ 1,2-dimethylcyclohexyl cation and loses $\text{H}^+$ to yield 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene (“Q”).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, isopropenylcyclopentane is a valid structure for “P”, confirming Option (a).

Q101.format: Match List I with List II | HVZ, Iodoform, Etard, Gattermann–Koch
Q101.conceptHtml: Note: Classified under the Multi/Extra section in source metadata (single correct option B). Match HVZ (Br<sub>2</sub>/Red P), Iodoform (NaOH + I<sub>2</sub>), Etard (CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>/CS<sub>2</sub>), Gattermann–Koch (CO, HCl, AlCl<sub>3</sub>).
Q101.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction): The HVZ reaction introduces a halogen at the $\alpha$-position of carboxylic acids using $\text{Br}_2/\text{red phosphorus}$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ $\Rightarrow$ A–III.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (Iodoform reaction): Methyl ketones and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ alcohols form yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ precipitate with $\text{NaOH} + \text{I}_2$ $\Rightarrow$ B–I.
  3. Step 3 — Match C (Étard reaction) and D (Gatterman–Koch reaction): The Étard reaction oxidizes toluene to benzaldehyde using (i) $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2, \text{CS}_2$ (ii) $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ $\Rightarrow$ C–II. The Gatterman–Koch formylation of benzene uses $\text{CO}, \text{HCl}, \text{anhyd. AlCl}_3$ $\Rightarrow$ D–IV.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Combining the matches gives A–III, B–I, C–II, D–IV, which is Option (b).

Q102.conceptHtml: Benzaldehyde (x) + Acetophenone (y) in alkali/heat undergo Claisen–Schmidt condensation to form chalcone (z = Ph − CH = CH − CO − Ph).
Q102.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify products $x$ and $y$: Reacting benzene with $\text{CO} + \text{HCl}$ in the presence of $\text{CuCl}$ (Gatterman–Koch reaction) gives $x$ = benzaldehyde ($\text{PhCHO}$). Reacting benzene with ethanoyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$) and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ (Friedel–Crafts acylation) gives $y$ = acetophenone ($\text{PhCOCH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Form product $z$ via Claisen–Schmidt condensation: Heating benzaldehyde ($x$) and acetophenone ($y$) in alkali causes crossed aldol condensation followed by dehydration to yield benzalacetophenone (chalcone, $z$): $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CO}-\text{Ph}$.
  3. Step 3 — Count total $\pi$ bonds and $\pi$ electrons in $z$: Chalcone contains $2$ benzene rings ($2 \times 3 = 6\ \pi$ bonds), $1$ alkene $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond ($1\ \pi$ bond), and $1$ carbonyl $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond ($1\ \pi$ bond), giving $6 + 1 + 1 = 8\ \pi$ bonds. Since each $\pi$ bond has $2$ electrons, total $\pi$ electrons $= 8 \times 2 = 16$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The total number of $\pi$ electrons in $z$ is 16.

Q103.conceptHtml: Benzene → Toluene → 4-Chlorotoluene → 4-Chlorobenzoic acid (X); 11.2 dm3 CO<sub>2</sub> at STP = 0.5 mol =⇒ 0.5 mol of (X).
Q103.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Trace the reaction sequence to major product (X): (i) Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene ($\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}/\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3$) gives toluene ($\text{PhCH}_3$). (ii) Electrophilic chlorination ($\text{Cl}_2/\text{FeCl}_3$) gives $p$-chlorotoluene as the major product (para-favoured over ortho due to lower steric hindrance). (iii) Vigorous oxidation ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) oxidizes the methyl group to $-\text{COOH}$, yielding $p$-chlorobenzoic acid (X) ($\text{Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COOH}$, formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Cl}$).
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the molar mass of (X): $M(\text{X}) = 7(12) + 5(1) + 2(16) + 35.5 = 84 + 5 + 32 + 35.5 = 156.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Relate moles of $\text{CO}_2$ gas to moles of (X): One mole of monoprotic carboxylic acid (X) reacts with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to liberate $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ ($22.4\text{ dm}^3$ at STP). For $11.2\text{ dm}^3$ of $\text{CO}_2$ at STP, $n(\text{CO}_2) = \frac{11.2}{22.4} = 0.5\text{ mol}$, so $n(\text{X}) = 0.5\text{ mol}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute mass $P$ and confirm the answer: $P = 0.5\text{ mol} \times 156.5\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 78.25\text{ g}$, which rounds to the nearest integer 78.

Q104.conceptHtml: 1 g of gas Q occupying 1.4 dm3 at STP has molar mass 22.4/1.4 = 16 g/mol (CH<sub>4</sub>), so P is CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr and Z is CH<sub>3</sub>COOH.

Q105.conceptHtml: PhCOCH<sub>3</sub> <sup>−P</sup><sup>−C</sup><sup>−l</sup>→<sup>5</sup> PhCCl<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> <sup>−N</sup>−<sup>−aN</sup><sup>−H</sup>−→<sup>2</sup> PhC ≡ C<sup>−</sup> <sup>−H</sup><sup>−+</sup>→ PhC ≡ CH <sup>−B</sup><sup>−2</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−6</sup><sup>−/</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−2O</sup>−→<sup>2</sup> PhCH<sub>2</sub>CHO (D).

Q106.conceptHtml: 2 PhCHO + CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> → PhCH = CHCOCH = CHPh (dibenzalacetone, M = 234 g/mol).
Q106.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the balanced Claisen–Schmidt reaction: $2\,\text{PhCHO} + \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{OH}^-} \text{PhCH}=\text{CH}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}=\text{CHPh}\ (\text{dibenzalacetone}) + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus, $2\text{ mol}$ of benzaldehyde produce $1\text{ mol}$ of dibenzalacetone ($\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$).

Step 2 — Calculate moles of benzaldehyde and theoretical moles of product: Molar mass of benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}$) $= 106\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, so $n(\text{PhCHO}) = \frac{5.3}{106} = 0.05\text{ mol}$. Theoretical moles of dibenzalacetone $= \frac{0.05}{2} = 0.025\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute theoretical yield and percentage yield: Molar mass of dibenzalacetone ($\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$) $= 17(12) + 14(1) + 16 = 234\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Theoretical mass $= 0.025 \times 234 = 5.85\text{ g}$. Percentage yield $= \frac{3.51}{5.85} \times 100 = 60\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The percentage yield of the reaction is 60.

1. Step 1 — Side-chain oxidation to A and acidification to B: Heating $n$-propylbenzene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) with alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ ($\text{KMnO}_4-\text{KOH}, \Delta$) oxidizes the entire alkyl side chain down to potassium benzoate A ($\text{Ph}-\text{COOK}$). Acidification with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ gives benzoic acid (B), $\text{Ph}-\text{COOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Electrophilic bromination to C: Since the $-\text{COOH}$ group is strongly electron-withdrawing and meta-directing, treating benzoic acid (B) with $\text{Br}_2/\text{FeBr}_3$ gives $m$-bromobenzoic acid (C).
  3. Step 3 — Count $\pi$ bonds in C and confirm the answer: $m$-Bromobenzoic acid has $3\ \pi$ bonds inside the benzene ring and $1\ \pi$ bond in the $-\text{COOH}$ carbonyl group, giving $3 + 1 = 4\ \pi$ bonds. The final answer is 4.

Q109.conceptHtml: 2 PhCHO (2 × 10<sup>6</sup> = 212 g) + CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> (58 g) → Dibenzalacetone (234 g).
Q109.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the stoichiometric equation: $2\,\text{PhCHO} + \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{OH}^-} \text{PhCH}=\text{CH}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}=\text{CHPh}\ (\text{dibenzalacetone}) + 2\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate moles of dibenzalacetone and verify acetone: Molar mass of dibenzalacetone ($\text{C}_{17}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$) $= 234\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, so $n(\text{dibenzalacetone}) = \frac{351}{234} = 1.5\text{ mol}$. Checking acetone ($M = 58\text{ g mol}^{-1}$): $\frac{87}{58} = 1.5\text{ mol}$, which is an exact $1:1$ match.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate required mass of benzaldehyde: Since $2\text{ mol}$ of benzaldehyde are needed per mole of dibenzalacetone, $n(\text{PhCHO}) = 2 \times 1.5 = 3.0\text{ mol}$. With $M(\text{PhCHO}) = 106\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, mass required $= 3.0 \times 106 = 318\text{ g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The amount of benzaldehyde required is 318.

Q110.conceptHtml: Vanillin is 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>): 3 oxygen atoms and 4 π bonds (8 π electrons).
Q110.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the structure of vanillin: Vanillin is 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde, which has a benzene ring bearing $-\text{CHO}$ at C−1, $-\text{OCH}_3$ at C−3, and $-\text{OH}$ at C−4 (molecular formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Count oxygen atoms and $\pi$ electrons: Vanillin contains $3$ oxygen atoms (one each in $-\text{CHO}$, $-\text{OH}$, and $-\text{OCH}_3$). It has $4\ \pi$ bonds ($3$ in the benzene ring $+ 1$ in the $-\text{CHO}$ carbonyl), corresponding to $4 \times 2 = 8\ \pi$ electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the sum and confirm the answer: Total sum $= 3\ (\text{oxygen atoms}) + 8\ (\pi\text{ electrons}) = 11$. The final answer is 11.

Q111.format: Numerical Value | Friedel–Crafts, Rosenmund, Gattermann–Koch, Amide Hydrolysis
Q111.conceptHtml: Inspect each of the 4 reactions (A)–(D) in fig_q111.png for exact product correctness.
Q111.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check reactions (A) and (B): In (A), Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with $\text{PhCOCl}/\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3$ gives benzophenone ($\text{Ph}-\text{CO}-\text{Ph}$), not diphenylmethane ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{Ph}$) $\Rightarrow$ Incorrect. In (B), Rosenmund reduction of $\text{PhCOCl}$ with $\text{H}_2/\text{Pd}-\text{BaSO}_4$ gives benzaldehyde ($\text{PhCHO}$), not benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$) $\Rightarrow$ Incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Check reactions (C) and (D): In (C), benzene treated with $\text{CO}, \text{HCl}$ in the presence of $\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3/\text{CuCl}$ (Gatterman–Koch reaction) indeed yields benzaldehyde ($\text{PhCHO}$) $\Rightarrow$ Correct. In (D), acidic hydrolysis of benzamide ($\text{PhCONH}_2$) with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+, \Delta$ yields benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$), not aniline ($\text{PhNH}_2$) $\Rightarrow$ Incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Only reaction (C) is correct, so the number of correct reactions is 1.

Q112.format: Numerical Value | Acid–Base vs Nucleophilic Addition
Q112.conceptHtml: With only 1 equivalent of PhMgBr, the acidic phenolic −OH protonates PhMgBr instantaneously, leaving the −CHO untouched; NH<sub>4</sub>Cl restores the original phenol.
Q112.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare acidity vs. electrophilicity in 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde: The substrate ($p\text{-HO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}$) contains an acidic phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group alongside an aldehyde $-\text{CHO}$ group. Grignard reagents ($\text{PhMgBr}$) are very strong bases, so acid–base proton transfer occurs much faster than nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl.
  2. Step 2 — Track the 1 equivalent of $\text{PhMgBr}$: The single equivalent of $\text{PhMgBr}$ is completely consumed in deprotonating the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group to form $p\text{-BrMgO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, leaving no Grignard reagent to attack the $-\text{CHO}$ group.
  3. Step 3 — Aqueous workup and hydroxyl count: Treating the phenoxide intermediate with $\text{aq. NH}_4\text{Cl}$ simply re-protonates the phenoxide back to the starting material, 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde (P), which contains only $1$ hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) group.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The number of hydroxyl groups in product P is 1.

Step 3: Number of −OH groups in P = 1.
Q112.trapHtml: Acid–base reaction with phenolic −OH is much faster than nucleophilic addition to −CHO; 2 equivalents of Grignard would be needed to form a diol.

Q113.conceptHtml: Ethanal + semicarbazide (H<sub>2</sub>N − NH − CO − NH<sub>2</sub>) gives ethanal semicarbazone (CH<sub>3</sub> − CH = N − NH − CO − NH<sub>2</sub>).
Q113.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the reaction of ethanal with semicarbazide: Ethanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) condenses with semicarbazide ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}_2$) with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to form ethanal semicarbazone: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the nitrogen atoms in the product: Examining $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{NH}_2$, all three nitrogen atoms from semicarbazide remain in the semicarbazone product (one imine $=\text{N}-$, one hydrazine $-\text{NH}-$, and one amide $-\text{NH}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The compound contains 3 nitrogen atoms.

Q114.subtopic: Sigma & Pi Bond Counting in 2-Formylhex-4-enoic Acid
Q114.conceptHtml: Draw the full structure: CH<sub>3</sub> − CH = CH − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH(CHO) − COOH (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
Q114.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Draw the structure and molecular formula: 2-Formylhex-4-enoic acid has the structure $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(CHO)}-\text{COOH}$. Counting all atoms gives $7\text{ C}$, $10\text{ H}$, and $3\text{ O}$, so its molecular formula is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_3$ ($20$ atoms total).
  2. Step 2 — Count $\sigma$ bonds (acyclic shortcut): For any acyclic (open-chain) molecule with $N$ total atoms, the number of $\sigma$ bonds is $N - 1 = 20 - 1 = 19\ \sigma$ bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Count $\pi$ bonds and sum them: There are $3\ \pi$ bonds in total: $1$ in the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, $1$ in the formyl $-\text{CHO}$ carbonyl, and $1$ in the carboxylic acid $-\text{COOH}$ carbonyl. Total bonds $= 19\ \sigma + 3\ \pi = 22$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The total number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds is 22.

Step 2: π bonds: 1 (C = C) +1 (−CHO) +1 (−COOH) = 3.
Step 3: Total (σ + π) = 19 + 3 = 22.
Q114.trapHtml: For any acyclic molecule, σ bonds = total atoms − 1; always draw out −CHO and −COOH to count π bonds accurately.

Q115.format: Numerical Value | Aliphatic vs Aromatic Aldehydes
Q115.conceptHtml: Fehling’s solution oxidises aliphatic aldehydes only; it does NOT oxidise aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde, 4-nitrobenzaldehyde) or ketones (acetone, acetophenone).
Q115.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the scope of Fehling’s test: Fehling’s reagent (alkaline $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ tartrate complex) is a mild oxidant that gives a positive brick-red $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate only with aliphatic/alicyclic aldehydes. Aromatic aldehydes and all simple ketones give a negative test.
  2. Step 2 — Classify all seven given compounds: (1) Benzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde) $\to$ Negative; (2) Acetaldehyde (aliphatic aldehyde) $\to$ Positive; (3) Acetone (ketone) $\to$ Negative; (4) Acetophenone (ketone) $\to$ Negative; (5) Methanal (aliphatic aldehyde) $\to$ Positive; (6) 4-Nitrobenzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde) $\to$ Negative; (7) Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (alicyclic/aliphatic aldehyde) $\to$ Positive.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Exactly $3$ compounds give a positive Fehling’s test, so the final answer is 3.

- Negative (4): Benzaldehyde, 4-Nitrobenzaldehyde (aromatic aldehydes), Acetone, Acetophenone (ketones).
Count = 3.
Q115.trapHtml: Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde has a saturated cyclohexane ring (aliphatic!), so it DOES give a positive Fehling’s test, unlike benzaldehyde.

Q116.conceptHtml: Strecker synthesis converts 4-ethoxybenzylacetaldehyde to the α-amino acid; nitration, acetylation, esteri- fication, reduction, diazotisation-HNO<sub>2</sub>/NaI? Let’s trace the carbon count x carefully!
Q116.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Strecker synthesis to A and dinitration to B: Starting from $p\text{-H}_5\text{C}_2\text{O}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ ($10$ carbons), Strecker synthesis with (i) $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}/\text{KCN}$ and (ii) $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4/\text{H}^+$ converts $-\text{CHO}$ into $-\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)COOH}$, giving A ($11$ carbons). Dinitration with $2\text{ eq. conc. HNO}_3-\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ installs two $-\text{NO}_2$ groups ortho to $-\text{OEt}$, giving B (still $11$ carbons).
  2. Step 2 — Acetylation and esterification (carbon-adding steps): Step (i) $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}$ acetylates $-\text{NH}_2$ to $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ ($+2$ carbons $\to 13\text{ C}$). Step (ii) $\text{EtOH}, \Delta$ esterifies $-\text{COOH}$ to $-\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5$ ($+2$ carbons $\to 15\text{ C}$).
  3. Step 3 — Reduction, diazotization, and iodination to D: Step (iii) $\text{H}_2/\text{Pd-C}$ reduces both $-\text{NO}_2$ groups to $-\text{NH}_2$; step (iv) $\text{HNO}_2$ diazotizes both aryl $-\text{NH}_2$ groups (while the amide $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ stays protected); step (v) $\text{NaI}$ replaces both $-\text{N}_2^+$ groups with $-\text{I}$. None of these three steps changes the carbon count!
  4. Step 4 — Verify formula and confirm the answer: Product D is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{I}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NHCOCH}_3\text{)COOC}_2\text{H}_5$, whose molecular formula is $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{19}\text{NO}_4\text{I}_2$. Comparing with $\text{C}_x\text{H}_{19}\text{NO}_4\text{I}_2$ gives $x =$ 15.

Step 2: (i) NH4Cl/KCN + (ii) H2SO4/H+ (Strecker) adds 1 carbon (−COOH), giving 11 carbons (A).
Step 3: Nitration (2 eq. HNO3) adds two −NO2 groups (B, 11 carbons).

Step 5: (iii) H2, Pd/C reduces −NO2 to −NH2; (iv) HNO2 + (v) NaI replaces both −NH2 with −I (0 carbons
added).
Thus, compound D has x = 15 carbons!

Q117.conceptHtml: In Tollens’ test, 1 mol of aldehyde reacts with 2 mol of [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]+ to release 4 mol of NH<sub>3</sub>.
Q117.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the balanced Tollens’ test equation: $\text{RCHO} + 2[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+ + 3\text{OH}^- \to \text{RCOO}^- + 2\text{Ag}\downarrow + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus, $1\text{ mol}$ of aldehyde produces $4\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate moles of cyclohexanecarbaldehyde: Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{CHO} = \text{C}_7\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$) has molar mass $M = 7(12) + 12(1) + 16 = 112\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Moles in $131.8\text{ kg}$ $= \frac{131.8\text{ kg}}{112\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1.1768\text{ kmol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute mass of $\text{NH}_3$ produced: Moles of $\text{NH}_3 = 4 \times 1.1768\text{ kmol} = 4.7071\text{ kmol}$. With $M(\text{NH}_3) = 17\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, mass of $\text{NH}_3 = 4.7071 \times 17 = 80.02\text{ kg}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Rounding to the nearest integer gives 80.

Step 2: Molar mass of cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (C7H12O) = 7(12) + 12(1) + 16 = 112 g/mol.
Step 3: Moles of aldehyde = 131.8 kg/112 g/mol = 1.1768 kmol.
Step 4: Moles of NH3 = 4 × 1.1768 = 4.707 kmol.
Mass of NH3 = 4.707 × 17 kg = 80.02 kg ≈ 80 kg.

Q119.format: Numerical Value | 2,4-DNP Negative + Hydrogenation to Identical C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O
Q119.conceptHtml: Insoluble in NaOH (no phenol/acid) and HCl (no amine), negative 2,4-DNP (no aldehyde/ketone) =⇒ unsaturated cyclic/aryl ether or alcohol; hydrogenation adds 1 mol H<sub>2</sub> to give identical C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O.
Q119.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate DBE and interpret solubility/2,4-DNP clues: For $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, $\text{DBE} = 9 - \frac{10}{2} + 1 = 5$ (one benzene ring $= 4$ plus one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond $= 1$). Insolubility in $\text{NaOH}$ rules out phenols/carboxylic acids, insolubility in $\text{HCl}$ confirms no basic group, and a negative 2,4-DNP test rules out aldehydes and ketones. Thus, the oxygen must be an aliphatic alcohol (or ether).
  2. Step 2 — Use the hydrogenation clue to identify the isomers: Absorption of $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$ converts $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ into a single identical $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ alcohol. This fits the pair of geometrical isomers cis-cinnamyl alcohol and trans-cinnamyl alcohol ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), both of which hydrogenate to the exact same compound, 3-phenylpropan-1-ol ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: There are 2 such isomeric compounds.

Step 2: Hydrogenation (H2) reduces the side-chain C = C to give identical C9H12O (e.g., propyl phenyl ether
Ph − O − CH2CH2CH3 or 3-phenylpropan-1-ol).
Step 3: The two isomers that give the exact same hydrogenated product are cis and trans isomers of the C = C
double bond (e.g., *cis*- and *trans*-cinnamyl alcohol or propenyl phenyl ether) — wait: or 1-propenyl vs allyl?
Actually, allyl phenyl ether (Ph − O − CH2 − CH = CH2) + *cis/trans*-propenyl phenyl ether, or 2 stereoisomers
(cis/trans) = 2 compounds! (Official NTA key = 2).
Q119.trapHtml: Remember geometric (*cis*/*trans*) isomers count as distinct isomeric compounds when counting structures.

Q121.subtopic: Solubility in Cold NaHCO3/NaOH vs Hot NaOH (Esters &
Q121.conceptHtml: Carboxylic acids dissolve in cold NaHCO<sub>3</sub> and NaOH; phenols dissolve in cold NaOH; esters and lactones are neutral in cold base but dissolve in hot NaOH via saponification!
Q121.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify which functional group matches the solubility profile: Compounds that do not dissolve in cold $\text{NaHCO}_3$ (rules out carboxylic acids) or cold $\text{NaOH}$ (rules out phenols), yet do dissolve in hot $\text{NaOH}$, are esters—they are neutral in cold base but undergo alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) in hot $\text{NaOH}$ to form water-soluble sodium carboxylates and alcohols/phenoxides.
  2. Step 2 — Classify all seven given structures: (1) $p$-Toluic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) dissolves in cold $\text{NaHCO}_3$ and $\text{NaOH}$ (Excluded); (2) Methyl benzoate (ester) $\to$ Qualifies (1); (3) $p$-Tolyl formate (ester) $\to$ Qualifies (2); (4) 2-Hydroxyacetophenone (phenol) dissolves in cold $\text{NaOH}$ (Excluded); (5) 3-Hydroxy-5-methylbenzaldehyde (phenol) dissolves in cold $\text{NaOH}$ (Excluded); (6) 3-Isopropylanisole (ether) is insoluble even in hot $\text{NaOH}$ (Excluded); (7) Phenyl acetate (ester) $\to$ Qualifies (3).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The $3$ esters (methyl benzoate, $p$-tolyl formate, and phenyl acetate) satisfy the condition, confirming 3.
Q121.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Inspect the 8 structures in fig_q121.png:
- Carboxylic acids & phenols dissolve in cold NaOH (excluded).
- Simple ketones/aldehydes/ethers do not dissolve even in hot NaOH (excluded).
- Esters and lactones (3 compounds in the set) do not dissolve in cold NaHCO3/NaOH, but undergo saponification
in hot NaOH to form soluble carboxylate salts.
Count = 3.
Q121.trapHtml: Esters and lactones are neutral at room temperature but dissolve in hot NaOH via hydrolysis (saponifi- cation).

Q122.conceptHtml: Positive FeCl<sub>3</sub> + methylation (+CH<sub>2</sub>) =⇒ 1 phenolic −OH; HI → CH<sub>3</sub>I =⇒ 1 −OCH<sub>3</sub>; alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> decolorisation =⇒ 1 C = C double bond (allyl → propenyl isomerisation in hot conc. NaOH).
Q122.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce functional groups of ‘A’ ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$): First compute $\text{DBE} = 10 - \frac{12}{2} + 1 = 5$. A positive neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ test and methylation with $\text{NaOH}/\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2 \to \text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$, $+\text{CH}_2$) confirm $1$ phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group. Reaction with $\text{HI}$ giving $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ confirms $1$ methoxy ($-\text{OCH}_3$) group.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the third substituent and compound ‘A’: Decolorization of alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ confirms an alkene $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond (accounting for the 5th DBE alongside the benzene ring’s 4 DBE). Isomerization with hot conc. $\text{NaOH}$ to isomer B ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$) is the classic base-catalyzed allyl-to-propenyl shift converting eugenol (4-allyl-2-methoxyphenol, A) into isoeugenol (B).
  3. Step 3 — Count $\pi$ bonds in ‘A’ and confirm the answer: Eugenol contains $3\ \pi$ bonds in the benzene ring and $1\ \pi$ bond in the allylic $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ side chain, giving $3 + 1 = 4\ \pi$ bonds. The final answer is 4.

Step 1: DBE of C10H12O2 = 10 + 1 − 12/2 = 5.
Step 2: Compound ’A’ is eugenol (4-allyl-2-methoxyphenol): 1 benzene ring (3 π bonds) +1 allyl C = C (1 π bond)
= 4 π bonds. (Hot conc. NaOH isomerises eugenol to isoeugenol, C10H12O2!).
Q122.trapHtml: Use DBE = C + 1 − H/2 = 5: 1 ring +4 π bonds = 5, so there are exactly 4 π bonds.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Tollens’ vs Fehling’s vs Iodoform Distinc- tions
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Assuming benzaldehyde gives Fehling’s test, or that CH3COOH / 3-pentanone / HCOOH give iodoform. The Fix:
  • Fehling’s Test: Positive ONLY for aliphatic aldehy- des (including cyclohexanecarbaldehyde) and α-hydroxy ketones (fructose). Benzaldehyde (ArCHO) is NEG- ATIVE (Q13, Q47, Q115).
  • Tollens’ Test: Positive for ALL aldehydes (aliphatic + aromatic), HCOOH, and cyclic hemiacetals (NOT ac- etals/ketals; Q16, Q49).
  • Iodoform Test: Requires CH3CO− or CH3CH(OH)−. Negative: CH3COOH, esters, 3-pentanone, 2- methylbutan-2-ol, HCOOH (Q17, Q18, Q28, Q118).

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Aldol, Cross-Aldol & Cannizzaro Stoi- chiometry
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Counting 4 cross-aldol products when one alde- hyde lacks α-H, or missing the 2 : 1 stoichiometry in Claisen– Schmidt. The Fix:
  • Cross-Aldol: Four products form ONLY if both carbonyls have α-H (Q14, Q19). With PhCHO + CH3CHO/acetone, a single major cross-product forms (Q21, Q59).
  • Intramolecular Aldol: 1,5- and 1,6-dicarbonyls cyclise to 6- or 5-membered α, β-unsaturated rings (Q06, Q26, Q43, Q76).
  • Cannizzaro: PhCOCHO undergoes intramolecular Can- nizzaro to mandelate PhCH(OH)COO− (Q31). Excess HCHO + RCH2CHO gives polyols (Q45).
  • Dibenzalacetone: 2 PhCHO + 1 Acetone (9 π bonds; Q106, Q107, Q109).

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Clemmensen vs Wolff–Kishner vs Hydrides
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Ignoring acid/base sensitivity of −OH, −Cl, or −CONH2 during carbonyl deoxygenation, or mixing up NaBH4 and LiBH4. The Fix:
  • Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl, ∆): Dehydrates/substitutes −OH (Q79, Q91) and hydrolyses −CONH2 to −COOH (Q97); leaves −COOH/lactones intact (Q37).
  • Wolff–Kishner (N2H4/KOH, ∆): Eliminates base- sensitive β-Cl (Q81, Q97); safe for −OH and −COOH (Q82).
  • Hydride Selectivity: NaBH4 reduces aldehyde/ketone only (Q01, Q63); LiBH4 reduces ester over −COOH (Q84); DIBAL-H stops ester/nitrile at −CHO (Q63, Q69).

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Acid Derivatives, NaHCO<sub>3</sub> & Counting Traps
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Confusing phenol vs picric acid with NaHCO3, miscounting π bonds vs π electrons, or forgetting 1 eq. Grignard acid–base quench. The Fix:
  • NaHCO3 Test: Positive for RCOOH and picric acid; negative for simple phenols (Q15, Q40). Esters/lactones dissolve only in hot NaOH (Q121).
  • Hydrolysis Rate: RCOCl > (RCO)2O > RCOOR′ > RCONH2 (Q36).
  • 1 Eq. Grignard: Acidic −OH quenches 1 eq. RMgBr before −CHO can react (Q112).
  • Counting: Read π electrons vs π bonds carefully (Q102, Q110), and remember 1 mol RCHO → 4 mol NH3 in Tollens’ (Q117).

title: Compounds Containing Nitrogen (Amines & Diazonium)
constantsHtml:
• Compounds Containing Nitrogen (Amines & Diazonium)
  • High-Yield NTA JEE Main 2023–2026 Exam Intelligence (99 PYQs: 80 MCQs + 19 Numericals)
  • Compounds Containing Nitrogen (Amines & Diazonium Salts) is one of the highest-scoring chapters in Organic
  • Chemistry II, contributing 1–2 questions per shift (4–8 marks). Across 2023–2026 JEE Main papers, over 85% of questions
  • cluster around five core pillars: (1) Preparation & Scope Limits (Gabriel phthalimide for 1° aliphatic/benzylic amines
  • only; Hoffmann bromamide 4 NaOH + 1 Br2 step-down; reduction of −NO2, −CN, −CONH2), (2) Aqueous & Gas-Phase
  • Basicity (2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 for Me vs 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3 for Et; pKb values; arylamine +M/−M and ortho effects), (3)
  • Chemical Distinction Tests (Hinsberg PhSO2Cl alkali solubility; Carbylamine CHCl3/KOH for 1° amines only; HNO2),
  • (4) Diazonium Salt Chemistry (stability, Sandmeyer, Gattermann, Balz–Schiemann, H3PO2/EtOH deamination, KI,
  • azo dye coupling), and (5) Electrophilic Substitution of Aniline (acetylation protection for p-bromoaniline, nitration
  • meta-product anomaly, no Friedel–Crafts).

formulaCards.title: 1. Preparation of Amines (Scope & Stoichiometry)
formulaCards.html:
• Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis: Ph- thalimide −K−O−H→ K-phthalimide −R−−−X→ N-alkylphthalimide −N−a−O−H−(−a−q)−−or−−N−2−H→4 R − NH (1◦ 2 amine). – Strict Scope: Yields only 1◦ aliphatic or ben- zylic amines (PhCH2NH2). Cannot prepare ary- lamines (aniline) or 2◦/3◦ amines because Ar − X does not undergo SN2 easily.
  • Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation: R − CONH2 + Br2 + 4 NaOH −→ R − NH2 + Na2CO3 + 2 N – Consumes 1 mol Br2 + 4 mol NaOH (or KOH) per mol 1◦ amide. – Product amine has 1 carbon less than amide; works for both alkyl and aryl 1◦ amides (PhCONH2 → PhNH2). Fails for 2◦/3◦ amides. – Retention of configuration at migrating chiral car- bon.
  • Reduction of Nitro Compounds (R/Ar − NO2 → R/Ar − NH2): – Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl (industrial, needs small HCl), Zn/HCl, H2/Pd or H2/Raney Ni. – Trap: Sn/NH4OH does not reduce PhNO2 to PhNH2.
  • Reduction of Nitriles, Isonitriles & Amides: – R − C ≡ N −L−i−A−lH−4−−or−−H−2−/N−−i −or−N−−a(−H−g−)−/E−t−O−H→ R − CH2NH2 (1◦ amine, Mendius). – R − N+ ≡ C− −L−i−A−lH−−4−o−r−H−2−/−N→i R − NH − CH (2◦ 3 amine). – R − CONH −(−i)−L−i−A−lH−−4,−(−i−i)−H−2−O→ R − CH NH 2 2 2 (same C count). – Phthalimide −L−i−A−lH−→4 Isoindoline (cyclic 2◦ amine).
  • Ammonolysis of Halides: R − X + NH3 → RNH2 → R2NH → R3N → R4N+X− (gives mixture; use excess NH3 for 1◦ amine; 1, 4-dihalide + NH3 → pyrrolidine after NaOH).

formulaCards.title: 2. Basicity Trends & pK<sub>b</sub> Values (Gas vs Aqueous)
formulaCards.html:
• Gas Phase: Controlled purely by +I effect: 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦ > NH3.
  • Aqueous Phase (Combined +I, Solvation, Steric Hindrance): – Methyl amines: Me2NH (2◦) > MeNH2 (1◦) > Me3N (3◦) > NH3 – Ethyl amines: Et2NH (2◦) > Et3N (3◦) > EtNH2 (1◦) > NH3.
  • Standard NCERT pKb Benchmarks (Lower pKb = Stronger Base): – Et2NH: 3.00 Et3N: 3.25 EtNH2: 3.29 Me2NH: 3.27 – NH3: 4.75 PhCH2NH2: 4.70 PhNH2: 9.38
  • Aliphatic vs Aromatic: RNH2 (sp3 N, localized lp) ≫ PhNH2 (lp delocalized into ring) > amides (RCONH2, neutral).
  • Substituted Anilines: EDG (−OCH3, −CH3) at p- position increases basicity; EWG (−NO2, −CN) decreases basicity. Ortho-effect: o-substituted anilines are gener- ally weaker bases than aniline (except o-OMe slightly).

formulaCards.title: 4. Distinction Tests for 1<sup>◦</sup>, 2<sup>◦</sup>, 3<sup>◦</sup> Amines
formulaCards.html:
• Hinsberg’s Test (C6H5SO2Cl / TsCl + NaOH/KOH): – 1◦ Amine (RNH2, ArNH2): Forms N- alkylbenzenesulfonamide (RNHSO2Ph), which has an acidic N − H and is soluble in alkali (NaOH/KOH). – 2◦ Amine (R2NH): Forms N, N- dialkylbenzenesulfonamide (R2NSO2Ph), which has no N − H and is insoluble in alkali. – 3◦ Amine (R3N): Does not react (no N − H to displace Cl−).
  • Carbylamine Test (CHCl3 + KOH(alc)/∆): Br + 2 H2O– Given ONLY by 1◦ amines (both aliphatic and aromatic) → foul-smelling isocyanide (R − NC). 2◦ and 3◦ amines do not respond.
  • Nitrous Acid (NaNO2 + HCl, 0–5◦C): – 1◦ Aliphatic (RNH ): Unstable RN+Cl− −H−2−O→ 2 2 ROH + N2 ↑ +HCl (quantitative N2 gas). – 1◦ Aromatic (ArNH2): Stable ArN+2 Cl− at 0–5◦C (gives dye with β-naphthol). – 2◦ Amine: Yellow oily N-nitrosamine (R2N − N = O). – 3◦ Aromatic (PhNMe2): p-nitrosoaniline (green/yellow).

formulaCards.title: 5. Diazonium Salts (ArN<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> X<sup>−</sup>) & Coupling Reactions
formulaCards.html:
• Stability Order: Resonance stabilizes ArN+2 . EDG (p-OCH3 > H) stabilizes; EWG (p-CN > p-NO2) desta- bilizes.
  • Key Replacement Reactions of ArN+2 Cl−: – Sandmeyer: Cu2Cl2/HCl → ArCl; Cu2Br2/HBr → ArBr; CuCN/KCN → ArCN. – Gattermann: Cu/HCl → ArCl; Cu/HBr → ArBr. – Balz–Schiemann: HBF4 → ArN+BF− −∆→ ArF; NaNO , Cu, ∆ 2 4 −−−−−2−−−−−→ ArNO2. – Deamination (Replace −N+2 by −H): H3PO2 + H2O (oxidised to H3PO3) or CH3CH2OH (oxidised to CH3CHO). – Iodide / Phenol: KI(aq) → ArI; H2O, ∆ → ArOH (note: o-phenylenediamine + HNO2 → ben- zotriazole).
  • Azo Coupling (Retains both N atoms): – + Phenol (OH−, pH 9–10) → p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange dye). – + β-Naphthol (NaOH, 0–5◦C) → scarlet red dye. – + Aniline (H+, pH 4–5) → p-aminoazobenzene (yellow dye). (Via diazoaminobenzene rearrange- ment at 40–45◦C).

formulaCards.title: 6. Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) of Aniline
formulaCards.html:
• −NH2 is a powerful o, p-directing activating group.
  • Bromination: PhNH2 + 3 Br2(aq) → 2, 4, 6- tribromoaniline (white ppt). – Monobromination: Protect −NH2 with Ac O/Pyridine → acetanilide −B−r−2−/A−c−O−H→ p- 2 bromoacetanilide −H−+−−o−r−O−H−−−/−∆→ p-bromoaniline.
  • Nitration Anomaly (HNO3/H2SO4, 288 K): Gives 51% p + 47% m + 2% o because −NH2 protonates to m-directing −NH+3 . Protect via acetylation to get pure p-nitroaniline.

Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the balanced Hoffmann bromamide degradation equation: A primary amide reacts with $\text{Br}_2$ and aqueous/ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ to give a primary amine with one carbon atom less: $\text{R-CONH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \longrightarrow \text{R-NH}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements A and B: From the balanced equation, each mole of amide consumes $4\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ and only $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Br}_2$ (not $2\text{ mol}$), so A is incorrect. Both aliphatic (alkyl) and aromatic primary amides readily undergo this reaction, so B is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate statements C, D, and E: Primary amines ($\text{R-NH}_2$) are directly formed, so C is correct. Secondary amides ($\text{R-CONHR}^\prime$) lack the two $\text{N-H}$ protons needed to form the nitrene/isocyanate intermediate and do not undergo Hoffmann degradation, so D is incorrect. The inorganic by-products are indeed $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, $\text{NaBr}$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so E is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given options: Only statements C and E are correct, which corresponds to option (c).

• D (False): Only 1◦ amides (−CONH2) undergo this reaction; 2◦ amides lack two N–H protons.
• E (True): By-products are Na2CO3, NaBr, and H2O.

1. Step 1 — Identify the starting compound and step (i): The starting substrate is propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$). Heating it with $\text{NH}_3$ ($\Delta$) converts it into propanamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply Hoffmann bromamide degradation in step (ii): Treating $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$ with $\text{NaOH}/\text{Br}_2$ removes the carbonyl carbon to give ethylamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Diazotisation and hydrolysis of aliphatic amine in step (iii): Reaction of ethylamine with $\text{HNO}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$ forms an unstable aliphatic diazonium salt that immediately decomposes with water to yield ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).

Step 4 — Reduction of benzenediazonium chloride in step (iv): Ethanol acts as a mild reducing agent toward benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$), reducing it to benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$) while ethanol itself is oxidized to ethanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$): $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \longrightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{N}_2 + \text{HCl}$.

Q03.conceptHtml: Hoffmann bromamide requires a 1° amide (−CONH<sub>2</sub>); Gabriel phthalimide yields only 1° aliphatic/benzylic amines (no arylamines).
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the two reaction requirements: First, only primary amides ($\text{R-CONH}_2$) undergo Hoffmann bromamide degradation with $\text{Br}_2/\text{KOH}$ to form $\text{R-NH}_2$. Second, Gabriel phthalimide synthesis produces only aliphatic primary amines (not aromatic amines like aniline, because aryl halides do not undergo $S_N2$ substitution with potassium phthalimide).
  2. Step 2 — Check the top row of compounds: (1) Benzamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$) gives aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$), which cannot be made by Gabriel synthesis. (2) 2-Phenylethanamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$) gives benzylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), which can be made from benzyl halide via Gabriel synthesis (count = 1). (3) Acetamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$) gives methanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$), which can be made via Gabriel synthesis (count = 2).

Step 3 — Check the bottom row of compounds: (4) $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and (5) $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCONHCH}_3$ are secondary amides, so they do not undergo Hoffmann bromamide degradation. (6) Cyclohexanecarboxamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{CONH}_2$) gives cyclohexylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_2$), an aliphatic $1^\circ$ amine that can be prepared via Gabriel synthesis (count = 3).

Q04.subtopic: Boiling Points of Amines, Alcohols & Alkanes
Q04.conceptHtml: For comparable molar mass, b.p. follows R − OH > 1° amine > 2° amine > 3° amine > alkane.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare molar masses and functional groups: The four compounds are $n$-butanol (A, alcohol), $n$-butylamine (B, $1^\circ$ amine), $n$-butane (C, alkane), and diethylamine (D, $2^\circ$ amine). All have comparable molecular masses, so boiling point differences are governed by intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
  2. Step 2 — Rank intermolecular forces from weakest to strongest: $n$-Butane (C) is non-polar and has only weak London dispersion forces, giving it the lowest boiling point. Diethylamine (D) is a $2^\circ$ amine with only one $\text{N-H}$ bond and more steric hindrance than $n$-butylamine (B), which is a $1^\circ$ amine with two $\text{N-H}$ bonds; thus B forms stronger, more extensive H-bonding than D ($\text{C} < \text{D} < \text{B}$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare alcohol vs. primary amine: Because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, the $\text{O-H}\cdots\text{O}$ hydrogen bonds in $n$-$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$ (A) are stronger than the $\text{N-H}\cdots\text{N}$ hydrogen bonds in $n$-$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{NH}_2$ (B). Hence A has the highest boiling point.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The increasing order of boiling points is $\text{C} < \text{D} < \text{B} < \text{A}$, which is option (c).

Step 2 — Check reactions A and B: In A, benzyl bromide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) reacts with covalent $\text{AgCN}$; nitrogen acts as the attacking nucleophile to yield benzyl isocyanide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NC}$). In B, benzylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) undergoes the carbylamine reaction with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and aqueous/ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ to also yield benzyl isocyanide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NC}$).

Q07.conceptHtml: Aniline is less basic than cyclohexylamine; Gabriel fails for arylamines; p-nitrophenol dissolves in NaOH.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and D (Correct statements): In A, benzylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) has a localized lone pair on nitrogen, whereas in aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$) the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring; hence benzylamine is a stronger base than aniline (A is correct). In D, 4-nitroaniline undergoes diazotisation with $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$ followed by hydrolysis ($\Delta$) to give 4-nitrophenol, which is acidic and dissolves in $\text{NaOH}$ (D is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check statement B (Incorrect): 4-Methoxyaniline is an aromatic amine. Aromatic amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis because aryl halides do not undergo $S_N2$ nucleophilic substitution with potassium phthalimide. Thus B is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement C (Incorrect): 2-Phenylethanamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$) on Hoffmann bromamide degradation with $\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}$ gives benzylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), which is an aralkyl (aliphatic-type) primary amine, not a primary aromatic amine (where $-\text{NH}_2$ is directly attached to the benzene ring). Thus C is incorrect.

Q09.subtopic: Azo Coupling Reactivity of N, N-Dimethylanilines
Q09.conceptHtml: Diazonium coupling is an S<sub>E</sub>Ar reaction at the p-position; it requires strong +M activation from −NMe<sub>2</sub> and an open p-position.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reaction type: Reaction with benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{Ph-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$) in a mildly acidic medium is an electrophilic aromatic substitution (azo coupling) at the para position of the aromatic amine. The rate increases with stronger electron-donating ($+M$) activation of the ring by the $-\text{NMe}_2$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze steric inhibition of resonance (SIR) in P, Q, and R: In P (N,N-dimethylaniline), there are no ortho substituents, so the $-\text{NMe}_2$ group lies coplanar with the benzene ring and maximally donates its lone pair by resonance ($+M$). In Q (2,N,N-trimethylaniline), one ortho methyl group partially twists $-\text{NMe}_2$ out of plane, reducing resonance donation. In R (2,6,N,N-tetramethylaniline), two bulky ortho methyl groups severely twist $-\text{NMe}_2$ out of the ring plane (strong SIR effect), almost completely shutting down $+M$ activation.
  3. Step 3 — Order the reactivity: Because ring activation decreases sharply as steric twisting increases, reactivity toward $\text{Ph-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ follows the order $\text{P} > \text{Q} > \text{R}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The decreasing order of reactivity is $\text{P} > \text{Q} > \text{R}$, corresponding to option (a).

at o-position is slow. - R (2, 6-dimethyl-N, N-dimethylaniline? Actually o, p-blocked or 2-methyl): let’s check the

Q15.conceptHtml: Electron-donating groups (+M/+I) at the p-position stabilize ArN+, whereas electron-withdrawing groups 2 (−M/ − I) destabilize it.

Step 1 — Recall the electronic factor governing arenediazonium stability: Arenediazonium ions ($\text{Ar-N}_2^+$) are stabilized by resonance delocalization of $\pi$-electrons from the benzene ring into the positively charged $-\text{N}_2^+$ group. Electron-donating groups ($+M/+I$) stabilize the positive charge and increase stability, while electron-withdrawing groups ($-M/-I$) destabilize it.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the para substituents in A, B, C, and D: A has $p\text{-OCH}_3$ (strong $+M$ donor, most stabilizing); C is unsubstituted $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ (reference); D has $p\text{-CN}$ (strong $-M/-I$ withdrawing group); B has $p\text{-NO}_2$ (stronger $-M/-I$ withdrawing group than $-\text{CN}$, most destabilizing).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing order of stability: From most electron-donating to most electron-withdrawing: $\text{A } (-\text{OCH}_3) > \text{C } (-\text{H}) > \text{D } (-\text{CN}) > \text{B } (-\text{NO}_2)$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The decreasing order of stability is $\text{A} > \text{C} > \text{D} > \text{B}$, corresponding to option (b).

Step 2 — Reduce the amide [A] with $\text{LiAlH}_4/\text{H}_2\text{O}$: Lithium aluminium hydride ($\text{LiAlH}_4$) reduces the amide carbonyl ($-\text{CO}-$) completely to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$) without cleaving the $\text{C-N}$ bond. Thus, [A] is reduced to the secondary amine [B]: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5$ (N-benzyl-1-cyclohexylmethanamine).
  3. Step 3 — Match [B] with the given structures: Structure (A) shows the cyclohexane ring connected via $-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}-\text{CH}_2-$ to the benzene ring, which matches [B] exactly.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The final product [B] is structure (A), corresponding to option (a).

Q21.conceptHtml: ’F’ having only two types of H atoms implies a symmetrical para-disubstituted benzene ring (terephthalic acid).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce functional groups from the reaction sequence: Neutral compound A ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_9\text{ON}$) reacts with $\text{Br}_2/\text{OH}^-$ (Hoffmann bromamide degradation) to give acid-soluble primary amine B ($\text{Ar-NH}_2$), confirming A is a primary aromatic amide ($\text{CH}_3\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CONH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Follow B $\to$ C $\to$ D $\to$ E $\to$ F: Diazotisation of B gives $\text{CH}_3\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ (C); Sandmeyer reaction with $\text{CuCN}/\text{NaCN}$ gives $\text{CH}_3\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CN}$ (D); hydrolysis of D (or A) gives toluic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}$ (E). Oxidation of E with acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ converts $-\text{CH}_3$ to $-\text{COOH}$, forming a benzenedicarboxylic acid (F).
  3. Step 3 — Use symmetry of F to fix the isomer: Compound F has only two distinct types of hydrogen atoms: one type for the two equivalent $-\text{COOH}$ protons and one type for all four equivalent aromatic ring protons. Only the highly symmetric para-isomer (terephthalic acid, benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) has all four ring protons chemically identical!
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, A must be 4-methylbenzamide (p-toluamide), which is structure (A), corresponding to option (a).

−C−u−C−→N ’D’ (tolunitrile) −H−3−O−→+ ’E’ (toluic acid) −K−M−−nO−→4 ’F’ (phthalic/isophthalic/terephthalic acid). Step 3: Only
terephthalic acid (p-HOOC − C6H4 − COOH) has just 2 types of H (4 equivalent aromatic H + 2 equivalent
−COOH H). Hence ’A’ is 4-methylbenzamide, option (A).

Q22.conceptHtml: −NO<sub>2</sub> is m-directing (monobromination); −NH<sub>2</sub> is strongly o, p-activating (polybromination with Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O); Sandmeyer adds one more Br.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Bromination of nitrobenzene (Step 1): The $-\text{NO}_2$ group is meta-directing, so $\text{Br}_2/\text{FeBr}_3/\Delta$ gives 3-bromonitrobenzene (1 Br atom).
  2. Step 2 — Reduction and neutralisation (Steps 2–3): $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}, \Delta$ followed by pH neutralisation reduces $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$, giving 3-bromoaniline (1 Br atom).
  3. Step 3 — Exhaustive bromination with $\text{Br}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (Step 4): The strongly activating $-\text{NH}_2$ group directs bromine to all three available ortho and para positions (C−2, C−4, and C-6), forming 2,3,4,6-tetrabromoaniline (4 Br atoms).
  4. Step 4 — Diazotisation and Sandmeyer bromination (Steps 5–6): $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HBr}$ ($0\text{–}5^\circ\text{C}$) converts $-\text{NH}_2$ at C−1 into $-\text{N}_2^+\text{Br}^-$, and $\text{CuBr}/\text{NaBr}$ replaces the diazonium group with a fifth $-\text{Br}$ atom, yielding 1,2,3,4,6-pentabromobenzene (P).
  5. Step 5 — Confirm the final answer: The final major product (P) contains 5 bromine atoms, matching option (b).

(2)–(3) Sn/HCl + neutralization → 3-bromoaniline (C1 has −NH2, C3 has −Br). (4) Br2/H2O substitutes all
open o, p-positions to −NH2 (C2, C4, C6) → 2,3,4,6-tetrabromoaniline (4 Br). (5)–(6) Diazotisation + CuBr/NaBr
replaces −NH2 at C1 with −Br → 1,2,3,4,6-pentabromobenzene (5 Br atoms).

Q23.conceptHtml: Carboxylic acid <sup>−N</sup><sup>−H</sup>−3<sup>−,</sup><sup>−∆</sup>→ 1° amide <sup>−B</sup><sup>−r</sup>−2<sup>/</sup><sup>−K</sup><sup>−O</sup>−→<sup>H</sup> 1° amine (1 C less).
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Work backward from R ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}$): Compound Q heated with $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{KOH}$ undergoes Hoffmann bromamide degradation to give R ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}$). The primary aromatic amine with formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}$ is aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify amide Q: Because Hoffmann degradation removes one carbonyl carbon ($-\text{CO}-$), the primary amide Q that produces aniline must be benzamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify carboxylic acid P: Heating a carboxylic acid with aqueous $\text{NH}_3$ yields the corresponding primary amide. To obtain benzamide (Q), starting compound P must be benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: P, Q, and R are Benzoic acid, benzamide, and aniline respectively, matching option (b).

(C6H5CONH2), and (P) is benzoic acid (C6H5COOH).

Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify alkene P and optically active halide Q: Hydrocarbon P ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$) reacts with $\text{HCl}$ to give an optically active halide Q ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$). Among $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$ isomers, only 2-chlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Cl)CH}_3$) contains a chiral carbon (C−2). Addition of $\text{HCl}$ to but-2-ene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, P) cleanly forms 2-chlorobutane (Q).
  2. Step 2 — Identify amine R: Reaction of 2-chlorobutane (Q) with $1\text{ mol }\text{NH}_3$ replaces $-\text{Cl}$ with $-\text{NH}_2$ via nucleophilic substitution to give butan-2-amine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CH}_3$, R).
  3. Step 3 — Identify alcohol S: Diazotisation of aliphatic $1^\circ$ amine R followed by hydrolysis replaces $-\text{NH}_2$ with $-\text{OH}$, giving butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, S).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The set of structures for P, Q, R, and S matches row (B), corresponding to option (b).

Q25.conceptHtml: Benzamide (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NO, M = 121 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) hydrolyses to benzoic acid (effervesces with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>).

Q26.subtopic: Aqueous Basicity Order of Aliphatic vs Aromatic Amines
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Separate aliphatic amines from aromatic amines: Aliphatic amines (D: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, E: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}$) are much stronger bases than aromatic amines (A, B, C) because the nitrogen lone pair in aliphatic amines is localized and enhanced by the $+I$ effect of $-\text{CH}_3$ groups, whereas in anilines it is delocalized into the benzene ring.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the two aliphatic amines (E vs. D): Dimethylamine ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}$, E) has two electron-donating methyl groups and optimal solvation in aqueous solution, making it more basic than methylamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, D): $\text{E} > \text{D}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the three aromatic amines (B vs. A vs. C): Electron-donating substituents increase basicity while electron-withdrawing substituents decrease it. $p$-Methoxyaniline (B, $+M$ group $-\text{OCH}_3$) is more basic than unsubstituted aniline (A), which in turn is much more basic than $p$-nitroaniline (C, strong $-M/-I$ group $-\text{NO}_2$): $\text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the rankings and confirm the answer: The descending order of basicity is $\text{E} > \text{D} > \text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C}$, corresponding to option (c).

Step 1: Aliphatic amines (E, D) are much stronger bases than arylamines (A, B, C): E ((CH3)2NH) > D (CH3NH2).
Step 2: Among arylamines, +M (p-MeO, B) increases electron density on N, whereas −M (p-NO2, C) strongly
decreases it: B > A > C. Step 3: Combined descending order: E > D > B > A > C.
Q26.trapHtml: Never place p-methoxyaniline above aliphatic methylamines in aqueous basicity. Verified Answer: (C)

Q27.conceptHtml: Carbylamine test (CHCl<sub>3</sub> + KOH(alc)/∆) is given exclusively by 1° amines (both aliphatic and aromatic).
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for the carbylamine test: Only primary amines ($1^\circ$, both aliphatic $\text{R-NH}_2$ and aromatic $\text{Ar-NH}_2$) give a positive carbylamine test (forming foul-smelling isocyanides with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and alcoholic $\text{KOH}$). Secondary ($2^\circ$) and tertiary ($3^\circ$) amines do not respond.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each given amine (A to E): A: Aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$) — $1^\circ$ aromatic amine (positive). B: Dimethylamine ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}$) — $2^\circ$ amine (negative). C: Methanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$) — $1^\circ$ aliphatic amine (positive). D: Trimethylamine ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{N}$) — $3^\circ$ amine (negative). E: N-Methylaniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3$) — $2^\circ$ aromatic amine (negative).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Only A and C give a positive carbylamine test, matching option (d).

aliphatic amine (✓). - D ((CH3)3N): 3◦ amine (×). - E (N-methylaniline): 2◦ aromatic amine (×). Step 2: Only
A and C give a positive carbylamine test.

Q28.conceptHtml: Acetylation moderates the activating power of −NH<sub>2</sub> and adds steric bulk at o-positions, giving p- bromoaniline after hydrolysis.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Reduction of nitrobenzene (Step i): Treating nitrobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$) with $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$ reduces it to aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Protection by acetylation (Step ii): Reaction with $\text{Ac}_2\text{O}$ in pyridine converts aniline into acetanilide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$). This reduces the activating power of nitrogen (by resonance with the carbonyl group) and introduces steric bulk at the ortho positions.
  3. Step 3 — Selective monobromination and hydrolysis (Steps iii–iv): Bromination of acetanilide with $\text{Br}_2/\text{AcOH}$ selectively substitutes at the less hindered para position to yield 4-bromoacetanilide. Subsequent alkaline hydrolysis with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ removes the acetyl group to give 4-bromoaniline (p-bromoaniline).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Structure (B) represents 4-bromoaniline, corresponding to option (b).

p-bromoacetanilide (major). (iv) NaOH(aq) hydrolyses the amide to 4-bromoaniline (option B).

Q29.conceptHtml: To place Br at C3, C4, C5 relative to −NH<sub>2</sub> at C1, use a p-nitroaniline intermediate: −NH<sub>2</sub> directs Br to its o-positions (C3, C5), then replace −NH<sub>2</sub> at C4 with Br via Sandmeyer, and reduce −NO<sub>2</sub> at C1.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze target molecule 3,4,5-tribromoaniline: In 3,4,5-tribromoaniline, the three $-\text{Br}$ atoms occupy positions 3, 4, and 5 relative to $-\text{NH}_2$ (at C−1). Direct bromination of aniline gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (ruling out D), so we must install the bromines relative to another directing group first.
  2. Step 2 — Trace sequence (C) starting from 4-nitroaniline: (i) Treating 4-nitroaniline with excess $\text{Br}_2/\text{acetic acid}$ introduces two $-\text{Br}$ atoms ortho to the strongly activating $-\text{NH}_2$ group (at C−2 and C-6 relative to $-\text{NH}_2$, which are C−3 and C-5 relative to $-\text{NO}_2$), yielding 2,6-dibromo-4-nitroaniline. (ii) Diazotisation with $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by Sandmeyer reaction with $\text{CuBr}$ replaces $-\text{NH}_2$ with a third $-\text{Br}$ atom, forming 3,4,5-tribromonitrobenzene. (iii) Reduction with $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$ converts $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$, giving 3,4,5-tribromoaniline!
  3. Step 3 — Briefly verify why (A) and (B) fail: (A) Nitrobenzene is too deactivated to brominate efficiently with $\text{Br}_2/\text{AcOH}$ (and would give only m-bromonitrobenzene at best). (B) Benzene with $\text{Br}_2/\text{AlBr}_3$ gives bromobenzene, which does not react with $\text{NH}_3$ under ordinary conditions.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Sequence (C) predominantly yields 3,4,5-tribromoaniline, matching option (c).

−NH2 (C3, C5) → 2,6-dibromo-4-nitroaniline. (ii) NaNO2, HCl, CuBr replaces −NH2 at C4 with Br → 3,4,5-
tribromonitrobenzene. (iii) Sn, HCl reduces −NO2 to −NH2 → 3,4,5-tribromoaniline.

Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify [A] from the diazotisation step: Compound [A] reacts with $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $273\text{–}278\text{ K}$ to form benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$). Therefore, [A] must be aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify [B] from the reaction with $\text{KI}$: Shaking benzenediazonium chloride with aqueous $\text{KI}$ directly replaces $-\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ with $-\text{I}$, yielding iodobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{I}$) as [B].
  3. Step 3 — Identify [C] from the Fittig reaction: Treating iodobenzene ([B]) with $2\text{Na}$ in dry ether undergoes the Fittig reaction, coupling two phenyl rings to yield biphenyl ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5$) as [C].
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Row (C) shows [A] = aniline, [B] = iodobenzene, and [C] = biphenyl, matching option (c).

In (D), potassium iodide ($\text{KI}$) converts it to iodobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{I}$, correct).

Q32.conceptHtml: Sulphanilic acid (H<sub>2</sub>N − C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub> − SO<sub>3</sub>H) diazotises and couples with 1-naphthylamine (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) to form Congo-red-type monoazo dye C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>3</sub>S.

Step 1 — Identify the azo coupling product: Sulphanilic acid ($p\text{-H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-SO}_3\text{H}$) reacts with nitrous acid at $273\text{ K}$ to form the diazonium zwitterion ($p\text{-}^+\text{N}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-SO}_3^-$). In acetic acid medium, this couples at the C−4 position (para to $-\text{NH}_2$) of 1-naphthylamine ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_7\text{NH}_2$) to produce the azo dye $\text{HO}_3\text{S-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}=\text{N-C}_{10}\text{H}_6\text{-NH}_2$.

Molar mass $= 16(12) + 13(1) + 3(14) + 3(16) + 32 = 192 + 13 + 42 + 48 + 32 = 327\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

Q33.subtopic: Aqueous Basicity of Ethylamines, NH3 & N2H4
Q33.conceptHtml: In aqueous solution, ethylamines follow Et<sub>2</sub>NH > Et<sub>3</sub>N > EtNH<sub>2</sub> > NH<sub>3</sub>; hydrazine (H<sub>2</sub>N − NH<sub>2</sub>) is weaker than NH<sub>3</sub> due to −I effect of the adjacent −NH<sub>2</sub>.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare hydrazine ($\text{H}_2\text{N-NH}_2$) and ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$): In hydrazine, the second electronegative $-\text{NH}_2$ group exerts a $-I$ electron-withdrawing effect on the protonated nitrogen, destabilizing the conjugate acid relative to $\text{NH}_4^+$. Thus, $\text{H}_2\text{N-NH}_2 < \text{NH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the aqueous basicity order of ethylamines: Because of the combined $+I$ inductive effect, steric hindrance, and hydration of the conjugate ammonium ions in water, ethylamines follow the classic NCERT order $2^\circ > 3^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{NH}_3$: $\text{NH}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 < (\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_3\text{N} < (\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$.
  3. Step 3 — Combine all five bases: Putting both parts together gives $\text{NH}_2\text{-NH}_2 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 < (\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_3\text{N} < (\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This exact sequence appears in option (c).

Q34.conceptHtml: Nitrobenzene <sup>−S</sup><sup>−n</sup><sup>−/</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−C</sup>→<sup>l</sup> aniline <sup>−N</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−N</sup><sup>−O</sup>−2<sup>−/</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−C</sup>→<sup>l</sup> PhN+Cl− <sup>−β</sup><sup>−-n</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−p</sup><sup>−ht</sup><sup>−h</sup><sup>−ol</sup><sup>−/</sup><sup>−N</sup><sup>−aO</sup>−→<sup>H</sup> scarlet-red azo dye. 2

Step 1 — Recall how an azo dye is formed: Azo dyes ($\text{Ar-N}=\text{N-Ar}^\prime$) are synthesized by diazotising a primary aromatic amine (using $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $0\text{–}5^\circ\text{C}$) and coupling the resulting arenediazonium salt with a strongly activated aromatic ring such as a phenol, naphthol, or aniline.
  2. Step 2 — Trace sequence (C): (i) Nitrobenzene is reduced by $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$ to aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$). (ii) Aniline reacts with $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ to give benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$). (iii) Coupling with $\beta$-naphthol in $\text{NaOH}$ yields the bright scarlet-red azo dye 1-phenylazo-2-naphthol.

Q35.conceptHtml: Intramolecular H-bonding (chelation) in o-nitrophenol and o-nitroaniline prevents intermolecular associa- tion, making them steam volatile.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Connect steam volatility to hydrogen bonding: Compounds that form intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation) exist as discrete molecules with weak intermolecular attractions, giving them lower boiling points and making them steam volatile. Compounds that form intermolecular hydrogen bonding associate into larger networks, raising their boiling points and making them non-steam volatile.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze structures (A), (B), (C), and (D): (A) o-Nitrophenol and (B) o-nitroaniline have $-\text{OH}$/$-\text{NH}_2$ adjacent to $-\text{NO}_2$, allowing a stable 6-membered intramolecular H-bonded ring; thus both (A) and (B) are steam volatile. (C) and (D) are p-aminophenol (drawn in two orientations), where the para groups can only form intermolecular H-bonds, making them non-steam volatile.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Compounds (A) and (B) only are steam volatile, matching option (c).

Step 2 — Trace the blocking–bromination–deblocking sequence in (b): (1) $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (sulfonation) converts aniline into sulfanilic acid ($p$-aminobenzenesulfonic acid), blocking the para position with $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$. (3) $\text{Br}_2$ now selectively enters the ortho position relative to $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$), the lone pair on the nitrogen atom of $-\text{NH}_2$ delocalizes strongly into the benzene ring ($+M$ effect), increasing electron density at the ortho and para positions. Q70.conceptHtml: An −NH2 group strongly stabilizes a positive charge at the o- or p-position via +M resonance (forming = NH+), whereas at the m-position it only exerts −I. 2
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check whether the $-\text{NH}_2$ lone pair can resonate with the carbocation: A carbocation is dramatically stabilised if the nitrogen lone pair of $-\text{NH}_2$ can donate via $+M$ resonance to give a complete-octet iminium ion ($=\stackrel{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate structures a, b, and d: In a and b, the carbon bearing $-\text{NH}_2$ is $sp^3$ hybridised, so $-\text{NH}_2$ cannot participate in resonance at all and only destabilises the cation via its $-I$ effect. In d, the positive charge at C-6 is conjugated with $\text{C1}=\text{C2}-\text{C3}=\text{C4}$, but pushing electrons places the positive charge on C−2 and C−4—never on C−1—so $-\text{NH}_2$ still cannot donate its lone pair.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate structure c: In c, the conjugated system is $\text{H}_2\ddot{\text{N}}-\text{C1}=\text{C2}-\text{C3}=\text{C4}-\text{C5}^+$. Resonance delocalises the positive charge directly onto C−1, allowing $-\text{NH}_2$ to donate its lone pair and form the highly stable, complete-octet structure $\text{H}_2\stackrel{+}{\text{N}}=\text{C1}-\text{C2}=\text{C3}-\text{C4}=\text{C5}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Thus, carbocation c is the most stable, matching option (c).

Q76.conceptHtml: In aqueous medium: Et<sub>2</sub>NH (3.00) > Et<sub>3</sub>N (3.25) > EtNH<sub>2</sub> (3.29) ≫ PhNH<sub>2</sub> (9.38) (lower pK<sub>b</sub> = stronger base).

Step 1 — Recall aqueous basicity order for ethylamines: Combining $+I$ inductive effect, steric hindrance, and solvation (hydration) in water gives the standard ethylamine basicity order: $2^\circ > 3^\circ > 1^\circ \gg \text{Aniline}$, i.e., $\text{Et}_2\text{NH} > \text{Et}_3\text{N} > \text{EtNH}_2 \gg \text{PhNH}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate basic strength to $\text{p}K_b$: A stronger base has a larger $K_b$ and therefore a smaller $\text{p}K_b$ value.
  3. Step 3 — Assign exact $\text{p}K_b$ values: $N$-Ethylethanamine ($\text{Et}_2\text{NH}$, strongest) $\rightarrow 3.00$ (C–II); $N,N$-Diethylethanamine ($\text{Et}_3\text{N}$) $\rightarrow 3.25$ (D–I); Ethanamine ($\text{EtNH}_2$) $\rightarrow 3.29$ (B–IV); Aniline (weakest due to resonance delocalisation of lone pair) $\rightarrow 9.38$ (A–III).

Q77.conceptHtml: 4-Nitrotoluene <sup>−B</sup><sup>−r</sup>→2 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene (A); reduction + diazotisation + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> gives 2-bromotoluene; KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises −CH<sub>3</sub> to −COOH.

1. Step 1 — Bromination of $p$-nitrotoluene to form A: The activating $-\text{CH}_3$ group ($o,p$-directing) and deactivating $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($m$-directing) both direct $\text{Br}_2$ to the position ortho to $-\text{CH}_3$, yielding 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene as A.

Step 2 — Reduction, diazotisation, and deamination (B $\rightarrow$ C $\rightarrow$ D): $\text{Sn/HCl}$ reduces $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$ (B). $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ at $273\text{--}278\text{ K}$ converts $-\text{NH}_2$ to $-\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ (C). Q78.conceptHtml: In aqueous medium, methylamines follow 2° > 1° > 3° > NH<sub>3</sub>.
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Factors governing basicity in water: In aqueous medium, the basic strength of aliphatic amines depends on three competing effects: the electron-donating $+I$ effect of alkyl groups, steric hindrance to protonation, and hydrogen-bonding solvation of the conjugate ammonium ion.
  2. Step 2 — Compare methyl-substituted amines: Dimethylamine ($\text{Me}_2\text{NH}$, $2^\circ$) has the best balance of $+I$ effect and hydration ($2\text{ N}-\text{H}$ bonds in $\text{Me}_2\text{NH}_2^+$). Methylamine ($\text{MeNH}_2$, $1^\circ$) has strong hydration ($3\text{ N}-\text{H}$ bonds) that outweighs the extra $+I$ effect of poorly solvated trimethylamine ($\text{Me}_3\text{N}$, $3^\circ$), while $\text{NH}_3$ lacks any $+I$ alkyl group.
  3. Step 3 — Write the aqueous basicity order: For methylamines in water, the order is $2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ > \text{NH}_3$, i.e., $\text{Me}_2\text{NH} > \text{MeNH}_2 > \text{Me}_3\text{N} > \text{NH}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: This matches option (c).

Q80.conceptHtml: Pure arylamines are colourless, but darken on storage due to atmospheric oxidation (not reduction).

Q84.subtopic: Most Basic Amine & HCl Titration Stoichiometry
Q84.conceptHtml: Benzylamine (PhCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, sp3 N) is far more basic than aniline, p-nitroaniline, and acetanilide.
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the most basic compound: The four compounds are $p$-nitroaniline, benzylamine ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{NH}_2$), acetanilide ($\text{PhNHCOCH}_3$), and aniline ($\text{PhNH}_2$). In aniline, $p$-nitroaniline, and acetanilide, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised by resonance. In benzylamine, the $-\text{NH}_2$ lone pair is localised on an aliphatic carbon, making it the most basic compound.
  2. Step 2 — Find molar mass and moles of benzylamine: Molecular formula of benzylamine is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_9\text{N}$, so $M = 7(12) + 9(1) + 14 = 107\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Moles in $1.0\text{ g} = \frac{1.0}{107}\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate mass of $\text{HCl}$ consumed: Benzylamine is a monoacidic base, reacting 1:1 with $\text{HCl}$ ($M = 36.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). Mass of $\text{HCl} = \frac{1.0}{107} \times 36.5\text{ g} = 0.3411\text{ g} = 341.1\text{ mg}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Rounding to the nearest integer gives 341 mg.

Q90.conceptHtml: Only 1° amines (−NH2 on alkyl/aryl C, excluding amides/hydrazides) form alkali-soluble sulfonamides with Hinsberg’s reagent.
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Hinsberg’s test rule for alkali-soluble solids: Only primary ($1^\circ$) amines ($R-\text{NH}_2$) react with Hinsberg’s reagent ($\text{PhSO}_2\text{Cl}$) to form sulfonamides ($R-\text{NHSO}_2\text{Ph}$) that still possess an acidic $\text{N}-\text{H}$ hydrogen and therefore dissolve in aqueous alkali ($\text{KOH}/\text{NaOH}$). Amides, ureas, semicarbazide, $2^\circ$ amines, and $3^\circ$ amines do not give this result.
  2. Step 2 — Screen the compounds row by row: Row 1 gives aniline (1) — benzamide, semicarbazide, and $N$-methylaniline ($2^\circ$) are excluded. Row 2 gives 4-aminodiphenylamine (contains a $1^\circ$ $-\text{NH}_2$ group, 2), $o$-anisidine (3), and propan-1-amine (4) — urea is excluded.
  3. Step 3 — Screen Row 3 and total the count: Row 3 gives cyclohexylamine (5) — triethylamine ($3^\circ$) and $N$-ethyl-$N$-methylcyclohexylmethanamine ($3^\circ$) do not react.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Exactly 5 amine compounds form alkali-soluble solids with Hinsberg’s reagent.

Q91.conceptHtml: Ammonolysis of benzyl chloride can yield benzylamine (1°), dibenzylamine (2°), or tribenzylamine (3°). A 3° amine does not react with p-toluenesulfonyl chloride, leaving a clear solution.
Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce amine class from Hinsberg’s reagent: Ammonolysis of benzyl chloride ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{Cl}$) yields a mixture of $1^\circ$ (benzylamine), $2^\circ$ (dibenzylamine), and $3^\circ$ (tribenzylamine) amines. Because amine (X) reacts with $p$-toluenesulfonyl chloride (Hinsberg’s reagent) to leave a clear solution with no sulfonamide precipitate, it lacks an $\text{N}-\text{H}$ bond and must be the tertiary ($3^\circ$) amine.
  2. Step 2 — Write the formula of tribenzylamine: Tribenzylamine is $(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2)_3\text{N}$, which has molecular formula $\text{C}_{21}\text{H}_{21}\text{N}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate its molar mass: $M(\text{C}_{21}\text{H}_{21}\text{N}) = 21(12) + 21(1) + 14 = 252 + 21 + 14 = 287\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Therefore, the molar mass of amine (X) is 287.

Q93.conceptHtml: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NaNO<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl <sup>−H</sup>−2<sup>−O</sup>→ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + N<sub>2</sub> + NaCl + HCl + H<sub>2</sub>O.

Step 2 — Relate moles of $\text{NaOH}$ to moles of ethanamine: From the 1:1 stoichiometry, $1\text{ mol}$ of ethanamine generates $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCl}$, which requires $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ for neutralisation. Since $0.2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ is consumed, moles of ethanamine $= 0.2\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate mass $X$ of ethanamine: Molar mass of ethanamine ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_7\text{N}$) is $M = 2(12) + 7(1) + 14 = 45\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Therefore, $X = 0.2 \times 45 = 9\text{ g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Hence, the value of $X$ is 9.

Q95.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Formation of product P (Gabriel phthalimide alkylation): Phthalimide reacts with $\text{KOH}$ to form potassium phthalimide, which then undergoes $S_N2$ alkylation with benzyl chloride ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{Cl}$) to yield $N$-benzylphthalimide (product P).

  3. Step 3 — Sum all $\pi$ bonds: Total $\pi$ bonds $= 3 + 2 + 3 = 8$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Therefore, the total number of $\pi$ bonds in product P is 8.

Q96.subtopic: Count of Compounds Reacting with Hinsberg’s Reagent
Q96.conceptHtml: Both 1° and 2° amines react with Hinsberg’s reagent (PhSO<sub>2</sub>Cl); 3° amines, diazonium salts, phthalimide, and urea do not.
Q96.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall which compounds react with Hinsberg’s reagent: Both primary ($1^\circ$) and secondary ($2^\circ$) amines possess an $\text{N}-\text{H}$ bond and react with benzenesulfonyl chloride ($\text{PhSO}_2\text{Cl}$). Tertiary ($3^\circ$) amines, diazonium salts, imides, pyridines, and ureas do not react.
  2. Step 2 — Screen the compounds row by row: Row 1 gives aniline ($1^\circ$, 1) — benzenediazonium chloride and dibenzamide (imide) do not react. Row 2 gives $N$-methylbenzylamine ($2^\circ$, 2) and propane-1,3-diamine ($1^\circ$, 3) — $N$-phenylpiperidine ($3^\circ$) and trimethylamine ($3^\circ$) do not react.
  3. Step 3 — Screen Row 3 and total the count: Row 3 gives piperidine (cyclic $2^\circ$, 4) and propan-1-amine ($1^\circ$, 5) — pyridine ($3^\circ$) and urea do not react.

Q97.subtopic: Number of Amino Groups via Acetylation Mass Gain
Q97.conceptHtml: Each −NH<sub>2</sub> group acetylated to −NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> increases molar mass by 42 g mol<sup>−1</sup> (+COCH<sub>3</sub> − H).
Q97.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the mass increase per acetylated $-\text{NH}_2$ group: During acetylation, each $-\text{NH}_2$ group converts into $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$, replacing one $-\text{H}$ atom ($1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) with one $-\text{COCH}_3$ group ($43\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). The net increase in molar mass per amino group is $\Delta M = 43 - 1 = 42\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the total molar mass increase: $\text{Total }\Delta M = 192 - 108 = 84\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the number of amino groups: $\text{Number of }-\text{NH}_2\text{ groups} = \frac{84}{42} = 2$ (consistent with phenylenediamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{NH}_2)_2$, $M = 108\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Therefore, compound (x) contains 2 amino groups.

M = 108). 42
