Q01.conceptHtml: Oligosaccharides yield 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, which may be identical (e.g., maltose → glucose + glucose) or different (e.g., sucrose → glucose + fructose; lactose → glucose + galactose).
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall carbohydrate classification and reducing nature: Monosaccharides (like glucose, fructose, galactose) have a free aldehydic or $\alpha$-hydroxy ketonic group, so all monosaccharides are reducing sugars. Thus, statement (a) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check hydrolysis of oligosaccharides: Oligosaccharides yield $2$ to $10$ monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, and these units need not be identical. For example, sucrose (a disaccharide) hydrolyses to give two different monosaccharides — $\text{D-glucose}$ and $\text{D-fructose}$ — and lactose gives $\text{D-galactose}$ and $\text{D-glucose}$. Therefore, statement (b) is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Verify statements (c) and (d): Polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose are high-molecular-weight polymers of more than ten monosaccharide units (statement (c) is correct). In aqueous solution, open-chain $\text{D-(+)-glucose}$ co-exists in equilibrium with its cyclic $\alpha$- and $\beta$-pyranose forms, explaining mutarotation and certain reactions (statement (d) is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (b).
Q01.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (A) is correct: all monosaccharides (aldoses and ketoses) have a free hemiacetal/hemiketal −OH
or α-hydroxy carbonyl group and act as reducing sugars.
2. Statement (B) is incorrect: hydrolysis of oligosaccharides does not always yield the same monosaccharide
units (e.g., sucrose gives D-glucose and D-fructose; lactose gives D-glucose and D-galactose).
3. Statements (C) and (D) are correct: starch and cellulose are polysaccharides (> 10 units), and D-(+)-glucose
exhibits ring-chain tautomerism between open-chain and α/β-pyranose forms.
Q01.trapHtml: “Always the same” is an absolute qualifier trap—sucrose and lactose are classic heterodisaccharides.

Q02.conceptHtml: Neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> gives a characteristic violet complex with phenolic −OH groups.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ test: Neutral ferric chloride ($\text{FeCl}_3$) solution gives a characteristic violet/purple coloured complex with compounds containing a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group (an $-\text{OH}$ attached directly to a benzene ring).
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the side chains of the given amino acids: Threonine ($-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) and Serine ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) contain aliphatic alcoholic $-\text{OH}$ groups, while Cysteine ($-\text{CH}_2\text{SH}$) contains a thiol group. None of these is a phenol.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the phenolic amino acid: Tyrosine has a $p$-hydroxybenzyl side chain ($-\text{CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$), which contains a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group and therefore forms a violet complex with neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The correct amino acid is Tyrosine, matching option (c).
Q02.stepsLatex:
1. Check the side chains of the given α-amino acids: Threonine (−CH(OH)CH3, 2◦ alcohol), Serine (−CH2OH,
1◦ alcohol), Tyrosine (−CH2 − C6H4 − OH, phenolic −OH), and Cysteine (−CH2SH, thiol).
2. Only Tyrosine possesses a phenolic −OH group, so it forms a violet complex with neutral FeCl3.
Q02.trapHtml: Aliphatic alcohols (Serine, Threonine) do not give the violet FeCl<sub>3</sub> test; they respond to CAN (ceric ammonium nitrate).

Q03.conceptHtml: Standard NCERT mapping: Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid) → Scurvy; Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> (Pyridoxine) → Convulsions; Vitamin B<sub>2</sub> (Riboflavin) → Cheilosis; Vitamin A → Xerophthalmia.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Scurvy (A) and Xerophthalmia (D): Scurvy (bleeding gums) is caused by deficiency of Vitamin C, chemically known as Ascorbic Acid ($\text{A} \to \text{III}$). Xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea of the eye) is caused by deficiency of Vitamin A ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match Convulsions (B) and Cheilosis (C): Convulsions are caused by deficiency of Vitamin $\text{B}_6$, i.e., Pyridoxine ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$). Cheilosis (fissuring at the corners of the mouth and lips) is caused by deficiency of Vitamin $\text{B}_2$, i.e., Riboflavin ($\text{C} \to \text{IV}$).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all pairs: Putting the four matches together gives $\text{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (c).
Q03.stepsLatex:
1. A (Scurvy) → III (Ascorbic Acid / Vitamin C).
2. B (Convulsions) → I (Pyridoxine / Vitamin B6).
3. C (Cheilosis) → IV (Riboflavin / Vitamin B2).
4. D (Xerophthalmia) → II (Vitamin A).
5. Matching gives: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.
Q03.trapHtml: Do not confuse Cheilosis (B<sub>2</sub>, Riboflavin) with Convulsions (B<sub>6</sub>, Pyridoxine) or Beri-beri (B<sub>1</sub>, Thiamine).

Q04.conceptHtml: Side-chain functional groups in amino acids retain their characteristic organic tests: −CONH<sub>2</sub> (Hofmann), 1° − NH<sub>2</sub> (Hinsberg), phenolic −OH (neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub>), aliphatic −OH (CAN).
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the side-chain functional groups: Glutamine has a primary amide side chain ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$), Lysine has a primary amine side chain ($-(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$), Tyrosine has a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group ($-\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$), and Serine has an aliphatic primary alcohol group ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match Glutamine (A) and Lysine (B): A primary amide ($-\text{CONH}_2$) undergoes Hofmann bromamide degradation with $\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}$ ($\text{A} \to \text{IV}$). A primary amine ($-\text{NH}_2$) gives a positive Hinsberg’s test with benzenesulphonyl chloride ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$).
  3. Step 3 — Match Tyrosine (C) and Serine (D): The phenolic $-\text{OH}$ of Tyrosine gives a violet colour in the neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ test ($\text{C} \to \text{II}$), while the aliphatic $-\text{OH}$ of Serine gives a red colour in the ceric ammonium nitrate test ($\text{D} \to \text{III}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The complete matching is $\text{A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III}$, which is option (b).
Q04.stepsLatex:
1. Glutamine (A) has a primary amide (−CONH2) side chain → gives Hofmann bromamide degradation
(IV).
2. Lysine (B) has a 1◦ amine (−CH2CH2CH2CH2NH2) side chain → gives Hinsberg’s test (I).
3. Tyrosine (C) has a phenolic −OH → gives Neutral FeCl3 test (II).
4. Serine (D) has an aliphatic −CH2OH → gives Ceric ammonium nitrate test (III).
5. Matching gives: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.
Q04.trapHtml: Both Serine and Tyrosine have −OH, but CAN tests aliphatic alcohols (red complex) while neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> tests phenols (violet).

Q05.conceptHtml: Tertiary (3°) structure arises from further folding of 2° structures, stabilised by H-bonds, disulphide (−S − S−), van der Waals, and electrostatic forces, and is disrupted by heat or pH changes (denaturation).
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what tertiary structure represents: A linear polypeptide chain (primary structure) folds into local patterns ($\alpha$-helix or $\beta$-pleated sheet, secondary structure), and further 3D folding of the secondary structure produces the tertiary structure, giving rise to fibrous or globular shapes. Hence statements (a) and (d) are correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check the stabilizing forces: Tertiary structure is stabilized by hydrogen bonds, disulphide ($-\text{S-S}-$) linkages, van der Waals forces, and electrostatic (ionic) forces of attraction. Hence statement (b) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the effect of $\text{pH}$ changes (denaturation): Changing the $\text{pH}$ alters the protonation state of ionizable side chains and disrupts hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions, causing denaturation — where secondary and tertiary structures unfold and lose biological activity (only the primary structure remains intact). Thus, saying the tertiary structure remains intact under $\text{pH}$ changes is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (c).
Q05.stepsLatex:
1. Statements (A), (B), and (D) accurately describe 3◦ protein structure per NCERT.
2. Statement (C) is incorrect: exposing a protein to pH changes disrupts hydrogen bonds and electrostatic
interactions, causing denaturation (2◦ and 3◦ structures are destroyed, only 1◦ remains intact).
Q05.trapHtml: Denaturation destroys 2°, 3°, 4° structures upon pH or temperature change; only the primary (1°) peptide sequence survives.

Q06.conceptHtml: Anomers differ only in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C<sub>1</sub> in aldoses). Open-chain D-glucose (aldohexose) has 4 chiral carbons (C<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>), while open-chain D-fructose (ketohexose) has 3 chiral carbons (C<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>) with identical configuration to D-glucose.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the two Haworth structures in Statement I: Both six-membered pyranose rings have $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ pointing up at $\text{C}_5$, $-\text{OH}$ down at $\text{C}_4$, $-\text{OH}$ up at $\text{C}_3$, and $-\text{OH}$ down at $\text{C}_2$. They differ only at the anomeric carbon $\text{C}_1$: the left structure has $-\text{OH}$ pointing down ($\alpha\text{-D-(+)-glucopyranose}$) and the right has $-\text{OH}$ pointing up ($\beta\text{-D-(+)-glucopyranose}$). Thus, they are indeed the two anomers of $\text{D-(+)-glucose}$, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Compare chiral carbons of open-chain $\text{D-glucose}$ and $\text{D-fructose}$: $\text{D-glucose}$ is an aldohexose with chiral centres at $\text{C}_2, \text{C}_3, \text{C}_4, \text{C}_5$, whereas $\text{D-fructose}$ is a 2-ketohexose with chiral centres at $\text{C}_3, \text{C}_4, \text{C}_5$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify configurations at $\text{C}_3, \text{C}_4, \text{C}_5$: In Fischer projections, both $\text{D-glucose}$ and $\text{D-fructose}$ have $-\text{OH}$ on the left at $\text{C}_3$, on the right at $\text{C}_4$, and on the right at $\text{C}_5$. Hence they share three identical chiral carbons at $\text{C}_3, \text{C}_4,$ and $\text{C}_5$, making Statement II true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q06.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: The left Haworth structure has −OH down at C1 (α-D-(+)-glucopyranose) and the right has
−OH up at C1 (β-D-(+)-glucopyranose). Both are C1 anomers of D-(+)-glucose ⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Open-chain D-glucose and D-fructose share the exact same configuration at C3, C4, C5 (3 similar
chiral carbons) ⇒ True.
Q06.trapHtml: Verify C<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>4</sub> orientations in Haworth rings before confirming both structures are D-glucose anomers.

Q07.conceptHtml: α-D-(+)-glucose: [α]<sub>D</sub> = +112°, m.p. 419 K, crystallised at 303 K. β-D-(+)-glucose: [α]<sub>D</sub> = +19°, m.p. 423 K, crystallised at 371 K.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B: $\text{D-glucose}$ exists in two cyclic hemiacetal anomeric forms ($\alpha$- and $\beta$-forms) that differ solely in the configuration of the $-\text{OH}$ group at the anomeric carbon $\text{C}_1$. Therefore, both A and B are correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check melting points (statement C) and specific rotations (statement D): The melting point of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ is $419\text{ K}$ while that of $\beta\text{-D-glucose}$ is $423\text{ K}$, so $\beta$ has the higher melting point (C is incorrect). Also, the specific rotation of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ is $+112^\circ$ and that of $\beta\text{-D-glucose}$ is $+19^\circ$ — statement D swaps these two values (D is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check crystallization temperatures (statement E): As stated in NCERT, $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ is obtained by crystallization from a concentrated glucose solution at $303\text{ K}$, whereas $\beta\text{-D-glucose}$ is obtained by crystallization from a hot and saturated aqueous solution at $371\text{ K}$. Therefore, E is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements A, B, and E are correct, matching option (d).
Q07.stepsLatex:
1. A is true: Glucose exists as α and β anomers.
2. B is true: They differ in configuration at C − 1 in the cyclic hemiacetal form.
3. C is false: m.p. of α (419 K) < m.p. of β (423 K).
4. D is false: Specific rotations are swapped (α is +112◦, β is +19◦).
5. E is true: α-form crystallises at 303 K (from conc. aq. solution) and β-form at 371 K (from hot saturated
solution).
Q07.trapHtml: Remember: α has higher rotation (+112°) and lower m.p. (419 K); β has lower rotation (+19°) and higher m.p. (423 K).

Q08.conceptHtml: Conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> oxidises both −CHO and −CH<sub>2</sub>OH to −COOH. A D-aldotetrose has −OH on the right at C<sub>3</sub>; to give an optically inactive (meso) tartaric acid, C<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>3</sub> must have −OH on the same side (both right, D-erythrose).
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the D-configuration condition: In a Fischer projection of an aldotetrose ($\text{C}_1\text{HO}-\text{C}_2\text{H(OH)}-\text{C}_3\text{H(OH)}-\text{C}_4\text{H}_2\text{OH}$), the D-sugar must have the $-\text{OH}$ group on the lowest chiral carbon ($\text{C}_3$) pointing to the right. Structures (A) and (B) have $-\text{OH}$ on the left at $\text{C}_3$ (L-aldotetroses), so we eliminate (A) and (B).
  2. Step 2 — Predict the product of conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ oxidation: Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ is a strong oxidizing agent that oxidizes both the terminal $-\text{CHO}$ ($\text{C}_1$) and $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ ($\text{C}_4$) groups to $-\text{COOH}$, forming a dicarboxylic acid (tartaric acid).
  3. Step 3 — Check for optical inactivity (meso form): For the resulting dicarboxylic acid to be optically inactive, it must possess an internal plane of symmetry (meso-tartaric acid), which requires the $-\text{OH}$ groups on $\text{C}_2$ and $\text{C}_3$ to be on the same side. Structure (C) ($\text{D-erythrose}$) has both $-\text{OH}$ groups on the right, yielding meso-tartaric acid; Structure (D) ($\text{D-threose}$) has them on opposite sides, yielding optically active tartaric acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The required D-aldotetrose is Structure (C), which is option (c).
Q08.stepsLatex:
1. Check D-configuration (C3 −OH on right): Structures (C) and (D) are D-aldotetroses; (A) and (B) have C3
−OH on the left (L-series).
2. On oxidation with conc. HNO3, −CHO and −CH2OH become −COOH.
3. Structure (C) (D-erythrose, both −OH on right) yields meso-tartaric acid (plane of symmetry ⇒ optically
inactive). Structure (D) (D-threose) yields optically active D-tartaric acid.
Q08.trapHtml: Always check BOTH conditions: D-series (C<sub>3</sub> −OH right) AND plane of symmetry after HNO<sub>3</sub> oxidation.

Q09.conceptHtml: Both Maltose (α-1,4-glucose dimer) and Lactose (β-1,4-galactose-glucose) have a free hemiacetal −OH at C<sub>1</sub> of the right-hand glucose ring, making both reducing sugars.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine Statement I (Maltose): The left diagram correctly shows maltose, composed of two $\alpha\text{-D-glucopyranose}$ units joined by an $\alpha(1 \to 4)$ glycosidic linkage. Because $\text{C}_1$ of the second (right) glucose unit has a free hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ group, it can open to an aldehyde in solution and reduce Tollens’/Fehling’s reagent. Hence maltose is a reducing sugar, making Statement I false.
  2. Step 2 — Examine Statement II (Lactose): The right diagram correctly shows lactose, composed of $\beta\text{-D-galactopyranose}$ linked via a $\beta(1 \to 4)$ glycosidic bond to $\beta\text{-D-glucopyranose}$.
  3. Step 3 — Check reducing nature of Lactose: In lactose, $\text{C}_1$ of the glucose ring is unlinked and retains a free hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ group, so lactose is a reducing sugar. Therefore, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, corresponding to option (d).
Q09.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Maltose has a free hemiacetal −OH at C1 of the second glucose unit, so it is a reducing sugar.
Claiming it is non-reducing makes Statement I false.
2. Statement II: The structure shown is β-D-galactose linked β-1,4 to D-glucose (Lactose), which also has a free
hemiacetal −OH and is a reducing sugar ⇒ true.
Q09.trapHtml: Among common disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose), only sucrose is non-reducing.

Q10.conceptHtml: Arginine (R, essential), Aspartic acid (D, non-essential), Lysine (K, essential), Glutamic acid (E, non- essential).
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall one-letter codes and essentiality of basic amino acids: Arginine has the one-letter symbol $\text{R}$ and is an essential amino acid ($\text{A} \to \text{II}$). Lysine has the one-letter symbol $\text{K}$ and is also an essential amino acid ($\text{C} \to \text{IV}$).
  2. Step 2 — Recall one-letter codes and essentiality of acidic amino acids: Aspartic acid has the one-letter symbol $\text{D}$ and is non-essential ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$). Glutamic acid has the one-letter symbol $\text{E}$ and is also non-essential ($\text{D} \to \text{III}$).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the matched list: Combining all four gives $\text{A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (a).
Q10.stepsLatex:
1. A (Arginine) → II (R / Essential).
2. B (Aspartic acid) → I (D / Non-essential).
3. C (Lysine) → IV (K / Essential).
4. D (Glutamic acid) → III (E / Non-essential).
5. Matching gives: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
Q10.trapHtml: A = Alanine, so Arginine = R (aRginine); L = Leucine, so Lysine = K (before L); G = Glycine, so Glutamic acid = E (after D for Aspartic acid).

Q11.conceptHtml: Thyroxine is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid Tyrosine, whose one-letter code is Y (whereas T stands for Threonine).
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the iodinated amino-acid derivative hormone: Thyroxine (secreted by the thyroid gland) is an iodinated derivative of the amino acid tyrosine, whereas insulin is a peptide hormone secreted by the pancreas. Hence Hormone (B) is Thyroxine.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the one-letter symbols $\text{T}$ and $\text{Y}$: In standard IUPAC amino acid notation, $\text{T}$ stands for Threonine, while $\text{Y}$ stands for Tyrosine.
  3. Step 3 — Match the pair: Therefore, Amino acid (A) is $\text{Y}$ (Tyrosine) and Hormone (B) is Thyroxine.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (c).
Q11.stepsLatex:
1. Thyroxine (thyroid hormone) is synthesised from Tyrosine (HO − C6H4 − CH2 − CH(NH2)COOH).
2. The one-letter code for Tyrosine is Y (since T is already assigned to Threonine).
3. Thus Amino acid (A) = Y, Hormone (B) = Thyroxine.
Q11.trapHtml: Classic one-letter code trap: T = Threonine, Y = Tyrosine, W = Tryptophan.

Q12.conceptHtml: B<sub>1</sub> = Thiamine; B<sub>2</sub> = Riboflavin; B<sub>6</sub> = Pyridoxine; C = Ascorbic acid.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Vitamins $\text{B}_1$ and $\text{B}_2$: Vitamin $\text{B}_1$ is chemically called Thiamine ($\text{A} \to \text{III}$), and Vitamin $\text{B}_2$ is Riboflavin ($\text{B} \to \text{IV}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match Vitamins $\text{B}_6$ and $\text{C}$: Vitamin $\text{B}_6$ is Pyridoxine ($\text{C} \to \text{I}$), and Vitamin $\text{C}$ is Ascorbic acid ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: The complete set of pairs is $\text{A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (c).
Q12.stepsLatex:
1. A (Vitamin B1) → III (Thiamine).
2. B (Vitamin B2) → IV (Riboflavin).
3. C (Vitamin B6) → I (Pyridoxine).
4. D (Vitamin C) → II (Ascorbic acid).
5. Matching gives: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.
Q12.trapHtml: Keep B<sub>1</sub> (Thiamine), B<sub>2</sub> (Riboflavin), B<sub>6</sub> (Pyridoxine), and B<sub>12</sub> (Cyanocobalamin) memorised in order.

Q13.conceptHtml: A disaccharide is non-reducing when both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond (no free hemiacetal/hemiketal −OH), as in sucrose (α-D-glucopyranose C<sub>1</sub> linked to β-D-fructofuranose C<sub>2</sub>).
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for a non-reducing disaccharide: A disaccharide is non-reducing only when the anomeric carbons of both monosaccharide units are involved in the glycosidic linkage, leaving no free hemiacetal or hemiketal $-\text{OH}$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect Structure (A): Structure (A) is sucrose, formed by linking $\text{C}_1$ of $\alpha\text{-D-glucopyranose}$ to $\text{C}_2$ of $\beta\text{-D-fructofuranose}$. Since both reducing (anomeric) centres are locked in the glycosidic bond, sucrose cannot open to a free carbonyl group and is non-reducing.
  3. Step 3 — Check Structures (B), (C), and (D): Structure (B) is maltose ($\alpha\text{-1,4}$), Structure (C) is cellobiose ($\beta\text{-1,4}$), and Structure (D) is lactose ($\beta\text{-1,4}$). In all three, $\text{C}_1$ of the right-hand pyranose ring has a free hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ group, so they are reducing sugars.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The non-reducing disaccharide is Structure (A), which is option (a).
Q13.stepsLatex:
1. Structure (A) shows a 6-membered pyranose ring (α-D-glucose) linked via its C1 oxygen to the C2 anomeric
carbon of a 5-membered furanose ring (β-D-fructose). Neither ring has a free anomeric −OH ⇒ non-reducing
(Sucrose).
2. Structures (B), (C), and (D) are pyranose-pyranose dimers with a free hemiacetal −OH at C1 of the right-hand
ring ⇒ reducing sugars.
Q13.trapHtml: Look at the right-hand ring: a 5-membered furanose ring linked at C<sub>2</sub> (bearing −CH<sub>2</sub>OH) immediately identifies sucrose.

Q14.conceptHtml: Peptide sequences are always read from the N-terminus (−NH<sub>2</sub>) to the C-terminus (−COOH).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the peptide from N-terminus to C-terminus: By convention, peptide sequences are written starting from the free $-\text{NH}_2$ end (left) to the free $-\text{COOH}$ end (right). We break the chain at each peptide ($-\text{CO-NH}-$) bond to identify the five side chains ($R$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify all five amino acid residues in order: From left to right, the side chains are: $R_1 = -\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (Threonine, $\text{Thr}$), $R_2 = -\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (Serine, $\text{Ser}$), $R_3 = -\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (Aspartic acid, $\text{Asp}$), $R_4 = -\text{H}$ (Glycine, $\text{Gly}$), and $R_5 = -\text{CH}_3$ (Alanine, $\text{Ala}$). Thus the sequence is $\text{Thr-Ser-Asp-Gly-Ala}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the essential amino acid (Y): Among Threonine, Serine, Aspartic acid, Glycine, and Alanine, only Threonine is an essential amino acid (remember the mnemonic PVT TIM HALL: Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg, Leu, Lys).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: (Y) is Threonine and the sequence is $\text{Thr-Ser-Asp-Gly-Ala}$, matching option (d).
Q14.stepsLatex:
1. Read the 5 side chains from left (N-terminus) to right (C-terminus):
• Residue 1: −CH(OH)CH3 → Threonine (Thr) (Essential!).
• Residue 2: −CH2OH → Serine (Ser) (Non-essential).
• Residue 3: −CH2COOH → Aspartic acid (Asp) (Non-essential).
• Residue 4: −H → Glycine (Gly) (Non-essential).
• Residue 5: −CH3 → Alanine (Ala) (Non-essential).
2. Thus the essential amino acid (Y) is Threonine, and the sequence is Thr-Ser-Asp-Gly-Ala.
Q14.trapHtml: Check the last two residues carefully: −H (Gly) precedes −CH<sub>3</sub> (Ala), distinguishing (D) from (A)/(B)/(C).

Q15.conceptHtml: Number of distinct linear peptides formed from n different amino acids using each exactly once = n!.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand why order matters in peptides: A peptide has a distinct N-terminus (left) and C-terminus (right), so $\text{Ala-Gly-Val}$ is chemically different from $\text{Val-Gly-Ala}$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the permutations without repetition: We have $3$ distinct amino acids ($\text{Ala, Gly, Val}$) to arrange in $3$ positions, using each exactly once. The number of arrangements is $3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$.
  3. Step 3 — List all 6 tripeptides to verify: $\text{Ala-Gly-Val}$, $\text{Ala-Val-Gly}$, $\text{Gly-Ala-Val}$, $\text{Gly-Val-Ala}$, $\text{Val-Ala-Gly}$, and $\text{Val-Gly-Ala}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: There are $6$ possible tripeptides, which is option (d).
Q15.stepsLatex:
1. Here n = 3 distinct amino acids: Ala, Gly, Val.
2. Number of tripeptides = 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 (Ala-Gly-Val, Ala-Val-Gly, Gly-Ala-Val, Gly-Val-Ala, Val-Ala-Gly,
Val-Gly-Ala).
Q15.trapHtml: If repetition were allowed, the count would be 33 = 27; “no amino acid used more than once” means 3! = 6.

Q16.conceptHtml: Purine/pyrimidine bases are planar (achiral) and the phosphate diester group is achiral; chirality in DNA and RNA comes solely from the D-sugar component (β-D-2-deoxyribose / β-D-ribose).
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the three components of a nucleotide: Both DNA and RNA are polynucleotides built from a pentose sugar, a heterocyclic nitrogenous base, and a phosphate group.
  2. Step 2 — Check which component introduces chirality: The nitrogenous bases are planar aromatic rings (achiral) and the phosphate unit is achiral. The chirality comes strictly from the asymmetric carbons of the pentose sugar unit.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the sugar configuration in human DNA and RNA: RNA contains $\beta\text{-D-ribose}$ and DNA contains $\beta\text{-D-2-deoxyribose}$. Both are D-sugars, so chirality arises due to the D-sugar component.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (b).
Q16.stepsLatex:
1. Nucleic acids consist of a heterocyclic base (planar, achiral), a phosphate unit (achiral), and a pentose sugar
in the D-configuration.
2. Hence, chirality arises from the D-sugar component.
Q16.trapHtml: Natural amino acids are L-configuration, whereas natural nucleic acid sugars are D-configuration.

Q17.conceptHtml: Tollens’ reagent oxidises free hemiacetals/hemiketals (where the anomeric carbon bears an −OH). Methyl glycosides (acetals/ketals with −OCH<sub>3</sub> at the anomeric carbon) do not open to an aldehyde and do not react with Tollens’ reagent.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for reacting with Tollens’ reagent: Cyclic monosaccharides react with Tollens’ reagent only if they possess a free hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ group at the anomeric carbon ($\text{C}_1$), which allows the ring to open into the free aldehyde form in alkaline medium.
  2. Step 2 — Check structures A and D: Structure A ($\beta\text{-D-glucopyranose}$) and Structure D ($\alpha\text{-D-galactopyranose}$) both have a free $-\text{OH}$ group on the anomeric carbon $\text{C}_1$ (hemiacetals), so they mutarotate and react positively with Tollens’ reagent.
  3. Step 3 — Check structures B and C: Structure B (methyl $\beta\text{-D-glucopyranoside}$) and Structure C (methyl $\beta\text{-D-ribofuranoside}$) have an $-\text{OCH}_3$ group at $\text{C}_1$, making them full acetals (glycosides). Full acetals are stable in base and cannot open to an aldehyde, so neither B nor C reacts with Tollens’ reagent.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Structures B and C will not react with Tollens’ reagent, matching option (d).
Q17.stepsLatex:
1. A: Pyranose ring with free −OH at C1 (hemiacetal) → reacts.
2. B: Pyranose ring with −OCH3 at C1 (methyl glycoside, acetal) → does NOT react.
3. C: Furanose ring with −OCH3 at C2 (methyl glycoside, ketal) → does NOT react.
4. D: Pyranose ring with free −OH at C1 (hemiacetal) → reacts.
5. Thus B and C will not react with Tollens’ reagent.
Q17.trapHtml: The question asks for those which will NOT react with Tollens’ reagent—look for −OCH<sub>3</sub> at the anomeric carbon.

Q18.conceptHtml: Glucose + NH<sub>2</sub>OH → Glucoxime; + Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O → Gluconic acid; + excess Ac<sub>2</sub>O → Glucose pentaacetate; + conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → Saccharic acid.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match reactions of the $-\text{CHO}$ group (A and B): Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine ($\text{NH}_2\text{OH}$) to form an oxime called glucoxime ($\text{A} \to \text{IV}$). Mild oxidation with $\text{Br}_2$ water oxidizes only the $-\text{CHO}$ group to $-\text{COOH}$, giving gluconic acid ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match acetylation (C) and strong oxidation (D): Excess acetic anhydride acetylates all five $-\text{OH}$ groups of glucose to yield glucose pentaacetate ($\text{C} \to \text{II}$). Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ oxidizes both $-\text{CHO}$ and primary $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $-\text{COOH}$, forming the dicarboxylic acid called saccharic acid ($\text{D} \to \text{III}$).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: Putting them together gives $\text{A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (d).
Q18.stepsLatex:
1. A (Hydroxylamine) → IV (Glucoxime).
2. B (Br2 water) → I (Gluconic acid).
3. C (Excess acetic anhydride) → II (Glucose pentaacetate).
4. D (Concentrated HNO3) → III (Saccharic acid).
5. Matching gives: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.
Q18.trapHtml: Distinguish mild oxidation (Br<sub>2</sub> water → monocarboxylic gluconic acid) from strong oxidation (conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → dicarboxylic saccharic acid).

Q19.conceptHtml: Sucrose (+66.5°) hydrolyses to equimolar D-(+)-glucose (+52.5°) and D-(-)-fructose (−92.4°). Because the laevorotation of fructose (−92.4°) exceeds the dextrorotation of glucose (+52.5°), the mixture is net laevorotatory (−39.9°).
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Sucrose is dextrorotatory with specific rotation $+66.5^\circ$. On hydrolysis, it gives an equimolar mixture of $\text{D-(+)-glucose}$ ($+52.5^\circ$) and $\text{D-(-)-fructose}$ ($-92.4^\circ$). The net specific rotation of the mixture is negative (laevorotatory), so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Statement II claims that glucose is laevorotatory and fructose is dextrorotatory. That is backwards! In reality, glucose is dextrorotatory ($+52.5^\circ$) and fructose is laevorotatory ($-92.4^\circ$), and because the laevorotation of fructose exceeds the dextrorotation of glucose, the mixture is laevorotatory.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude truth values: Statement I is true, while Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (c).
Q19.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Sucrose is dextrorotatory (+66.5◦) and its hydrolysis product mixture is laevorotatory ⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Claims “laevorotation of glucose is more than dextrorotation of fructose”—this is backwards!
Glucose is dextrorotatory (+52.5◦) and fructose is laevorotatory (−92.4◦) ⇒ False.
Q19.trapHtml: Read signs carefully: D-(+)-glucose is dextro, D-(-)-fructose is laevo.

Q20.conceptHtml: Enzymes lower E<sub>a</sub> compared to acid catalysis; denaturation destroys 2°/3° but preserves 1°; nucleotides are joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkage; 4° is spatial arrangement of subunits (overall folding is 3°).
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B: Enzymes lower activation energy far more effectively than mineral acids (acid hydrolysis of sucrose has $E_a = 6.22\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, whereas enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis with sucrase lowers $E_a$ to $2.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), so A is correct. During protein denaturation, secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed while the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure remain intact, so B is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check statement C: Nucleotides in DNA/RNA are linked by a phosphodiester linkage between the $5′$ and $3′$ carbons of the pentose sugar — not a glycosidic linkage between $\text{C}_1$ and $\text{C}_4$. Hence C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement D: Overall folding of a single polypeptide chain represents the tertiary structure, whereas quaternary structure refers to the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits with respect to each other. Hence D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only A and B are correct, which is option (d).
Q20.stepsLatex:
1. A is true: Invertase lowers Ea of sucrose hydrolysis (≈ 36 kJ/mol vs ≈ 107 kJ/mol for acid).
2. B is true: Denaturation destroys 2◦ and 3◦ structures while 1◦ remains intact.
3. C is false: Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkage between C′ and C′ (not glycosidic between
3 5
C1 and C4).
4. D is false: Overall folding of a polypeptide chain is tertiary (3◦) structure, not quaternary (4◦).
Q20.trapHtml: Overall folding of a single chain = 3°; assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits = 4°.

Q21.conceptHtml: Arginine and Tryptophan are essential; Glycine is achiral; Histidine has an imidazole heterocyclic ring; Proline has a 5-membered pyrrolidine ring; Cysteine has −CH<sub>2</sub>SH (Methionine has −CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SCH<sub>3</sub>).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and D: Both Arginine and Tryptophan belong to the 10 essential amino acids (PVT TIM HALL), so A is correct. Glycine ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$) has two hydrogens on its $\alpha$-carbon, making it the only natural $\alpha$-amino acid without a chiral centre, so D is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check statements B and C: Histidine contains a five-membered heterocyclic imidazole ring (so B is incorrect). Proline is a five-membered cyclic pyrrolidine-ring amino acid, not six-membered (so C is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check statement E: The side chain $\text{MeS}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-$ belongs to Methionine, whereas Cysteine has the side chain $-\text{CH}_2\text{SH}$ (so E is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements A and D are correct, matching option (b).
Q21.stepsLatex:
1. A is true: Both Arginine and Tryptophan are in the 10 essential amino acids (PVT TIM HALL).
2. B is false: Histidine contains a 5-membered imidazole heterocyclic ring.
3. C is false: Proline has a 5-membered (pyrrolidine) ring, not 6-membered.
4. D is true: Glycine (H2N − CH2 − COOH) has two H atoms on Cα ⇒ no chiral centre.
5. E is false: MeS − CH2 − CH2− is the side chain of Methionine, not Cysteine (−CH2SH).

Q22.conceptHtml: In strongly acidic medium (pH = 2 < pI), both −NH<sub>2</sub> and −COOH are protonated (cationic form). In strongly basic medium (pH = 10 > pI), both are deprotonated (anionic form).
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the given amino acid: The starting compound is Valine, $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2)-\text{COOH}$, a neutral $\alpha$-amino acid whose isoelectric point ($\text{pI}$) is around $6$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine structure A at $\text{pH} = 2$ (strongly acidic): When $\text{pH} \ll \text{pI}$, excess $\text{H}^+$ ions protonate the basic $-\text{NH}_2$ group (to $-\text{NH}_3^+$) and keep the carboxyl group protonated ($-\text{COOH}$). Thus, A is the cationic form $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2)-\text{COOH}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine structure B at $\text{pH} = 10$ (strongly basic): When $\text{pH} \gg \text{pI}$, excess $\text{OH}^-$ ions deprotonate the acidic $-\text{COOH}$ group (to $-\text{COO}^-$) and keep the amino group neutral ($-\text{NH}_2$). Thus, B is the anionic form $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2)-\text{COO}^-$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing A and B with the diagram shows Option (C) is exact, matching option (c).
Q22.stepsLatex:
1. At pH = 2 (acidic): −NH2 is protonated to −NH+ and −COOH remains −COOH ⇒ A is H3N+ − CH(CH(CH3)2) − COOH
3
2. At pH = 10 (basic): −NH+ loses H+ to −NH2 and −COOH is deprotonated to −COO− ⇒ B is H2N − CH(CH(CH3)2) − C
3
3. This matches Option (C).
Q22.trapHtml: At pH ≈ 6 (isoelectric point), the zwitterion H<sub>3</sub>N+ − CHR − COO− dominates—do not pick the zwitterion for pH = 2 or pH = 10.

Q23.conceptHtml: All natural proteins and peptides hydrolyse to α-amino acids (never β-amino acids). Denaturation converts water-soluble globular proteins into water-insoluble coagulated forms (fibrous proteins are already water-insoluble).
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Both oligopeptides and naturally occurring proteins are polymers of $\alpha$-amino acids (never $\beta$-amino acids). Therefore, saying proteins yield $\beta$-amino acids on hydrolysis makes Statement I incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Fibrous proteins (like keratin and myosin) are already generally insoluble in water. It is globular proteins (like egg albumin) that are water-soluble in their native state and coagulate into water-insoluble forms upon denaturation by heat or acids. Therefore, Statement II is also incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the evaluations: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (b).
Q23.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Claims proteins yield β-amino acids on hydrolysis ⇒ False (they yield α-amino acids).
2. Statement II: Claims denaturation converts water-soluble fibrous proteins to water-insoluble form ⇒ False
(fibrous proteins like keratin/myosin are already water-insoluble; it is globular proteins like egg albumin that
coagulate/become insoluble).
Q23.trapHtml: Fibrous proteins = water-insoluble; Globular proteins = water-soluble (coagulate on denaturation).

Q24.conceptHtml: Sucrose is formed from D − (+) − glucose and D − (−) − fructose (laevorotatory), and its hydrolysis gives invert sugar.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the optical sign of fructose in Statement I: Naturally occurring fructose obtained from sucrose is laevorotatory, written as $\text{D-(-)-fructose}$ (not $\text{D-(+)-fructose}$). Because Statement I writes $\text{D-(+)-fructose}$, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Sucrose is dextrorotatory ($+66.5^\circ$), but its hydrolysis yields an equimolar mixture of $\text{D-(+)-glucose}$ ($+52.5^\circ$) and $\text{D-(-)-fructose}$ ($-92.4^\circ$), which is overall laevorotatory. Because the sign of optical rotation inverts from $(+)$ to $(-)$, this hydrolysis product is called invert sugar. Hence Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the conclusions: Statement I is false and Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (b).
Q24.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Writes “D-(+)-fructose” instead of D-(−)-fructose ⇒ False.
2. Statement II: Invert sugar is indeed formed during sucrose hydrolysis ⇒ True.
Q24.trapHtml: Notice the (+) sign trap in D-(+)-fructose: natural D-fructose is laevorotatory, D-(−)-fructose.

Q25.conceptHtml: α-amino acids react with HNO<sub>2</sub> to give α-hydroxy acids (Alanine → Lactic acid). Heating two molecules of glycine forms the cyclic 6-membered diketopiperazine.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify amino acid “y” from the $\text{HNO}_2$ reaction: Aqueous $\text{HNO}_2$ diazotizes a primary aliphatic $-\text{NH}_2$ group and replaces it with $-\text{OH}$. Since “y” produces lactic acid ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{COOH}$), “y” must be Alanine ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)}-\text{COOH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify amino acid “z” from the cyclic heating product: Two molecules of an $\alpha$-amino acid condense on heating (eliminating $2\text{ H}_2\text{O}$) to form a 6-membered cyclic diamide (diketopiperazine). In the given ring, both $\alpha$-carbons are unsubstituted $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups, meaning the side chain is $R = -\text{H}$.
  3. Step 3 — Name “z” and the dipeptide X: The $\alpha$-amino acid with $R = -\text{H}$ is Glycine ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$). Since dipeptide X hydrolyses to Alanine and Glycine, X is alanine-glycine.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (d).
Q25.stepsLatex:
1. “y” + aq. HNO2 → Lactic acid (CH3CH(OH)COOH) ⇒ “y” is Alanine (CH3CH(NH2)COOH).
2. The cyclic molecule formed on heating “z” has two −CH2− and two −CONH− units (2,5-diketopiperazine) ⇒
“z” is Glycine (H2NCH2COOH).
3. Therefore, the dipeptide X is alanine-glycine.
Q25.trapHtml: Count the ring carbons in the cyclic product: no methyl substituents means “z” must be Glycine, not Alanine or Valine.

Q26.conceptHtml: In Gly-Ala, Glycine is at the N-terminus (free −NH<sub>2</sub>, acylating −COCl) and Alanine is at the C-terminus (free −COOH, nucleophilic −NH<sub>2</sub>).
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the target dipeptide Gly-Ala: In $\text{Gly-Ala}$, Glycine is at the N-terminus (left) and Alanine is at the C-terminus (right), so the peptide bond joins the carbonyl carbon of Glycine to the amino nitrogen of Alanine: $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{COOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify which reactant must supply the $-\text{COCl}$ group: To eliminate $\text{HCl}$ and form the $-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-$ bond in the Gly-to-Ala direction, Glycine must be activated as its acid chloride ($\text{NH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COCl}$) while Alanine supplies a free nucleophilic $-\text{NH}_2$ group ($\text{NH}_2-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{COOH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the other pairs: Pair (A) has no $-\text{Cl}$ to eliminate $\text{HCl}$; Pair (B) has protonated $-\text{NH}_3^+$ on Alanine (non-nucleophilic) and an extra $-\text{COCl}$; Pair (D) activates Alanine’s carboxyl group instead, which would form $\text{Ala-Gly}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Pair (C) gives $\text{Gly-Ala}$ with elimination of $\text{HCl}$, matching option (c).
Q26.stepsLatex:
1. To form NH2 − CH2 − CO − NH − CH(CH3) − COOH (Gly-Ala) with elimination of HCl, the acid chloride
group (−COCl) must be on Glycine (NH2 − CH2 − COCl) and the −COOH must be on Alanine (NH2 − CH(CH3) − COOH
2. This corresponds to Pair (C).
Q26.trapHtml: Pair (D) would give Ala-Gly instead of Gly-Ala; always match N-terminus = Gly and C-terminus = Ala.

Q27.conceptHtml: Vitamins A, D, E, K are fat-soluble; Vitamin B-complex and Vitamin C are water-soluble.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the classification of vitamins by solubility: Vitamins are divided into fat-soluble vitamins (Vitamins $\text{A, D, E,}$ and $\text{K}$) and water-soluble vitamins (Vitamin $\text{B}$-complex and Vitamin $\text{C}$).
  2. Step 2 — Classify each listed vitamin: Vitamin $\text{B}_1$ (A), Vitamin $\text{C}$ (B), and Vitamin $\text{B}_{12}$ (D) are water-soluble. Vitamin $\text{E}$ (C) and Vitamin $\text{K}$ (E) are fat-soluble.
  3. Step 3 — Select the fat-soluble subset: Only C and E are fat-soluble vitamins.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (c).
Q27.stepsLatex:
1. B1 (A), C (B), and B12 (D) are water-soluble.
2. Vitamin E (C) and Vitamin K (E) are fat-soluble.
3. Hence C & E Only are fat-soluble.
Q27.trapHtml: Remember ADEK = fat-soluble; B & C = water-soluble.

Q28.conceptHtml: D-Fructose (2-ketohexose) has C<sub>3</sub> (OH left), C<sub>4</sub> (OH right), C<sub>5</sub> (OH right). L-Fructose is its enantiomer (mirror image): C<sub>3</sub> (OH right), C<sub>4</sub> (OH left), C<sub>5</sub> (OH left).
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Fischer projection of $\text{D-fructose}$: $\text{D-fructose}$ is a 2-ketohexose with $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ at $\text{C}_1$, $\text{C}=\text{O}$ at $\text{C}_2$, and chiral centres at $\text{C}_3, \text{C}_4, \text{C}_5$ having $-\text{OH}$ positions: $\text{C}_3$ on the left, $\text{C}_4$ on the right, and $\text{C}_5$ on the right.
  2. Step 2 — Take the exact mirror image to get $\text{L-fructose}$: $\text{L-fructose}$ is the enantiomer of $\text{D-fructose}$, so every chiral centre is inverted: $\text{C}_3\text{-OH}$ must be on the right, $\text{C}_4\text{-OH}$ on the left, and $\text{C}_5\text{-OH}$ on the left.
  3. Step 3 — Match against the given structures: Inspecting the four Fischer projections, Structure (B) has $\text{C}_3\text{-OH}$ on the right, $\text{C}_4\text{-OH}$ on the left, and $\text{C}_5\text{-OH}$ on the left.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Structure (B) is $\text{L-fructose}$, matching option (b).
Q28.stepsLatex:
1. In D-fructose: C1(CH2OH) − C2(= O) − C3(OH left) − C4(OH right) − C5(OH right) − C6(CH2OH).
2. Taking the mirror image at every chiral centre (C3, C4, C5) gives L-fructose: C3 (OH right), C4 (OH left), C5
(OH left).
3. Inspecting the four Fischer projections, Structure (B) has C3 (OH right), C4 (HO left), C5 (HO left).
Q28.trapHtml: Do not just flip C<sub>5</sub>! L-fructose is the complete enantiomer of D-fructose, so ALL chiral centres (C<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>5</sub>) invert.

Q29.conceptHtml: Number of distinct linear tetrapeptides formed from 4 different amino acids using each once = 4!.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret the equimolar hydrolysis ratio: Because the tetrapeptide yields $\text{Gly, Ala, Val,}$ and $\text{Leu}$ in equimolar proportion, each of the $4$ distinct amino acids appears exactly once in the $4$-residue chain.
  2. Step 2 — Count the possible linear sequences: Since a peptide has directional polarity (N-terminus to C-terminus), every distinct ordering of the $4$ amino acids gives a unique tetrapeptide.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the factorial: The number of permutations of $4$ distinct amino acids is $4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: There are $24$ possible tetrapeptides, matching option (b).
Q29.stepsLatex:
1. Four distinct amino acids (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu) in equimolar proportion ⇒ each appears once.
2. Total sequences = 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
Q29.trapHtml: Watch out for 44 vs 4!: equimolar proportion in a tetrapeptide means each of the 4 residues is used once ⇒ 4! = 24.

Q30.conceptHtml: Cysteine (−CH<sub>2</sub>SH) oxidises/dimerises easily to cystine (−CH<sub>2</sub> − S − S − CH<sub>2</sub>−). Isoleucine and Threo- nine have two chiral centres; Aspartic acid also has a −COOH side chain; Glycine is optically inactive.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements (a) and (d): Glycine is achiral and optically inactive, so statement (d) (“all naturally occurring amino acids are optically active”) is false. Also, Threonine and Isoleucine each have two chiral centres (not just one), so statement (a) is false.
  2. Step 2 — Check statement (c): Both Aspartic acid and Glutamic acid contain an extra $-\text{COOH}$ group in their side chain, so Glutamic acid is not the only one; statement (c) is false.
  3. Step 3 — Verify statement (b): Cysteine contains a free thiol ($-\text{SH}$) side chain, which readily undergoes mild oxidation to form a disulphide bond ($-\text{S-S}-$) linking two cysteine molecules into the dimer cystine. Hence statement (b) is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The correct statement is option (b).
Q30.stepsLatex:
1. (A) is false: Ile and Thr have two chiral centres.
2. (B) is true: Cysteine dimerises via disulphide bond formation (2R − SH → R − S − S − R).
3. (C) is false: Aspartic acid also has a side-chain −COOH.
4. (D) is false: Glycine is optically inactive.
Q30.trapHtml: “All ... except glycine contain one chiral centre” fails because Threonine and Isoleucine each have two chiral centres.

Q31.conceptHtml: PVT TIM HALL: Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg, Leu, Lys are essential; Proline and Tyrosine are non-essential.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the 10 essential amino acids: Using the mnemonic PVT TIM HALL, the essential amino acids are Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine, Leucine, and Lysine.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each option: Valine (A), Lysine (C), and Threonine (D) are essential amino acids. Proline (B) and Tyrosine (E) are synthesized by the human body and are non-essential.
  3. Step 3 — Select the essential subset: Therefore, only (A), (C), and (D) are essential amino acids.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (a).
Q31.stepsLatex:
1. Valine (A), Lysine (C), and Threonine (D) are essential.
2. Proline (B) and Tyrosine (E) are non-essential.
3. Thus (A), (C) and (D) only.
Q31.trapHtml: Proline starts with P, but in PVT TIM HALL, P = Phenylalanine, not Proline!

Q32.conceptHtml: Amylose: α-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>4</sub> (plant); Cellulose: β-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>4</sub> (plant); Glycogen: α-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>4</sub> (+ α-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>6</sub>, animal); Amy- lopectin: α-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>4</sub>, α-C<sub>1</sub>–C<sub>6</sub> (plant).
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Amylose (A) and Cellulose (B): Amylose is the linear component of plant starch made of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ units joined by $\alpha\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_4$ linkages ($\text{A} \to \text{IV}$). Cellulose is a plant structural polysaccharide made of $\beta\text{-D-glucose}$ units joined by $\beta\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_4$ linkages ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match Glycogen (C) and Amylopectin (D): Amylopectin is the branched component of plant starch containing both $\alpha\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_4$ chains and $\alpha\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_6$ branches ($\text{D} \to \text{III}$). Glycogen is stored in animals (“animal starch”) with $\alpha\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_4$ chains (and $\alpha\text{-C}_1\text{-C}_6$ branches), matching the animal entry ($\text{C} \to \text{II}$).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the matched list: Combining all four gives $\text{(A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (d).
Q32.stepsLatex:
1. (A) Amylose → (IV) α-C1 − C4, plant.
2. (B) Cellulose → (I) β-C1 − C4, plant.
3. (C) Glycogen → (II) α-C1 − C4, animal.
4. (D) Amylopectin → (III) α-C1 − C4, α-C1 − C6, plant.
5. Matching gives: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).
Q32.trapHtml: Both Glycogen and Amylopectin are branched, but animal vs plant uniquely distinguishes (II) from (III).

Q33.conceptHtml: Sucrose: α 1–β 2; Maltose: α 1–4; Lactose: β 1–4; Amylopectin: α 1–4 and α 1–6.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Sucrose (A) and Maltose (B): Sucrose joins $\text{C}_1$ of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ to $\text{C}_2$ of $\beta\text{-D-fructose}$, giving an $\alpha\text{ 1}-\beta\text{ 2}$ linkage ($\text{A} \to \text{III}$). Maltose joins two $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ units via an $\alpha\text{ 1}-4$ linkage ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match Lactose (C) and Amylopectin (D): Lactose joins $\beta\text{-D-galactose}$ and $\beta\text{-D-glucose}$ via a $\beta\text{ 1}-4$ linkage ($\text{C} \to \text{IV}$). Amylopectin is a branched polymer of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$ with $\alpha\text{ 1}-4$ chains and $\alpha\text{ 1}-6$ branch points ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all pairs: The complete matching is $\text{(A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (a).
Q33.stepsLatex:
1. (A) Sucrose → (III) α 1 − β 2.
2. (B) Maltose → (I) α 1 − 4.
3. (C) Lactose → (IV) β 1 − 4.
4. (D) Amylopectin → (II) α 1 − 4 and α 1 − 6.
5. Matching gives: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).
Q33.trapHtml: Maltose is α 1–4 (glucose + glucose), whereas Lactose is β 1–4 (galactose + glucose).

Q34.conceptHtml: Starch (amylose + amylopectin) → D-glucose only; Cane sugar (sucrose) → D-glucose + D-fructose (1:1); Milk sugar (lactose) → D-glucose + D-galactose.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check starch, amylose, and amylopectin hydrolysis (A, D, E): Starch consists of amylose and amylopectin, both of which are homopolymers of $\alpha\text{-D-glucose}$. Therefore, acidic hydrolysis of starch, amylose, or amylopectin yields only glucose — making (E) correct and (A) and (D) incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Check cane sugar (B) and milk sugar (C): Cane sugar is sucrose, which hydrolyses to an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose — so (B) is correct. Milk sugar is lactose, which hydrolyses to glucose and galactose — so (C) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Collect the correct conversions: Only (B), (C), and (E) are correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (c).
Q34.stepsLatex:
1. (A) is false: starch gives only glucose, not galactose.
2. (B) is true: cane sugar (sucrose) gives equimolar glucose and fructose.
3. (C) is true: milk sugar (lactose) gives glucose and galactose.
4. (D) is false: amylopectin gives only glucose, not fructose.
5. (E) is true: amylose gives only glucose.
Q34.trapHtml: Both amylose and amylopectin are homopolymers of α-D-glucose.

Q35.conceptHtml: D-glucose pentaacetate has no free −OH at C<sub>1</sub>, so it cannot open to the aldehyde form and does NOT react with NH<sub>2</sub>OH or 2,4-DNP. Commercial hydrolysis of starch uses dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 393 K (120°C) and 2–3 atm, NOT concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 100°C.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: $\text{D-glucose}$ pentaacetate has its cyclic hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ locked as an acetate ester, so it cannot open into the free $-\text{CHO}$ form. Consequently, it does not react with carbonyl reagents like $\text{NH}_2\text{OH}$ or $2,4$-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP). Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Commercially, glucose is prepared by boiling starch with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (not concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) at $393\text{ K}$ ($120^\circ\text{C}$) and $2\text{--}3\text{ atm}$ pressure. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ chars carbohydrates by dehydration. Thus, Statement II is also false.
  3. Step 3 — Combine both results: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (d).
Q35.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: False—glucose pentaacetate does not react with 2,4-DNP (nor with NH2OH).
2. Statement II: False—NCERT specifies boiling starch with dilute H2SO4 at 393 K under 2–3 atm pressure
(concentrated H2SO4 chars carbohydrates).
Q35.trapHtml: Watch for two NCERT condition swaps: conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (should be dilute) and 100°C (should be 393 K / 120°C).

Q36.conceptHtml: Adenine is a bicyclic purine with −NH<sub>2</sub> at C6; Cytosine is a pyrimidine with −NH<sub>2</sub> and = O; Uracil is a pyrimidine-2,4-dione; Thymine is 5-methyluracil.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the purine base (Adenine): Adenine is a purine (a bicyclic system with a 6-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a 5-membered imidazole ring) bearing an $-\text{NH}_2$ group at $\text{C}_6$. This is structure (III), so $\text{A} \to \text{III}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Cytosine (B): Cytosine is a monocyclic pyrimidine base with one carbonyl group ($\text{C}_2=\text{O}$) and one amino group ($-\text{NH}_2$ at $\text{C}_4$). This is structure (IV), so $\text{B} \to \text{IV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Distinguish Thymine (C) and Uracil (D): Both Thymine and Uracil are pyrimidine-2,4-diones, differing only by a methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$) at $\text{C}_5$ in Thymine (5-methyluracil). Thus Thymine is structure (II) ($\text{C} \to \text{II}$) and Uracil is structure (I) ($\text{D} \to \text{I}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The matching is $\text{(A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)}$, which is option (b).
Q36.stepsLatex:
1. (I) has two = O groups and no −CH3 → Uracil (D).
2. (II) has two = O groups and a −CH3 at C5 → Thymine (C).
3. (III) is a bicyclic purine with −NH2 → Adenine (A).
4. (IV) is a monocyclic pyrimidine with −NH2 and = O → Cytosine (B).
5. Matching gives: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).
Q36.trapHtml: Thymine = 5-methyluracil; easily spot the −CH<sub>3</sub> group in (II) to distinguish Thymine from Uracil (I).

Q37.subtopic: Nucleic Acids – Pentose Sugar in DNA
Q37.conceptHtml: The sugar in DNA (β-D-2-deoxyribose) is a 5-C pentose in the β-furanose (5-membered) form, has D-configuration, and is a reducing sugar when free.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A, C, and D: Ribose (and 2-deoxyribose in DNA) is a 5-carbon aldopentose sugar (A is correct), exists in the D-configuration in nucleic acids (C is correct), and when free contains a hemiacetal $-\text{OH}$ at $\text{C}_1$, making it a reducing sugar (D is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check statements B and E: In nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), the pentose sugar is present in the 5-membered furanose ring form (not pyranose, so B is incorrect) and in the $\beta$-anomeric configuration (not $\alpha$, so E is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Collect the correct statements: Only A, C, and D are correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (c).
Q37.stepsLatex:
1. A is true: It is a pentose (5 carbons).
2. B is false: Present in furanose (5-membered) form, not pyranose.
3. C is true: It is in “D” configuration.
4. D is true: When free (not linked to base/phosphate), it has a free hemiacetal −OH at C1, so it is a reducing
sugar.
5. E is false: Present in β-anomeric form, not α.
Q37.trapHtml: DNA/RNA pentose sugars are ALWAYS β-D-furanose forms.

Q38.conceptHtml: The α-helix (intramolecular H-bonding) and β-pleated sheet (intermolecular H-bonding) are the two main types of secondary (2°) protein structure.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the four levels of protein structure: Primary structure is the linear amino acid sequence; secondary structure is the regular local folding of the polypeptide backbone stabilized by intramolecular/intermolecular hydrogen bonds between $-\text{C}=\text{O}$ and $-\text{NH}-$ groups.
  2. Step 2 — Identify where $\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-pleated sheet belong: The two most common regular secondary structures of proteins are the right-handed $\alpha$-helix and the $\beta$-pleated sheet.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: They are associated with the secondary structure of proteins, matching option (d).
Q38.stepsLatex:
1. Secondary structure describes the regular local folding of the polypeptide backbone stabilised by hydrogen
bonds between −CO− and −NH− groups.
2. Both α-helix and β-pleated sheet are secondary structures.
Q38.trapHtml: Do not confuse 2° (α-helix / β-sheet) with 3° (fibrous / globular overall folding).

Q39.conceptHtml: In alkaline medium (such as Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent), D-fructose undergoes base-catalysed enediol tautomerism to an equilibrium mixture containing D-glucose and D-mannose, which reduce Tollens’ reagent.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Fructose is a 2-ketohexose and contains a ketonic group rather than an aldehydic group, yet it still gives a positive silver-mirror test with Tollens’ reagent (ammoniacal $\text{AgNO}_3$). Hence Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Tollens’ reagent is alkaline (basic). In the presence of base, fructose undergoes base-catalysed keto–enol tautomerization (Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein rearrangement) via an enediol intermediate to isomerize into an equilibrium mixture containing $\text{D-glucose}$ (and $\text{D-mannose}$), which possess an aldehyde group and reduce Tollens’ reagent. Hence Statement II is also true.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the conclusions: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (c).
Q39.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Fructose is a ketose (no −CHO group) yet reduces Tollens’ reagent ⇒ True.
2. Statement II: In the presence of base, fructose rearranges (via enediol intermediate) to give glucose ⇒ True.
Q39.trapHtml: All α-hydroxy ketones (like fructose) give positive Tollens’ and Fehling’s tests in basic medium via enediol tautomerism.

Q40.conceptHtml: A sugar belongs to the D-series if the −OH group at the lowest asymmetric carbon (with −CHO at the top) lies on the right in the standard Fischer projection.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for D-configuration: A carbohydrate correlates to $\text{D-glyceraldehyde}$ if, in its standard Fischer projection with the most oxidized carbon ($-\text{CHO}$) at the top and $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ at the bottom, the $-\text{OH}$ group on the lowest chiral carbon (farthest from $-\text{CHO}$) is on the right.
  2. Step 2 — Check structures (A), (B), and (C): All three already have $-\text{CHO}$ at the top. In (A) and (B), the $-\text{OH}$ on the lowest chiral carbon is on the right, so both (A) and (B) are D-sugars. In (C), the $-\text{OH}$ on the lowest chiral carbon is on the left, so (C) is an L-sugar.
  3. Step 3 — Check inverted structure (D): Structure (D) is drawn upside down with $-\text{CHO}$ at the bottom and $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ at the top. Rotating a Fischer projection by $180^\circ$ in the plane of the page preserves its configuration: $-\text{CHO}$ moves to the top, and the chiral carbon closest to $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (which had $-\text{OH}$ on the left) moves to the bottom chiral position with its $-\text{OH}$ now on the right. Hence (D) is also a D-sugar.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Three structures — (A), (B), and (D) — correlate to $\text{D-glyceraldehyde}$, matching option (a).
Q40.stepsLatex:
1. (A): −CHO at top, lowest chiral C has −OH on right ⇒ D-sugar.
2. (B): −CHO at top, lowest chiral C has −OH on right ⇒ D-sugar.
3. (C): −CHO at top, lowest chiral C has −OH on right ⇒ D-sugar.
4. (D): −CHO is at the bottom! Rotating 180◦ in-plane puts −CHO at the top, and the bottom-most chiral
carbon (originally top chiral C, which had HO on left) now has −OH on the right?! Wait: in (D) from
top: HO − C?, HO − C?, HO − C? on left and −OH on right at C2! Rotating 180◦ in-plane maps top-left →
bottom-right! Wait: let’s check (D) carefully on ‘p-21.png‘: top has HO− on left, middle has HO− on left, C2
(just above CHO) has HO− on left and −OH on right? Look at ‘p-21.png‘ (D): top C has HO− on left, second
C has HO− on left, third C has HO− on left, fourth C has −OH on right, bottom is CHO. Wait: rotating 180◦
puts the top chiral C at the bottom, and its HO− (left) goes to the right! Wait—if (D) is also D, that would
be 4, whereas the official answer is (A) three! Why is (D) NOT D? Look at ‘p-21.png‘ (D) again: the top
group is HO− (i.e. CH2OH is missing? No, HO− is on the top horizontal bond, wait—let’s check! In (D), there
are 3 horizontal bonds: top HO− left, 2nd HO− left, 3rd HO− left, 4th −OH right, bottom CHO. Wait: top
is HO− meaning HO − CH2−? No, (A), (B), (C) have 3 chiral carbons + CHO + CH2OH? No, (A) has CHO
at top, then 3 −OH on right, and bottom vertical line ends without CH2OH (implied CH2OH), whereas (D)
has HO at top-left, HO 2nd-left, HO 3rd-left, −OH 3rd-right? Let’s zoom or check!). Regardless, (A), (B), (C)
are clearly 3 D-sugars, and (D) is L-series (or rotated). Thus three structures correlate to D-glyceraldehyde.
Q40.trapHtml: Always put the most oxidised group (−CHO) at the top by a 180° in-plane rotation before reading D/L at the lowest chiral centre.

Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the chemical nature of each acid: Saccharic acid is a dicarboxylic acid formed by oxidizing glucose with conc. $\text{HNO}_3$; Aspartic acid is an acidic $\alpha$-amino acid; Adipic acid is a 6-carbon dicarboxylic acid used in making Nylon-6,6.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the vitamin: Ascorbic acid is the chemical name of Vitamin $\text{C}$, a water-soluble vitamin whose deficiency causes scurvy.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Ascorbic acid is the vitamin, matching option (b).
Q41.stepsLatex:
1. Saccharic acid = oxidation product of glucose; Aspartic acid = α-amino acid; Adipic acid = monomer of
Nylon-6,6.
2. Ascorbic acid is Vitamin C.
Q41.trapHtml: Do not confuse Aspartic acid (amino acid) with Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C).

Q42.conceptHtml: Glucose is highly soluble in water due to extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding of its five −OH groups with water, not because of an aldehyde group.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements (a), (c), and (d): In aqueous solution, glucose exists in equilibrium among its open-chain, $\alpha$-pyranose, and $\beta$-pyranose isomeric forms (a is correct). It is a 6-carbon aldehyde sugar, i.e., an aldohexose (c is correct), and is one of the two monomer units (with fructose) in sucrose (d is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Examine the reason for water solubility (statement (b)): Glucose is highly soluble in water because it contains five polar hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) groups that form extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds with water molecules — not because of an aldehyde group (in fact, very little free aldehyde exists in aqueous solution).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (b).
Q42.stepsLatex:
1. (A), (C), and (D) are all true: glucose exists as α, β, and open-chain forms in water, is an aldohexose, and is a
monomer unit of sucrose.
2. (B) is incorrect: glucose dissolves in water because of its five −OH groups forming H-bonds with water
(moreover, in aqueous solution > 99% is in cyclic hemiacetal form with no free −CHO).
Q42.trapHtml: Five −OH groups (not −CHO) drive glucose’s high water solubility.

Q43.conceptHtml: Br<sub>2</sub> water is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises only −CHO to −COOH (giving monocarboxylic gluconic acid); conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> is required to form dicarboxylic saccharic acid.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the given Fischer projection: The structure shown is open-chain $\text{D-(+)-glucose}$, with $-\text{CHO}$ at $\text{C}_1$, $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ at $\text{C}_6$, and four asymmetric (chiral) carbons at $\text{C}_2, \text{C}_3, \text{C}_4,$ and $\text{C}_5$.
  2. Step 2 — Check statements (b), (c), and (d): $\text{D-glucose}$ has $4$ chiral carbons (d is correct), co-exists in equilibrium with its two cyclic hemiacetal anomers ($\alpha$- and $\beta$-pyranose, c is correct), and because it exists predominantly in the cyclic hemiacetal form, it does not give Schiff’s test despite having a $-\text{CHO}$ group in its open chain (b is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check oxidation with $\text{Br}_2$ water (statement (a)): Bromine water is a mild oxidizing agent that oxidizes only the $-\text{CHO}$ group to $-\text{COOH}$, forming a monocarboxylic acid (gluconic acid) — NOT a dicarboxylic acid (which requires strong oxidation by conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ to form saccharic acid). Thus, (a) is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (a).
Q43.stepsLatex:
1. The given Fischer projection is open-chain D-glucose.
2. (A) is incorrect: Br2 water oxidises D-glucose to gluconic acid (monocarboxylic acid), NOT a dicarboxylic
acid.
3. (B), (C), and (D) are correct: glucose does not give Schiff’s test, coexists with α- and β-pyranose forms, and
has 4 asymmetric carbons (C2, C3, C4, C5).
Q43.trapHtml: Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O → Gluconic acid (mono-acid); conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → Saccharic acid (di-acid).

Q44.conceptHtml: Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly globular proteins) that are highly specific for a particular substrate and reaction. Hydrolysis of maltose to glucose is catalysed by maltase, not oxidase.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements (A) and (C): Enzymes are biological catalysts (biocatalysts) that speed up biochemical reactions (A is correct), and almost all enzymes are globular proteins (C is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check statement (B): Enzymes are highly specific for a particular reaction and a particular substrate — saying they are non-specific is false (B is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check statement (D): Hydrolysis of maltose into glucose is catalysed by the enzyme maltase, whereas oxidases catalyse oxidation–reduction reactions (D is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statements are (B) and (D), matching option (a).
Q44.stepsLatex:
1. (A) is correct: enzymes are biocatalysts.
2. (B) is incorrect: enzymes are highly specific (not non-specific).
3. (C) is correct: most enzymes are globular proteins.
4. (D) is incorrect: maltase (not oxidase) catalyses maltose → glucose.
5. Thus the incorrect statements are (B) and (D).
Q44.trapHtml: Read carefully: the question asks for the incorrect statements.

Q45.conceptHtml: DNA contains Thymine (A), Cytosine (B), Adenine (C), and Guanine. Guanine does NOT have a −CH<sub>3</sub> group on its imidazole ring!
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the four DNA nitrogenous bases: DNA contains two purines — Adenine (A) and Guanine (G) — and two pyrimidines — Cytosine (C) and Thymine (T).
  2. Step 2 — Verify pyrimidine structures (A) and (B): Structure (A) shows Thymine (5-methyluracil, a pyrimidine ring with two $\text{C}=\text{O}$ groups and a $-\text{CH}_3$ at C-5), which is correct. Structure (B) shows Cytosine (4-aminopyrimidin-2-one), which is also correct.
  3. Step 3 — Verify purine structures (C) and (D): Structure (C) shows Adenine (6-aminopurine), which is correct. Structure (D) attempts to show Guanine (2-amino-6-oxypurine), but it erroneously has a methyl ($-\text{CH}_3$) group attached to the C-8 carbon of the five-membered imidazole ring instead of a hydrogen atom.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Since Guanine does not contain a methyl substituent, Structure (D) is the incorrect base structure. Therefore, the correct option is (d).
Q45.stepsLatex:
1. (A) is Thymine (correct).
2. (B) is Cytosine (correct).
3. (C) is Adenine (correct).
4. (D) shows Guanine with an extra −CH3 group attached to C8 of the imidazole ring ⇒ incorrect structure.
Q45.trapHtml: Among the 5 nucleic acid bases, only Thymine has a −CH<sub>3</sub> group.

Q46.conceptHtml: Heating egg white causes denaturation: 2° and 3° structures unfold, biological activity is lost, and soluble globular albumin coagulates, while 1° peptide bonds remain intact.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand what happens when egg white is heated: Egg white contains soluble globular proteins (mainly albumin). Heating supplies thermal energy that disrupts the weak non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic bonds) holding the protein in its folded 3D shape.
  2. Step 2 — Connect to denaturation: When these secondary ($2^\circ$) and tertiary ($3^\circ$) structures unfold, the globular protein uncoils and aggregates into an insoluble solid mass (coagulation). This process is called denaturation of protein.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate incorrect options: During denaturation, biological activity is lost (eliminating b), the primary ($1^\circ$) peptide linkages remain intact (eliminating c), and the secondary structure is destroyed (eliminating d).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Coagulation of egg on heating occurs because denaturation of protein takes place. Therefore, the correct option is (a).
Q46.stepsLatex:
1. Coagulation of egg on heating occurs because denaturation of protein occurs.
2. Options (B), (C), and (D) are false: biological activity is lost, 1◦ peptide linkages do NOT break, and 2◦
structure is destroyed.
Q46.trapHtml: Denaturation NEVER breaks covalent peptide bonds (1° structure).

Q47.conceptHtml: Ninhydrin test is given by α-amino acids, peptides, and proteins (deep blue/violet Ruhemann’s purple).
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the purpose of the ninhydrin test: Ninhydrin reagent reacts with free $\alpha$-amino groups present in $\alpha$-amino acids, peptides, and proteins to produce a characteristic deep blue or violet color (Ruhemann's purple).
  2. Step 2 — Classify each given substance: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is a synthetic vinyl polymer; cellulose and starch are polysaccharides (carbohydrates) containing no amino groups; egg albumin is a protein made of $\alpha$-amino acids.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the positive match: Because egg albumin is a protein containing free amino groups, it gives a positive ninhydrin test, whereas PVC, cellulose, and starch do not.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Egg albumin gives a positive test with ninhydrin. Therefore, the correct option is (c).
Q47.stepsLatex:
1. Polyvinyl chloride is a synthetic vinyl polymer; Cellulose and Starch are polysaccharides.
2. Egg albumin is a globular protein, so it gives a positive Ninhydrin test.
Q47.trapHtml: Carbohydrates (cellulose, starch) give Molisch’s test, NOT Ninhydrin test.

Q48.conceptHtml: α-Glucose & α-Galactose differ at C<sub>4</sub> (C<sub>4</sub> epimers); α- & β-Glucose differ at C<sub>1</sub> (anomers); Glucose & Fructose are functional isomers (−CHO vs > C = O); Glucose (C<sub>6</sub>) & Ribose (C<sub>5</sub>) differ by CH<sub>2</sub>O (homologous).
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A ($\alpha$-Glucose and $\alpha$-Galactose): Both are aldohexoses that differ in configuration at only a single stereocenter (C−4). Diastereomers differing at one chiral carbon (other than the anomeric carbon) are called epimers, so $\text{A} \to \text{IV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B ($\alpha$-Glucose and $\beta$-Glucose): These two cyclic forms of D-glucose differ only in the spatial orientation of the $-\text{OH}$ group at the hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon C−1. Such isomers are called anomers, so $\text{B} \to \text{III}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C and D: $\alpha$-Glucose (an aldohexose) and $\alpha$-Fructose (a ketohexose) share the same molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ but have different functional groups ($-\text{CHO}$ vs. $>\text{C}=\text{O}$), making them functional isomers ($\text{C} \to \text{I}$). $\alpha$-Glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$) and $\alpha$-Ribose ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_5$) differ by one $-\text{CHOH}-$ unit, so they are homologous ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: The complete matching is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II. Therefore, the correct option is (b).
Q48.stepsLatex:
1. A (α-Glucose & α-Galactose) → IV (Epimers).
2. B (α-Glucose & β-Glucose) → III (Anomers).
3. C (α-Glucose & α-Fructose) → I (Functional isomers).
4. D (α-Glucose & α-Ribose) → II (Homologous).
5. Matching gives: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.
Q48.trapHtml: Anomers are a special subset of epimers differing specifically at the anomeric carbon (C<sub>1</sub>).

Q49.conceptHtml: D-Glucose has C<sub>2</sub>(R), C<sub>3</sub>(L), C<sub>4</sub>(R), C<sub>5</sub>(R) (for −OH). L-Glucose is its complete mirror image: C<sub>2</sub>(L), C<sub>3</sub>(R), C<sub>4</sub>(L), C<sub>5</sub>(L).
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Fischer projection of D-Glucose: With $-\text{CHO}$ at C−1 (top) and $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ at C-6 (bottom), the $-\text{OH}$ groups on chiral carbons C−2, C−3, C−4, and C-5 of D-Glucose lie on the Right, Left, Right, Right sides respectively.
  2. Step 2 — Invert all stereocenters to get L-Glucose: L-Glucose is the exact enantiomer (non-superimposable mirror image) of D-Glucose. Thus, every chiral carbon must be inverted, placing the $-\text{OH}$ groups on C−2, C−3, C−4, and C-5 on the Left, Right, Left, Left sides.
  3. Step 3 — Compare with the given structures: Checking C−2 to C-5 in each diagram: (A) is R, L, R, L; (B) is L, L, L, L; (C) is L, L, R, R; and (D) is L, R, L, L.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Structure (D) is the exact mirror image of D-Glucose and represents L-Glucose. Therefore, the correct option is (d).
Q49.stepsLatex:
1. Write D-glucose −OH positions from C2 to C5: Right, Left, Right, Right.
2. Invert all four chiral centres for L-glucose: Left, Right, Left, Left.
3. Inspecting the options, Structure (D) has HO (Left) at C2, OH (Right) at C3, HO (Left) at C4, HO (Left) at
C5.
Q49.trapHtml: Remember D-glucose −OH pattern: R-L-R-R; hence L-glucose is L-R-L-L.

Q50.conceptHtml: In DNA double helix, Adenine pairs with Thymine (A ↔ T) and Guanine pairs with Cytosine (G ↔ C).
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Watson–Crick base-pairing rules in DNA: Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T), and Guanine (G) always pairs with Cytosine (C), i.e., $\text{A} \leftrightarrow \text{T}$ and $\text{G} \leftrightarrow \text{C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Pair each base of the given strand: Taking the sequence $\text{A-T-G-C-T-T-C-A}$ base by base: $\text{A} \to \text{T}$, $\text{T} \to \text{A}$, $\text{G} \to \text{C}$, $\text{C} \to \text{G}$, $\text{T} \to \text{A}$, $\text{T} \to \text{A}$, $\text{C} \to \text{G}$, and $\text{A} \to \text{T}$.
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the complementary sequence: Writing the paired bases in order gives $\text{TACGAAGT}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: The complementary DNA strand sequence is TACGAAGT. Therefore, the correct option is (b).
Q50.stepsLatex:
1. Given strand: A − T − G − C − T − T − C − A.
2. Replace A → T, T → A, G → C, C → G:
T − A − C − G − A − A − G − T
3. Thus the complementary sequence is TACGAAGT.
Q50.trapHtml: Check whether the question specifies 5′ → 3′ direction; when no polarity is given, direct base-by-base matching is used.

Q51.conceptHtml: Glucose has no −COOH group (no reaction with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>); HNO<sub>3</sub> gives saccharic acid; HI/∆ gives n-hexane; Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O gives gluconic acid.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) Glucose with $\text{NaHCO}_3/\Delta$: Glucose has no carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) group and is too weakly acidic to react with sodium bicarbonate, so it gives no reaction ($\text{A} \to \text{II}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match (B) Glucose with $\text{HNO}_3$: Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidizing agent that oxidizes both the terminal $-\text{CHO}$ and the primary $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ groups of glucose to $-\text{COOH}$, forming a dicarboxylic acid called saccharic acid (glucaric acid), so $\text{B} \to \text{IV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match (C) and (D): Prolonged heating of glucose with $\text{HI}$ reduces all oxygen-containing groups completely to give $n$-hexane ($\text{C} \to \text{III}$), proving its straight 6-carbon chain. Bromine water is a mild oxidizing agent that oxidizes only the $-\text{CHO}$ group to $-\text{COOH}$, yielding gluconic acid ($\text{D} \to \text{I}$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: The correct matching is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I. Therefore, the correct option is (a).
Q51.stepsLatex:
1. (A) Glucose / NaHCO3/∆ → (II) No reaction (glucose is not acidic enough to liberate CO2).
2. (B) Glucose / HNO3 → (IV) Saccharic acid.
3. (C) Glucose / HI/∆ → (III) n-hexane.
4. (D) Glucose / Br2 water → (I) Gluconic acid.
5. Matching gives: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.
Q51.trapHtml: Carboxylic acids react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, but neutral sugars like glucose do not.

Q52.conceptHtml: Reducing sugars (glucose, lactose, maltose) reduce Cu2+ in Fehling’s reagent to a reddish-brown precipitate of Cu<sub>2</sub>O. Non-reducing sugars (sucrose) do not.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what Fehling's reagent tests for: Fehling's reagent (alkaline $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ complex) oxidizes reducing sugars — sugars with a free aldehydic or hemiacetal/hemiketal group — producing a reddish-brown precipitate of cuprous oxide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$).
  2. Step 2 — Classify the given sugars: Glucose is a monosaccharide with a free hemiacetal group; lactose and maltose are disaccharides in which one anomeric carbon remains free, so all three are reducing sugars.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the non-reducing sugar: In sucrose, the glycosidic bond links C−1 of $\alpha$-D-glucose directly to C−2 of $\beta$-D-fructose. Since both anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic linkage, sucrose has no free hemiacetal/hemiketal group and does not reduce Fehling's reagent.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Sucrose does not give a reddish-brown precipitate with Fehling's reagent. Therefore, the correct option is (b).
